#6839. Inside Danielle Lauder’s Barbie Dream Closet

Designed by AMMOR Architecture, the ultra-pink, mega dressing room is a cinematic fantasy come to life.

Cher Horowitz had a touch-screen conveyer belt in her color-coded closet. Carrie Bradshaw kept her Manolos in an unusually spacious high-fashion-filled walk-in. And Margot Robbie’s Barbie displayed her hot-pink wardrobe like doll’s packaging in her wall-free fantasy villa. Danielle Lauder, the great-granddaughter of Estée Lauder, created her own iteration of the dream closet—this time, in real life.

Her own inspiration? “I always thought of Belle in Beauty and the Beast in the library, just rolling around on her ladder,” she says. “I’m not much of a reader, but as a collector, I knew that’s what I wanted.”

Her wish list for the jewel-box space also included curving walls, glossy pink lacquer, illuminated marble, and a capsule-shaped vanity inspired by the makeup collection she designed for Estée Lauder in 2019. The beauty empire was founded by—and named after—her great-grandmother in 1946; and her father, William P. Lauder, serves as the chairman of the board. (Danielle now oversees her own production company, Act 4 Artists.)

To make her dream a reality, Lauder turned to architects Goil Amornvivat and Thomas Morbitzer, founders of New York City–based AMMOR Architecture. The duo had instant chemistry with Lauder, who was especially taken with the meticulous diorama they created for her.

“Tom and I both love Barbie,” says Amornvivat. “So we tweaked our design process to make an architectural model that was more like a dollhouse, where you could switch out surfaces.” Their efforts worked on Lauder, herself a Barbie fan, and the pair walked away with the commission to not just create the dressing room but to overhaul the entire industrial-style apartment in the West Village of Manhattan, which was then being used as an art studio.

“They both really understood and saw my vision,” says Lauder. “Plus, they were the most excited, which made me more excited. Goil is like the Energizer Bunny.”

The 250-square-foot dressing room is, Lauder says, “the biggest room in the apartment besides the living room.” It’s also where Lauder spends the most time. She enters just off the primary bedroom via an arched passageway finished in custom bronze plaster, emerging from the dark portal into a pink fantasia where her expansive fashion collection is arrayed like a personal boutique. “The idea was for it to be part display area but also a functional closet,” she says.

At the center is a custom pink vanity outfitted with fluted drawers, dual-sided mirrors, and a top made of richly veined Midnight Rose marble, sourced from New York Stone. Lauder keeps her collection of vintage and reissued Estée Lauder compacts in the drawers. “I love collecting them and having them out on display or in a nice drawer,” says Lauder. “They’re beautiful little artifacts.”

On the curving walls, rounded niches display shelving and racks against illuminated stone, part of Lauder’s request for layered lighting. “I love the backlit marble,” she says. “It’s so flattering.” She keeps her enviable bag and shoe collection on permanent display, maintained with help from her housekeeper. Lauder draws from the selection on a daily basis, with particular affection for family heirlooms such as her mom’s vintage Dolce & Gabbana handbags.

Overhead, Amornvivat and Morbitzer devised a futuristic lighting installation, stretching mesh taut over an oval-shaped light source to create a seamless surface. “The light in there is controllable by color, and it's dimmable,” notes Morbitzer. “It’s kind of like a skylight, which was important because it’s the only room without windows,” adds Amornvivat.

The bespoke elements continue: heated floors, an ice maker, a perfume bar, plenty of drawers, and a pair of walk-in closets cleverly concealed behind matching lacquered doors. “The whole room is custom millwork,” says Amornvivat.

And Lauder did get the sliding ladder of her dreams. “That was my hill to die on,” she says. “I’ve always struggled to reach things in my closet, so it was definitely practical. And my grandfather had one in his apartment in the library when I was growing up, and I just loved it.”

Now that the closet is complete, Lauder has a hard time leaving. “I spend more time in here than I do probably even sleeping in bed,” she says with a laugh. The space is remarkably faithful to the original idea that Amornvivat and Morbitzer presented in their dollhouse diorama. “I wanted it to be totally mine, feminine and fun, and still very warm and inviting,” she says. “It’s become my ultimate bachelorette hub.”

Geoffrey Montes is an associate editor at ELLE Decor with a serious love for all things real estate and design. Before that, he worked at Architectural Digest, Galerie, and Preservation magazines, covering everything from jaw-dropping listings to world-famous architects and design events like Salone del Mobile and Homo Faber.

#6835. Front Office: Radhi Devlukia

The host of the A Really Good Cry podcast turned to designer Jess Cooney to create a home office-meets-studio made for deep conversations.

Radhi Devlukia isn’t afraid of tears. On her podcast, A Really Good Cry, the whole point is to get personal, and to do so with guests as varied as supermodel Miranda Kerr, dermatologists, hospice nurses, personal finance advisors—and Devlukia’s husband, fellow podcaster Jay Shetty.

Now, two years into the show, Devlukia, a best-selling author, cook, and founder of beverage company Juni, is unveiling a new studio and office space located within her and Shetty’s Los Angeles house. Devlukia turned to designer Jess Cooney, who has a namesake Berkshires-based interiors firm, to craft a space designed to support these really good cries. Cooney had never tackled a podcast studio before but was ready for the challenge, which included building a room that could both serve as a set—technical components, artificial light, and all—as well as a welcoming home office.

From the start, Cooney knew what the space would not include. “We wanted to move away from the tropes usually seen in podcast studios, like styled bookshelves or cluttered backgrounds that detract from the people being interviewed, and also anything logo or merch heavy,” she says. “And toward something that felt warmer and more inviting.”

Instead, she took cues from spaces like fashion designer Bella Freud’s London apartment, Jean Cocteau’s Villa Santo Sospir in the Côte d’Azur, and Paloma Elsesser’s home by Gregory Rockwell. The resulting office, says Cooney, “has this incredible womb-like, feminine atmosphere that cocoons and holds you.”

Below, Devlukia takes our Front Office survey, giving a behind-the-scenes look at her new home base.

Radhi Devlukia: The hanging art piece in the middle of the window, Kissed by Katie Burdon.

When you need to lock in and power through work, what’s your setup?

Doors open, facing the window, instrumental music playing. I also move areas a lot during work hours to stay focused, so sometimes I’m at the desk, sometimes on the swivel chairs, sometimes on the floor by the window!

I have articles printed about my grandma and grandad on my canvas memory wall. They taught at schools in Africa in the 1970s and there were articles written about how much they were doing for the community. I also have vintage ceramics—I love the mix of old and new.

It really depends. If there are two of us, we’re on the swivel chairs. If there are a few of us, we’re around the marble table. We love keeping things casual at the office so sometimes people sit on the cozy rug or wherever feels comfortable.

What was the best meeting you’ve had there?

We have had so many creative meetings in this office. It’s such a calming and flowing environment. The whole rebrand of the podcast was ideated in this new office, which I’m obsessed with now.

What would you change about it if you could?

Maybe just having the ability to shoot with the blinds open.

What’s the funniest thing that happened there?

My team loves to prank me, so there’s been a lot of laughter in our office!

Annie Goldsmith is the senior editor and digital lead at ELLE Decor, where she covers design, culture, style, and trends. She previously held positions at The Information, covering technology and culture, and Town & Country, writing about news, entertainment, and fashion. Her work has also appeared in Vogue, Rolling Stone, and the SF Standard.

#6834. IDC Report Finds Significant Gap Between AI Spending and Measurable Financial Returns

Nearly 70% of organizations report a significant gap between artificial intelligence spending and measurable financial returns, according to a recent survey by IDC.

The research firm's 2026 Worldwide AI Economics and Cost of Ownership Survey found that 69% reported such a gap, while only 15% had achieved an AI return on investment exceeding 100%.

In a separate May 2026 survey, 73% of respondents identified excessive AI costs as a significant risk.

IDC highlighted the findings in an October 20 analysis examining what enterprise customers expect from AI technology vendors.

Enterprise customers are placing greater emphasis on measurable business outcomes when evaluating AI products, according to IDC.

The firm identified three priorities for vendors: demonstrating financial value, addressing governance and security requirements, and building support beyond IT departments.

The analysis also highlighted the gap between initial agentic AI deployments and broader adoption. Although 80% of organizations have started deploying agentic AI, only 17% are using it across the enterprise.

IDC said evaluating AI investments can be difficult when the technology changes how employees work and how business processes operate.

The firm expects AI infrastructure capacity to catch up with demand around 2029, potentially easing costs. Until then, vendors face pressure to demonstrate the long-term financial value of their products.

AI funding decisions involve a broad range of executives. IDC's September 2026 C-Suite Tech Survey found that CIOs and CTOs were involved in 63% of those decisions, business-function executives in 62%, and chief financial officers in 61%.

A separate IDC survey found that 42% of CEOs planned to hire a chief AI officer within the next 12 months.

Buyers also reported concerns about the products and terms vendors offer. Limited integration with existing systems, insufficient model and data transparency, and concerns about vendor lock-in were each cited by 34% of respondents.

Overpromising and underdelivering, along with unclear pricing models, were each cited by 31%.

IDC said vendors need to substantiate financial returns and address security and governance requirements while working with decision-makers across IT, finance, and other business departments.

For more information, go to the IDC blog.

#6830. Dakota Johnson’s Latest Dose of Pajama Dressing Is All About Mismatched Prints

Whether hitting the red carpet in a little lingerie-inspired slip or dressing up a long ivory robe for an event, Dakota Johnson has long loved a good pajama dressing moment. And on Thursday night, she gave her go-to style another spin—this time with a breezy two-piece set that could seriously take her from a night out to a night in.

Courtesy of Italian label Loretta Caponi, the ensemble was composed of a long-sleeve midi dress and relaxed trousers, each crafted from black satin, adorned with delicate gold floral embroidery, and trimmed with scalloped lace. The loose dress, with its choker collar, deep V neckline and drop shoulders, was secured in the front by a line of buttons—which Johnson left undone, wearing the piece as a robe. The coordinating trousers were defined by a pleated waist and fluid silhouette.

Underneath, the Fifty Shades of Grey actor embraced another one of her favorite trends—naked dressing—with a sheer black lace cami that was embroidered with a floral design of its own. And, for a third pop of pattern, she grabbed a small leopard-print Valentino bag.

Johnson wore the look to Thursday night’s Los Angeles screening of Flesh Impact, Maggie Gyllenhaal’s forthcoming short film that imagines what Marilyn Monroe’s life might have been like had she lived to be 100 years old. For the project, Johnson transformed into Monroe at the height of her fame, blonde hair and all. It premiered at Venice Film Festival in September, though a theatrical or streaming release date has not yet been announced.

#6828. Report: Global Ransomware Attacks Rise 23% in Q3

Global ransomware activity increased 23% in the third quarter of 2026, with organizations in North America and Europe accounting for the largest share of attacks, according to cybersecurity firm NCC Group.

The company's Cyber Threat Intelligence Report Review of Q3 2026 recorded 2,865 ransomware victim claims, up from 2,325 in the previous quarter.

Despite the quarterly increase, attacks declined 26% month over month in September to 821. North America recorded the most attacks that month with 390, followed by Europe with 211.

The industrial sector accounted for 29% of quarterly attacks, while Qilin remained the most active ransomware group for the sixth consecutive quarter, recording 365 victims. The Gentlemen followed with 356, and INC Ransom ranked third with 109.

The report highlighted a July cyber attack against a small UK power generation facility that forced operations to stop for approximately four days.

Although the incident did not affect the national electricity grid, it demonstrated how cyber attacks can disrupt physical infrastructure.

The security researchers said the incident was consistent with techniques previously associated with Iranian-affiliated campaigns, including attacks against internet-exposed industrial controllers.

However, the UK government has not formally attributed the attack, and the techniques used remain unconfirmed.

The report also identified growing security challenges as organizations connect traditional IT networks with operational technology (OT) systems for remote maintenance and centralized management.

The firm recommended network segmentation, stronger privileged-access controls, and continuous monitoring of OT environments.

The research found that more than 40 vulnerabilities affecting enterprise applications, VPN appliances, e-mail gateways, and management platforms were added to CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog during the quarter.

The report examined Gunra, a ransomware-as-a-service operation that has targeted 53 victims across multiple industries as of Q3.

According to the cybersecurity company, Gunra exploited vulnerabilities CVE-2024-55591 and CVE-2025-24472 in internet-facing Fortinet devices to gain access to corporate networks.

The group also used stolen credentials, session hijacking, and administrative tools to move between systems before deploying ransomware.

Other emerging ransomware groups included Deadlock and Storm, with the latter claiming 78 victims by the end of September.

Researchers also observed initial access brokers advertising compromised VPN, Remote Desktop Protocol, and SSH access, alongside access to cloud identities, source code repositories, and security management platforms.

The quarterly review also highlighted BraZetsu, an AI-enhanced Windows malware framework that evolved into a specialized initial access toolkit.

According to the report, BraZetsu uses AI models to automate victim profiling, analyze compromised environments, and identify valuable corporate systems.

The framework searches for enterprise software, financial data, digital certificates, and cloud credentials, helping operators identify compromised access that can be sold to other cyber criminals.

The cybersecurity firm also identified risks involving legitimate AI agents, including prompt injection, excessive permissions, and unintended access to external systems.

The report cited incidents involving U.S. and Australian government systems as examples of agents accessing resources beyond their intended scope.

Researchers warned that these incidents do not necessarily involve malicious intent but can create consequences resembling conventional cyber intrusions.

For the full report, visit the NCC Group site.

#6823. Microsoft Expands Protections and Controls for Sovereign Cloud

Microsoft is introducing new tools within its sovereign cloud offerings designed to give organizations tighter control over where their data resides, who can access it, and how critical systems operate, especially in light of AI becoming a bigger part of enterprise infrastructure.

In a recent announcement, Douglas Phillips, president and chief technology officer of Microsoft Specialized Clouds, outlined updates spanning public cloud, private cloud, and partner environments. The changes target governments, regulated industries, and organizations that need tighter control over sensitive workloads without abandoning cloud-based AI capabilities.

"Digital sovereignty should give organizations greater control and security over the technology they depend on, while continuing to innovate," Phillips wrote.

One of the biggest additions is Microsoft's Sovereign Control Panel, which will enter public preview at Microsoft Ignite. Available through the Azure portal, the tool will give IT administrators one place to manage data sovereignty settings, spot compliance issues, and identify potential risks that could disrupt operations.

Microsoft is also tightening controls over who can access sensitive systems. Its Data Guardian feature will require oversight by personnel based in Europe when Microsoft engineers access certain production systems in the European Union and European Free Trade Association. Another tool, Production Touch Ledger, will keep tamper-resistant records of that access, giving organizations a clearer picture of who accessed their systems and what they did.

Microsoft is also giving customers more control over encryption. External key management with Azure Managed HSM is now generally available, letting organizations keep their main encryption keys on hardware they own or manage outside Microsoft's cloud.

The company is also expanding its Sovereign Private Cloud offerings, giving organizations more options to run systems with or without an internet connection. New capabilities include GitHub Enterprise Local, GitHub Copilot with locally hosted AI models, and additional data services running on Azure Local.

The push for greater operational control comes as Microsoft is also reconsidering how enterprises should secure increasingly autonomous AI systems.

As reported by Redmond magazine, Microsoft is expanding Project Perception to address risks posed by what the company calls "agentic insiders," AI agents capable of accessing sensitive information and performing actions without constant human supervision.

That initiative introduces plans for Guardian Agents, specialized security agents designed to monitor other AI systems, evaluate their behavior and intervene when their actions become risky.

"Monitoring and securing those agents must become continuous," said Hayete Gallot, executive vice president of Microsoft Security.

Project Perception is about limiting what AI agents can do. Microsoft's sovereign cloud expansion tackles a different set of questions: where those systems run, who gets to administer them, and how the data stays protected.

Taken together, the two efforts point to a shift in Microsoft's enterprise AI strategy. The company is putting more weight on oversight, not just automation.

Phillips said AI is making these questions more pressing as organizations roll out intelligent systems across sensitive business processes and critical infrastructure.

For more information, go to the Microsoft blog.

Chris Paoli (@ChrisPaoli5) is the associate editor for Converge360.

#6818. Cisco Intros Privileged Infrastructure Access for People and AI Agents

Cisco has introduced Privileged Infrastructure Access, an approach to infrastructure administration that gives people and AI agents temporary, task-specific permissions instead of leaving standing privileges available after their work is done.

In a recent blog post, Cisco's Matt Caulfield described a system that uses cryptographic identity to connect an administrator or agent to the infrastructure needed for a particular task. Access is governed by short-lived privileges, with session recording providing a record of the work performed.

"If there is no work being done, no privilege exists," Caulfield wrote. Cisco positions the offering as a way to bring identity controls directly into infrastructure operations while reducing dependence on static credentials, shared secrets, and broad access.

The announcement follows Cisco's previously announced Teleport partnership and its Infrastructure Identity concept, which connects the identity of a person or machine with the resources it can access, the actions it performs, and the permissions governing those actions.

Caulfield described a gap between the controls organizations apply to workforce applications and those used to administer network infrastructure. Companies have invested in single sign-on, multifactor authentication, and risk-based controls for application access, he wrote, but those protections often do not follow an engineer logging into a router or switch.

Instead, infrastructure access may depend on long-lived credentials, shared accounts, or separate policy systems. According to Cisco, that separation makes it harder to enforce least privilege and establish which person or system performed a particular action.

The company illustrates the problem with an administrator updating hundreds of switches during a maintenance window. If some updates fail, the administrator needs to troubleshoot before the window closes. The permissions available to handle that work, however, may cover more infrastructure and remain active longer than the task requires.

Traditional privileged access management can reduce risk through credential vaulting and rotation, Caulfield wrote. But he argued that operational friction can undermine those controls when teams create exceptions to complete urgent work. Those exceptions can leave credentials and privileges usable after the immediate need has passed.

Cisco's stated objective is to give infrastructure teams a consistent route to the devices they manage while providing security teams with policy enforcement, temporary permissions, and a record of activity. The company describes operational convenience as part of the design, rather than treating access governance solely as a credential-management problem.

Privileged Infrastructure Access makes access an on-demand action, according to the announcement. Cryptographic identity establishes the actor, and the resulting connection provides only the privileges needed to complete the task. Those privileges expire when the task concludes.

For customers using Cisco Identity Services Engine (ISE) and Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus (TACACS+), the offering can draw on existing policy and device context to govern access to Cisco routers and switches. Cisco says customers can extend the same access model to other infrastructure, including servers, Kubernetes clusters, and cloud resources.

#6813. Survey Finds 84% of Organizations Reported at Least One AI-Related Incident in the Past Year

Companies are running into problems as they give artificial intelligence more control over critical business applications, with 84% reporting at least one AI-related incident in the past year, according to a new survey from identity security firm Delinea.

The company's 2026 Application Access Governance report found that some organizations have experienced incorrect financial transactions and AI actions they couldn't trace or explain. The findings raise concerns about whether enterprises have enough oversight of AI systems that can make decisions and take actions on their own

The findings are based on an independent survey of 1,000 senior finance and finance technology leaders in the United States and United Kingdom. The AI-specific analysis included 879 respondents whose organizations use the technology in critical business applications.

The report found that 35% of surveyed organizations have deployed AI agents capable of taking actions within business applications. However, only 11% of organizations using AI said their governance and security controls were keeping pace with deployment.

Delinea also found gaps in centralized visibility into agent deployment and permissions, including who owns agents and who approved their use.

Some respondents reported segregation-of-duties conflicts involving AI, while others identified agents that continued operating after the employees who deployed them had left the organization.

The research also highlighted gaps in monitoring access across business systems. Only 46% of respondents said they continuously monitor and manage cumulative access risks across applications.

Those gaps can make it difficult to identify segregation-of-duties conflicts, in which a person or agent has permissions across systems that should be kept separate.

Despite those issues, 95% of respondents said they were confident their access controls would withstand scrutiny in an external audit.

However, 26% reported access-related audit findings that had recurred in consecutive years, while 25% said some findings had remained unresolved for three or more years.

Only 22% of organizations had a single named owner for each application, with ownership tracked in one system of record.

Meanwhile, 60% reported an increase over the past two years in the number of critical applications operating outside the scope of access governance or Sarbanes-Oxley Act compliance.

The findings highlight the oversight challenges associated with giving AI agents authority to act within business systems, particularly when organizations cannot consistently identify who owns an agent or trace its actions.

Frank Vukovits, chief security scientist at Delinea, said organizations remain responsible for the actions AI agents take within their systems.

"When an agent can approve a transaction or change permissions, the business owns the outcome. You need to know what every agent can do, who owns it, and who approved it, before an auditor asks or your financials are misstated," Vukovits said.

For the full report, go to the Delinea site.

#6808. Report: Cyber Criminals Move Toward More Targeted Phishing Attacks

Cyber criminals are moving away from mass phishing scams and focusing on more targeted attacks, increasingly using trusted websites and services to trick victims, according to a new report from KnowBe4. The security firm found that spear-phishing attacks increased 41% over the past year.

The company's Phishing Threat Trends Report, Vol. 8 found that overall phishing volume increased 29.8% year over year. Organizations received an average of one dangerous e-mail for every 733 messages, but the bigger concern is how attackers are changing their approach.

Rather than sending the same fraudulent message to thousands of people, criminals are spending more time researching their targets and creating convincing messages that appear to come from trusted coworkers, businesses, and technology platforms.

The findings are based on threat data from KnowBe4 Defend, the company's inbound e-mail security platform, which processes approximately 1.15 billion event signals daily.

KnowBe4 found that several traditional phishing methods declined significantly compared with 2025. Mobile-focused scams dropped 47.3%, advance-fee fraud fell 31.3%, and missed-message scams declined 11.3%.

Meanwhile, spear phishing increased 41.1%, pre-attack reconnaissance rose 33.7%, and company impersonation climbed 28%.

The shift suggests that attackers are finding more value in carefully crafted scams that exploit existing business relationships and workplace routines.

Business e-mail compromise (BEC) remains particularly common, accounting for 51.2% of phishing e-mails analyzed in the report. Human resources, finance departments, and executive leadership are among the most frequently targeted groups.

Attackers also appear to be timing their campaigns around normal business activity. KnowBe4 found that 90.4% of phishing messages arrive Monday through Friday, with Monday accounting for the largest share at 20.6%.

One of the report's more troubling findings involves the growing use of legitimate technology platforms to deliver malicious content.

KnowBe4 found that phishing attacks were twice as likely to originate from legitimate infrastructure in the third quarter of 2026 compared with the previous quarter.

That includes AI services, where attackers are taking advantage of trusted domains to host fake developer consoles, login prompts, and credential-stealing pages. The report also identified a 228% increase in AI-brand impersonation attacks between March and August.

Because these malicious pages can operate on legitimate domains with valid security certificates, users may not see the usual warning signs associated with suspicious websites.

"For years, security advice has focused on a predictable checklist: Check the sender address, hover over the link, and look for the padlock," said Jack Chapman, senior vice president of threat intelligence at KnowBe4.

"While still foundational, that guidance is becoming less useful by the day."

The findings echo a recent report about management software and AI e-mail assistants. Research from Fortra and Barracuda showed how criminals are using legitimate administrative tools and hidden AI instructions to manipulate users and compromise systems.

#6802. Study: Sign-In Problems Are Primary Drivers of Help Desk Tickets

Sign-in problems account for up to 53% of help desk tickets at individual enterprises, but network issues can take significantly longer to resolve, according to a new study from ControlUp.

Analyzing 1,069,110 help desk tickets, the IT operations company identified password resets, account lockouts, and multifactor authentication (MFA) issues as major drivers of support demand.

At one large enterprise, account-related tickets took a median of 11 minutes to resolve, compared with 50 hours for network problems. Meanwhile, 87% of network and phone tickets were reassigned between teams, compared with 20% of account tickets.

MFA enrollment and re-enrollment problems appeared at 40% of organizations, with one in five linking these issues to employees replacing or upgrading their phones. Virtual desktop problems appeared at 55% of organizations analyzed.

Traditional phone support remained a major channel for IT assistance.

Among organizations that recorded how support requests were submitted, 57% reported that phone calls accounted for approximately two-thirds or more of contacts. At one organization, that figure reached 99%.

Machine-generated tickets from monitoring, security, backup, and patching systems appeared at half of the organizations studied. At 15%, automated tickets represented between 25% and 50% of all requests.

The research covered enterprises across retail, healthcare, financial services, manufacturing, construction, energy, and IT services.

ControlUp said the findings highlight the need to evaluate recurring problems and their operational impact rather than relying solely on ticket volume and resolution speed.

"IT organizations have traditionally measured support performance by how quickly they close tickets, but that doesn't tell the whole story," said Simon Townsend, senior vice president of marketing and office of the CTO at ControlUp.

"A password reset that takes a few minutes and an infrastructure failure that disrupts an entire location shouldn't carry the same operational weight."

For more information, go to the ControlUp site.

#6797. Enterprise AI Spending Outpaces Adoption Growth, Report Finds

Enterprise AI spending is growing faster than the number of organizations paying for it, according to a new Menlo Ventures report that points to a shift from buying access for employees to financing work performed by agents.

The venture capital firm's 2026 State of Enterprise AI report estimates deployment spending reached a $176.8 billion annualized run rate by September, up from $33 billion in 2025. The share of enterprises paying for AI rose from 55% to 65%.

A larger bill can reflect broader use inside an organization, but it does not independently establish that the additional work is useful or profitable.

Menlo's methodology describes revenue figures as annualized run rates. The $176.8 billion estimate therefore should not be read as $176.8 billion already spent during the first nine months of 2026.

The report also distinguishes unusually heavy spenders from the typical respondent. Average reported spending reached 4.7 times the prior year's level, while the median reached 2.2 times. That gap suggests a smaller group of large spenders drove the average substantially.

The practical implication is that an industry growth figure may be a poor benchmark for an individual organization's budget. Buyers need to understand their own workload growth and the results it produces.

"Agents are changing the economics of software," Menlo principal Derek Xiao said in the firm's announcement.

Menlo reports that agents account for 80% of tokens on OpenRouter, a service providing access to multiple models. That measures activity on one platform, rather than all enterprise AI use. Token consumption also measures processing volume, rather than completed business outcomes.

An agent that makes repeated attempts can consume more resources without delivering proportionately more value. For procurement teams, the relevant comparison is consequently the cost of completing acceptable work, including the review it requires.

Menlo estimates that Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google capture 69% of enterprise AI deployment spending. That measure is distinct from their shares of enterprise language-model API spending, a narrower category. The figures should not be used interchangeably.

The report draws on a Morning Consult survey of nearly 400 U.S. enterprise decision-makers responsible for more than $4 billion in AI spending. Market totals are modeled estimates informed by surveys, public filings, and third-party reports. Menlo discloses investments in Anthropic and OpenRouter.

A separate announcement from Information Services Group describes buyers putting more emphasis on the economics and reliability of production deployments. ISG says ongoing security and observability work remains necessary as organizations scale.

That provides a useful distinction between market demand and business value. Suppliers can generate growing revenue while customers still determine which deployments justify the cost.

For enterprise leaders, the new spending estimate strengthens the case for examining usage beyond license counts. It leaves the harder purchasing question with the customer: How much worthwhile work did the increased spending actually buy?

Menlo's State of Enterprise AI report is available here.

#6796. Are Zen Hotels Now Putting Us to Sleep?

Rich, layered maximalism is the latest form of escapism—historically inspired decor spiked with creative contemporary flair. Get ready to Instagram every nook.

Above: One of the cottages at Little Saint in Healdsburg, CA.

On the top floor of a Gilded Age McKim, Mead & White mansion in New York, now reincarnated as the Fifth Avenue Hotel, Martin Brudnizki recently put the finishing touches on a two-bedroom suite dubbed the Flâneur Penthouse. With his hallmark exuberance, the Elle Decor A-List designer arrayed the space with distinctive flourishes: a spirited Scalamandré wallcovering trimmed in grosgrain ribbon, bespoke furnishings mixed with French Art Deco pieces, India-inspired inlaid nightstands, Japanese-style lamps, and Murano glass ceiling lights. Each element connects to an imagined narrative that shaped Brudnizki’s vision for the hotel: “this cinematic idea of the home of a flâneur who has traveled the world, has seen and acquired a lot, and put it together here,” the designer says. “It’s a multicultural journey.”

Hotels in this vein tend to be -owner-operated properties looking to carve out a niche. One could trace a baroque family tree that links mold-breaking 1980s boutique hotels like Ian Schrager and Philippe Starck’s Royalton in New York to Jacques Garcia’s interiors for the Hôtel Costes and L’Hotel in Paris to Ilse Crawford’s Ett Hem in Stockholm to Kelly Wearstler’s Proper Hotel in Austin.

Fulk’s hospitality design, like Brudnizki’s, embraces spaces inspired by history and storytelling, with an emphasis on artistry, material richness, and character. Both men’s work is rooted in tradition, with idiosyncratic twists that feel fresh. And they have plenty of kindred spirits working in a diversity of styles, including such designers as Lorenzo Castillo, Kit Kemp, and Laura Gonzalez. While far from a coherent movement, the sumptuous, high-impact aesthetics practiced by these designers just might be today’s most zeitgeisty current.

Take Fulk’s Cottages at Little Saint in Healdsburg, California, each one an elevated boho mashup of influences. “Sixties and ’70s rock and roll, and a sort of Laurel Canyon meets Northern California spirit,” explains the designer. “The cottages feel utterly like nowhere else.” And that, of course, is the point.

For his part, Brudnizki doesn’t care much for maximalism as a label. In the case of his glamorously moody interiors for the Broadwick Soho in London—shimmering surfaces, lavishly upholstered furnishings, a riot of pattern—everything began with an idea he describes as “Studio 54 meets your grandmother’s Soho townhouse, a disco granny kind of thing.”

Then there are the roughly dozen memorable properties created by Kit and Tim Kemp under their Firmdale Hotels group. The most recent is the Warren Street Hotel in New York, with the forthcoming Bedford Place Hotel slated to open next year in London next to the British Museum. “It’s about personality, a sense of arrival, and fun,” says Kit Kemp, who outfits each of her hotels with a more-is-more mix of her ebullient textiles and wallpapers in splashy colors, animated by art and craft.

Kimberley Cohen, the creative director behind Maisons Pariente, says her family’s small portfolio of hôtels de charme are about creating a residential-feeling experience that is also “something you have never seen, that you would not do in your own home.” She has worked with Brudnizki on Le Grand Mazarin in Paris, with Charles Zana on two hotels in the South of France, and with Pierre Yovanovitch on a Méribel chalet. Her latest project, opening this winter, is a Courchevel retreat named Saint Roch, with interiors by Friedmann & Versace that channel the chic romanticism of traditional dachas.

Next up for Brudnizki, meanwhile, is the Knox Hotel, set to open soon in Dallas, new territory for him. As for what one should expect of the decor, he sums it up as “100 percent unapologetic glamour. It won’t be boring.”

This story originally appeared in the November 2026 issue of ELLE Decor.

ELLE Decor features director Stephen Wallis has spent three decades covering art, design, and culture. He was previously the consulting features editor for Galerie and held top positions at Architectural Digest and Departures. His writing has appeared in numerous publications, including The New York Times, T magazine, WSJ magazine, Esquire, Town & Country, Veranda, and Cultured. He is the author of Fontainebleau, a history of the iconic Miami Beach hotel, and Jim Thompson: Beyond Silk, Beyond Thailand.

#6795. QQ: Exactly Whomst Has Joe Jonas Dated Over the Years?

According to an Us Weekly insider, “Things started to shift as Joe got busier with work commitments and they were spending more time apart,” and though rumor has it that Joe “may have reconnected with a former girlfriend” (per Deuxmoi), he has yet to confirm any of this so...stand by for updates!

And if you’re wondering which of Joe’s former girlfriends he may have reconnected with, that’s fair, because there’s a lot of them! From Sophie Turner to Gigi Hadid to Taylor Swift, Joe has romanced his fair share of famous ladies, and the time has come to take a walk down memory lane. Meet ’em all here.

Joe and fellow former Disney star AJ Michalka dated way back in the day after the Jonas Brothers and her group, Aly & AJ, went on tour together. The two were a thing for about a year and a half before breaking it off, and AJ later admitted during a May 2026 appearance on Call Her Daddy that Joe was her first kiss.

“We met on tour,” she said of Joe. “The Jonas Brothers opened for us, and that’s when we started—like, there was a spark. I was like, ‘Oh, this would be fun.’ We started dating on that.”

Taylor Swift (you might’ve heard of her?) and Joe dated for roughly three months in 2008, but things did NOT end well. After they broke up, Taylor went on The Ellen Show and revealed that he'd dumped her during a 27-second phone call.

The two have since made up (she did send his baby a present, after all!), but that 27-second phone call will forever live in infamy.

Camilla Belle and Joe met when she starred in the Jonas Brothers’ “Lovebug” music video, and they began dating right after the musician ended things with Taylor Swift. Tay wasn’t too happy about the timing, and actually told Us Weekly, “They’ve been together since we broke up. That’s why we broke up—because he met her.”

FWIW, Camilla and Joe only dated for about seven months between October 2008 and July 2009 before going their separate ways, with a rep for Camilla saying, “There is no third party involved and they care deeply about each other and will remain friends.”

Joe met Demi Lovato on the set of the forever iconic Disney movie Camp Rock in 2007, but they didn’t start dating until 2010, and the relationship was shorter than you might have realized.

“We eventually dated for a month. I really got to know her and got to see the ins and outs of what she was struggling with, like drug abuse,” Joe later recounted to Vulture in 2013. “I felt like I needed to take care of her, but at the same time, I was living a lie because I wasn’t happy but felt like I had to stay in it for her because she needed help. I couldn’t express any of that, of course, because I had a brand to protect.”

Thankfully, both Demi and her relationship with Joe are in a much better place now.

Shortly after Joe and Demi ended things, Joe began dating Twilight star Ashley Greene in the summer of 2010. Joe called this his “first serious relationship,” and in that same 2013 Vulture interview, he explained why things went south: “We were together for almost a year. I was living out in L.A. by myself, and at the end of the day, long distance didn’t work. It’s incredibly difficult.”

What’s probably most, uhm, notable about this romance is that years later, during a Reddit AMA, Joe revealed that he lost his virginity to Ashley. His exact words, you ask? Ahem: “I lost my virginity to this girl named Ashley. You can probably just Google it.”

Joe and Blanda Eggenschwiler, a Swiss-born model and graphic designer, reportedly began dating in November 2012 after being introduced by a mutual friend and were together for almost two years. At the time, Joe called Blanda “someone I really care about” and said “we get each other.”

Sadly, no word on why they called it quits. A rep for Joe simply confirmed to Us Weekly that “Joe and Blanda have mutually decided to part ways” but “the split was amicable and the two remain friends, with great respect for one another.”

Joe dated yet another super-famous lady when he coupled up with Gigi Hadid in June 2015. At the time, Taylor Swift insisted it was totally fine that one of her BFFs was dating one of her exes, and Gigi even brought him to Taylor’s Fourth of July party. But after five months together, things seemed to end on a sour note.

The model ultimately began dating Zayn Malik two weeks after her split from Joe, of which he said publicly, “I think it’s interesting that she moved on so quickly. I mean it was definitely very quick.” Joe proceeded to unfollow Gigi on social media and delete a picture of himself with Zayn. Yikes.

And if that wasn’t enough, when Joe was asked to play “Shag, Marry, Kill” with his exes on Watch What Happens Live, Joe chose to marry Demi, shag Taylor, and kill Gigi. Okay!

Joe and his ex-wife Sophie Turner first sparked dating rumors in October 2016, and soon thereafter, the actor was spotted spending the holidays with the musician and his family. They kept their relationship pretty private at the beginning, but once they got engaged in October 2017, they started sharing their love with the public.

In July 2019, they tied the knot at Château du Martinet in Provence (that is, after a very campy Vegas ceremony a month prior), and went on to welcome two daughters together. Fans were then shocked when TMZ broke the news of their split in September 2023. Three days later, Joe and Sophie released a statement on Instagram, sharing that they’d “mutually decided to amicably end our marriage.”

It took a full year, but in September 2024, their marriage was officially dissolved.

Romance rumors between Joe and model Stormi Bree initially began swirling when they were spotted walking through a private airport terminal in Los Cabos, Mexico in January 2024. Soon after, the celebs continued to take their love ~international~ with trips to Aspen and even Australia ahead of the Jonas Brothers’ February shows in Sydney.

Fast-forward to March of that year, and a source told Us Weekly that “Joe is still dating Stormi and things are going really well. They haven’t used the love word yet, but they’ve been seeing each other for a few months now and have been getting more serious over the past several weeks.” Meanwhile, “He hasn’t introduced his kids to Stormi yet, but if things continue going well like they have been, then he would definitely be open to them meeting sometime soon.”

Sadly, by June 2024, these two were done, with multiple outlets reporting on the split. But the musician didn’t fly solo for long, because just two weeks after, he was snapped with...

Joe and Lebanese actor Laila Abdallah raised eyebrows when they were photographed looking very coupley on a beach in Athens, Greece. However, a source later told Us Weekly that the two were “just friends” and “were together at the One and Only opening in Greece” with a group that included Luke Evans and Liam Hemsworth.

Joe was first linked to Puerto Rican model Tatiana Gabriela in September 2025, with a source later telling People that they “first started to get to know each other late last summer.”

The two kept the cuteness going for just about a year before Us Weekly revealed in November 2026 that the couple had called it quits, with a source saying, “They had a really fun summer traveling together, but then things shifted in the relationship. Things started to shift as Joe got busier with work commitments and they were spending more time apart.”

#6794. Sauer Celebrates 85 Years With a New Assouline Book

Gabriel Sauer and Stephanie Wenk on how jewelry connects us to the real world.

For 85 years, Brazilian jewelry house Sauer has built a world of its own, one where vibrant gemstones, unexpected materials, and an adventurous spirit come together. Founded by Jules Sauer, a pioneering gem hunter whose fascination with Brazil’s natural treasures helped shape the country’s gemstone industry, the house has always approached jewelry a little differently. Today, that same curiosity remains at its core, even as a new generation takes over.

To celebrate its 85th anniversary, Sauer is looking both backward and forward with the release of a new Assouline book highlighting its remarkable history, out December 5, alongside an anniversary collection that reimagines some of the house’s most recognizable designs. For creative director Stephanie Wenk and third-generation family member Gabriel Sauer, the milestone is about more than honoring the past. It’s an opportunity to reflect on how a family business rooted in tradition can continue to evolve without losing what makes it special.

Stephanie Wenk, creative director of Sauer.

The anniversary collection is a testament to that philosophy. Drawing on an extraordinary archive of gemstones, some of which have been tucked away for decades, Wenk brings new life to Brazilian imperial topaz, aquamarines, and other precious stones through unexpected combinations. It’s an approach that feels true to the house’s history while pushing its creative boundaries. But beyond the jewelry itself, Sauer’s story is one of family, discovery, and a deep connection to Brazil. From Jules’s early adventures to the house’s growing international presence, each chapter has been shaped by a love of experimentation and embracing the unexpected. As the brand celebrates this milestone, Wenk and Sauer share how they’re staying true to the house’s original spirit.

The cover of Sauer: Dialogues Between Worlds from Assouline.

Gabriel Sauer: We’ve been with the company for almost 14 years now. The anniversary is an important milestone for the company, but it also marks more than 10 years of our generation of the Sauer family leading the business. I think we now have the material and the maturity to showcase our vision for the future of the company. It’s important that, in a book like this, we can tell a little bit about the past but also share our vision for the future. If we had done this book five years ago, it wouldn’t have had the same substance that it has now. We had the idea in previous years, but I feel that the timing came naturally.

Stephanie Wenk: I think it was the adventurous spirit of Sauer. Jules was always very nonconformist in everything he did, from his discoveries to his travels. He did things differently and in his own way. I think that’s what continues to inspire us today. While making the book, we were also talking about the history with Gabriel’s dad and the rest of the family. It’s very inspiring. Jules’s spirit is still very much alive.

GS: It was interesting to have these conversations with the second generation of the family while putting the book together. The story of how Jules came to Brazil and founded the company still shapes how we approach business and challenges today. He was an optimist with a deep passion for craftsmanship and gemstones, something we continue to carry forward. Every time we revisit his story, we’re reminded of our values and purpose.

I also learned more about the historical context of some of his discoveries. During the war, American companies were coming to Brazil to mine minerals for the war effort, and some of that activity was connected to his earlier explorations. I hadn’t fully understood how his discoveries fit into that period of history, so it was fascinating to learn about that connection.

GS: Working in a family business is a great responsibility. It’s also a challenge because we’re the third generation, and most family businesses don’t survive beyond the third generation. One of the biggest lessons I’ve learned is the importance of giving each generation creative freedom. Every family has its own formula, and there’s no single formula that works for everyone. In our family, we’ve always welcomed new generations and allowed them to express their vision for the future without having someone hovering over their heads. I think this philosophy came from Jules and [his wife] Zilda together, and it’s been an invaluable lesson in how to run a family business.

I remember that, when I was a kid, my grandfather used to carry gemstones in his pocket and give them to people with whom he felt a good connection or energy. He would say that gemstones take billions of years to form in nature and that they carry the heart of our world inside them. I would see the impact that these gifts had on people. He was passionate about honoring gemstones and bringing out their best qualities. That’s something we continue to express through our designs. A lot of our creations begin with the stone itself, sometimes even with one specific gemstone.

SW: We’re very lucky because we have this amazing inventory of stones, and I’m always discovering new ones. I think about 80 percent of the stones we used in this collection came from our archives. We used a lot of Brazilian stones, like imperial topaz and aquamarine, which are also very important to our history. Our signature elements are really important to our vocabulary, our DNA, and the foundations of our designs, but the stones play a very big role. There are a lot of one-of-a-kind pieces in this collection, including more high jewelry than we usually do, as well as some brooches. Some of the stones have been in our archives for 40 years, so it’s really special.

SW: Researching, introducing, and combining different materials is very important to our work, and it’s something I’m really drawn to. I love exploring the dialogue between different materials, how one enhances the other, and how combining them can give a new perspective to a material you might not normally imagine alongside a precious stone. We’ve been doing it since the beginning. We manufacture everything ourselves, so we also have the opportunity to test materials and develop ideas. Sometimes that process takes a long time, and you have to be able to experiment. It’s really valuable that we’re able to do that.

GS: Since we started as a stone-cutting workshop, we’ve always explored different types of stones and how we can cut and use them in different ways. This exploration of different forms and creative applications is something that’s ingrained in our DNA.

SW: We revisited a few pieces, but it’s also a collection that looks very much toward the future. We reinterpreted the Constellation ring, one of our most iconic designs, which won the De Beers prize. We also combined elements of Constellation with Illusion, another design from about 10 years ago. It was an opportunity to experiment with both designs and bring them together in a new way. We also revisited signature elements, like the use of onyx and lapis lazuli, as well as our distinctive framing techniques, and developed those ideas further.

GS: We also created a new version of an archival necklace incorporating pearls, revisiting a design language that’s been part of the house for years.

SW: I think all of our collections revolve around art, nature, and spirituality, so it felt very natural. Collaborating with artists, bringing in a contemporary vision, working across different disciplines, and interpreting different worlds are all part of that. I have a lot of different interests, including music, texture, design, art, and cinema. I don’t like to look at other jewelry. I prefer to look at things that inspire me, and I think that shows in what we do. Bringing that perspective into the house felt like a very natural evolution.

GS: I think it’s definitely something we inherited from previous generations and have carried forward. Jules was always passionate about art. He was a collector himself, and previous generations had already explored partnerships and collaborations with artists. When Stephanie started exploring this as well, it came very naturally because she’s so passionate about art. We’ve been fortunate to collaborate with some incredible artists. It wasn’t something that was particularly planned. It happened naturally, and eventually we realized that art had become one of the main pillars of the brand. We then started collaborating with art fairs as well, and we felt that establishing the art prize was a way to give back.

GS: We wanted to tell the story of how Jules first came to Brazil, which is very inspiring, but also highlight the different explorations and discoveries he participated in. For example, there was the discovery of emeralds in Brazil and how he worked with the GIA [Gemological Institute of America] to establish that the stones were actually emeralds. It was a very important milestone for Brazil as a gemstone producer.

He was also an advocate for gemstones and traveled around the world, giving speeches about removing the label of “semiprecious” from certain stones. He used to say that gemstones are a one-time harvest and that every gemstone is precious. He had an amethyst with an amazing color that he considered incredibly valuable, and he wouldn’t sell it at any price. Today, we can see that many different gemstones are recognized in the market and have very high values. He was really ahead of his time.

SW: I hope they understand the history of the brand, Jules’s story, and all the wonders of Brazil, especially because we have so many stones that are unique to the country. I also hope they see the creativity, the craftsmanship, and the different perspectives that define Sauer. It’s about understanding how you can take a heritage brand into the future while still respecting its past. Heritage shouldn’t be something that limits you but something that gives you more to build upon.

GS: I think we’ll always preserve it because whenever someone discovers Sauer, one of the first things they want to understand is how the company came to be and what makes us different. It’s inspiring to see how excited our team at the Madison Avenue store is to share that story. As we expand internationally, our Brazilian heritage will always remain an important part of our identity. I also feel that the pillars of the brand are timeless. Everyone can relate to nature, art, and spirituality, and people often find their own meaning in our jewelry. We’re also a multigenerational company, with people from the first and second generations alongside Gen Z. That range of perspectives keeps us fresh and allows us to continue evolving while staying true to our roots.

SW: We have a growing community of younger clients, and it’s interesting to see how different generations influence one another. Sometimes it’s the sons and daughters who influence their mothers. There’s a lot of meaning and symbolism in the jewelry. It helps people build connections and create their own personal interpretations. It’s all about connecting.

GS: I hope we still have the same energy and free spirit that we have today. I don’t necessarily think in terms of becoming a huge company with lots of stores. That’s not our approach. Of course, we may open new stores in new places, but I think it’s more about being in the right places and achieving greater global recognition. I feel that jewelry connects you to the real world. We live in a very digital world, and I think jewelry offers an opportunity to give clients real experiences and enhance human connection.

SW: I hope we continue to inspire people, connect stories, and create new stories through jewelry. I want more and more people to discover Sauer. Jewelry is very intimate. It’s something you wear on your body forever. You might wear an engagement ring for 40 years without ever taking it off. There’s almost nothing else in the world that you could wear every single day for your entire life. That intimacy and the fact that something can hold so much meaning are really unique to jewelry. Even before language existed, humans were adorning themselves.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

#6793. The Story Behind Peggy Scott’s Wedding Dress

The Gilded Age threw the wedding of the year for the fan-favorite character, played by Denée Benton

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

It’s 88 degrees on a humid June day in Troy, New York, and Denée Benton stands in a local church’s outbuilding, posing in Peggy Scott’s wedding dress, not breaking a sweat.

It has been a long, hot day of filming, and the cast and crew are scheduled to keep going for many more hours. To get to this photo shoot, I had to walk past a cramped church hallway where Cynthia Nixon, Audra McDonald, and John Douglas Thompson sat together in various stages of Gilded Age undress, trading inside jokes. Everyone on set is in a state of elation, both because of the long-planned-for episode featuring the wedding of Peggy and Dr. William Kirkland and because it’s the day of Game 4 of the Knicks’s historic NBA run. A few hours after I leave set, Nixon will post a reel of the cast reacting to the Knicks win in their Gilded Age finery. But even amidst all of this excitement, Benton in her wedding dress steals the show.

Writers, production assistants, costume designers, and even Jordan Donica, who plays Dr. Kirkland, gather to watch the shoot. Benton, in the middle of it all, is poised in the gown of white lace, a corset underneath, dress lines crisp, makeup unsmudged, a picture of bridal serenity. Later, Kasia Walicka Maimone, the show’s costume designer, will tell me she spied Benton doing breathing exercises in the church pews, just to maintain her stamina.

Peggy has been a fan favorite since her introduction in the show’s first episode. An ambitious, upper-class Black woman in Gilded Age America, she is an anomaly in period television. Her storyline has introduced viewers to the world of the Black elite, a burgeoning class that emerged during Reconstruction and would dominate Black political and cultural life to the present day. Popular nonfiction books like Our Kind of People have documented the history of this group, but they have been largely absent from television. Even Black weddings, of any time period, are rarely portrayed on American TV. So how do you design a dress for a wedding that hasn’t been seen before?

“The Gilded Age,” as the period between the 1870s and 1890s is known, “was famous for its excitement [around fashion],” says Walicka Maimone. “How do we represent this excitement? How do we pull out from the historical research things that we, the modern audience, are going to be excited about? We have this giant library of about 50 to 60,000 images that we’ve collected since season 1 … but there’s always manipulation that I apply to it.” Peggy’s wedding dress “resonates with a lot of elements from the period, but it’s not a direct quote of any one specific dress.…What was really important to both Denée and me was the composite of the silhouette [and] the texture of the lace,” a detail that was “referred to in the script directly by her mother-in-law.”

“The speed that we had to accomplish the design and execution and put it on the screen was astronomical,” Walicka Maimone says. “Hundreds of hands altogether contribute to the making. Each dress takes about six to eight weeks to be built.” Those working on the final bridal look included the in-house costume-design team, milliners for the veil and hat, a jeweler in Rome who designed Peggy’s earrings, and on-set tailors who maintained the costume during filming.

“My wedding dress had over 75 buttons going down the back. Amber, my head dresser, buttoned each one by hand. The craftsmanship was really unbelievable,” Benton tells me a few months later. “It felt powerful to me, spiritually. It felt like we were embodying a moment for a lot of people. I have never seen a luxury Black wedding of the 1800s on any screen, on a stage, in any popular media. And so it really feels like we’re getting to be a part of a pop-culture history moment.”

Peggy is a child of post-Reconstruction America. Her father, Arthur, experienced enslavement, but she is part of the first generation of Black people born into freedom and citizenship. The thrill of watching her on screen is seeing a character who relishes pushing against the boundaries of what that might mean. She is both an avatar of modern viewers’ desires and a fantasy of what Black womanhood might have looked like in a time of dynamic social change and fabulous dressing. For Peggy, the question of a wedding and marriage takes on additional significance.

“Because the law of the land during enslavement recognized enslaved people as property, [and] therefore not protected by the law, nor were there unions, whether they were chosen unions or forced unions … they could be separated at any moment. The law did not protect the sanctity of marriage for Black people, for enslaved people,” explains historian Erica Armstrong Dunbar, who is chair of the African-American Studies department at Emory University, in addition to a consultant on The Gilded Age.

Marriage for the Gilded Age generation of Black people was an assertion of agency and an act of claiming Black humanity. The ability to choose partners and form Black families—and have those family bonds legally protected—was a radical act in the aftermath of slavery. All of this history can inform the context of Peggy Scott’s marriage, but what that wedding might look like on screen is another question.

“When we first started talking about the season and the wedding, Sonja Warfield [the episode’s writer] and Julian Fellowes [The Gilded Age’s creator] were very invested in the notion of the jumping of the broom and that being a part of African American wedding tradition,” Armstrong Dunbar explains. Jumping the broom was a wedding tradition practiced by some enslaved people, a ceremonial act to mark a bond that by definition was not legally recognized.

“I immediately was like, but that’s not really happening in the 1880s,” Armstrong Dunbar explains. “People were actually distancing themselves from many of the traditional experiences connected to the weddings of enslaved people.”

Fellowes, Warfield, and Gilded Age executive producer Salli Richardson-Whitfield and producer Davita Scarlett, however, were all adamant about including this practice in the wedding episode. Many of them had participated in broom-jumping ceremonies in their own weddings; the practice became popular again in the 1970s, ’80s, and ’90s as post–Civil Rights era couples looked to include specifically African American rituals in their wedding ceremonies.

But part of the pleasure of The Gilded Age is watching how the show plays with historical conventions and anachronisms to further draw viewers into characters’ lives. In this case, the writers and producers decided to give Peggy’s father, Arthur, who was once enslaved, the task of handing the broom he used in his wedding ceremony to his daughter, a moment that recognizes the family’s beginnings and its triumph of seeing a freeborn daughter legally wed. “It really encapsulated the way in which people try to meld traditions when they’re bringing their families together,” says Scarlett. “It just felt too delicious and too interesting and too thematically rich to pass up.”

“I knew that we were going to be doing Peggy getting married, and I claimed it. I said, ‘No one else is allowed to direct this wedding but me,’ ” says director Richardson-Whitfield. “I just wanted to make sure that it was as lush and gorgeous and special as anything else that we’ve done on the show.”

This included the decision to feature a gospel choir. “We specifically chose also to do it a cappella and not have any instruments with the music because I felt like those beautiful Black voices were enough to fill the church,” she says. An a cappella chorus singing spirituals would have been, like the broom jumping, frowned upon by many upper-class Black people in the 1880s, but that tension provided another opportunity to deepen the wedding scenes. “Just because we are African American people doesn’t mean we all think the same thing,” Richardson-Whitfield says. “It’s nice to be able to explore different kinds of Black people.”

The show’s commitment to nuance and its willingness to acknowledge the historical existence of different kinds of marginalized people means its fan base stretches far and wide. Recently, the creative agency Little Big World hosted a Gilded Age drag ball and panel on queer black history with Benton, activist and Gilded Age fan Brittany Packnett Cunningham, and queer historian Hugh Ryan. The event was packed.

“I think that people see Peggy as this sort of doll princess,” Benton tells me, “but as the actor playing her … bell hooks has this quote that’s like, ‘Queer not as in who I sleep with, but queer as in at odds with everything around me.’ That is Peggy. Period. There was not really a class of professional women [during the Gilded Age]; you were either aristocracy or you were working class. And then to be a Black professional, she really is one of one moving through this space in her time. And I find that to be very queer.”

“That’s one of the two powers of history work for me,” says Ryan. “One is seeing … ‘Oh, things actually were really different back then. So that means they could be really different in the future.’ And I think that's liberatory. But the other part, and this is where I think The Gilded Age shines … is getting people excited. I was in a panel with 60 Black queer folk in a Black queer space in Bed-Stuy talking about the Gilded Age and Black drag kings in vaudeville. That conversation only happens because beautiful art sparks our interest and allows us to see a place in the past.”

“As an artist, you can’t really ask for more than to do something that is popular and meaningful at the same time,” Benton says. “The sweet spot.”

#6791. 35 of the Best ’90s Christmas Movies to Give You Extra Nostalgia

From the classics (Home Alone) to the deeply unsettling (also Home Alone).

To be honest, movies made in the 1990s are kind of all over the place—but that’s what we loved about the decade. You never knew what to expect, and Christmas and holiday movies were no exception. The decade was filled with a bunch of auteurs making daring choices (a.k.a. everything Tim Burton made, but particularly the movie that's somehow about Halloween and Christmas simultaneously), some insta-classics (Muppet Christmas Carol), and some pretty wild setups that have aged *weirdly* but still give us the nostalgia feels (While You Were Sleeping, Home Alone, The Santa Clause, and a whole bunch more).

Seriously, go back to some of your old faves and remember how we just accepted Arnold Schwarzenegger as a normal salesman from Minnesota (Jingle All the Way). To be even more honest, the '90s production speed couldn't hold a candle to the streaming era. These days, there are hundreds of Christmas movies released across various streaming network every year. We’ve only been able to scrounge up 30ish holiday movies for the whole decade.

Beyond the classics you know and love, there are a bunch of movies on here you probably missed the first time around—or haven't watched in actual decades. If you're here because you grew up on '90s movies, allow us to refresh your memory with some underrated classics and tell you where you can watch all your old faves. And, if you're here because you want something different for your holiday-viewing experience because you've already watched Elf 10,000 times, start at the top of this list and work your way down. Happy holiday viewing!

The Halloween-Christmas crossover no one expected, The Nightmare Before Christmas is a gorgeous stop-motion piece of art that's aged better than anyone expected. Tim Burton is a vocal lover of the holidays (this is the first of two times he'll be on this list), and his deeply weird vision is surprisingly moving—who hasn't felt like Jack Skellington desperately wishing for Christmas but also not totally doing it right?

Christmas movie, or movie that takes place during Christmas? While You Were Sleeping sees Sandra Bullock's Lucy save a man from an oncoming train, but not before he falls into a coma. While unconscious, hijinx ensue, and his family mistakes Lucy for his fiance. A classic '90s rom-com, this basically started a nationwide obsession with Sandra Bullock, Bill Pullman, and falling in love in snowy Chicago.

We realize that there are more beloved Muppet movies out there, but this one is *it* for us. Michael Caine is giving it 110 percent here, which means you get some seriousness alongside the giggles. Also, it contains both the scariest scene (hello, Ghost of Christmas Future) and the most bittersweet scene (hello, Beaker and the scarf) in a Christmas movie ever.

The Christmas movie to end all Christmas movies came to us in 1990. Home Alone follows a kid abandoned by his family on Christmas who must protect his home against two Grinch-like burglars.

Same, same, but different. Home Alone 2 follows the same abandoned kid, this time left adrift in New York City. The film sees the return of our beloved burglars, plus a cameo from a pre-political Donald Trump. Ah, simpler times.

Tim Burton is back, and with a newer, bleaker vision of the holiday season. Like some of its neighbors on this list, Batman Returns is a movie that takes place over the holidays, not a holiday movie. If you want a classic Burton look at the nightmare beauty of Christmas, wrapped in a cat woman suit and a cape, return to this movie during the holiday season.

Praise be! The best-selling gospel album of all time! If you're only familiar with the music, you should absolutely watch this Whitney Houston, Courtney B. Vance, Denzel Washington love triangle Christmas movie, in which Denzel plays a literal angel. If you grew up watching this, you know it's the corny, sweet, heartwarming goodness the holiday needs.

This is...a weird movie, and not just because it features the message that Christmas is all about buying sh*t you don't need. Arnold Schwarzenegger is...improbably cast as a frustrated mattress salesman from Minneapolis, and it only gets weirder from there. But if you're watching it for the nostalgia factor or just to remember how wild it really was, go for it!

Nothing says the '90s like Jonathan Taylor Thomas, heartthrob of millions of teen girls. This admittedly out-there premise features JTT as a noncommittal boarding school teen whose dad promises him a Porsche - if he makes it home in time for Christmas dinner. A weird, wacky road trip ensues (and life lessons are learned, obv).

If you loved the Olsen twins, this was probably a repeat watch in your house (guilty as charged). It's a deeply '90s TV movie that—fun fact—was the first time they ever portrayed separate characters. This one's a wild ride, quite literally, as the kiddos are just trying to get to grandma's and instead go on a bunch of adventures in a delivery truck. Just go with it, it's sweet.

This movie is a pretty obvious attempt to capture the magic of the original - which came out in 1988, so it unfortunately doesn't make the list. It's also basically the same movie in an airport. But it's still fun to watch Bruce Willis grumble, "Just once, I’d like a regular, normal Christmas" to himself while getting into a bunch of action shenanigans.

This is another action movie that didn't *have* to be set around Christmas—but it's more fun that way. Geena Davis is the coolest as a suburban housewife with amnesia. who turns out to be a hardcore assassin, alongside Samuel L. Jackson. This movie has an improbably happy ending, which, if that doesn't make it a Christmas movie, we don't know what does!

This early Nora Ephron film is absolute chaos (which is probably why you've never heard of it), but you can't beat the star-studded cast of Steve Martin, Rita Wilson, Rob Reiner, and Adam Sandler, just to name a few. And they're doing all the slapstick simultaneously, which will at least make for an entertaining hour and a half.

Did you know there was a direct-to-video Beauty and the Beast holiday special? Because we sure didn't. But, basically, it takes place in the middle of the first movie, where the Beast hates Christmas (and joy, apparently), and Belle has to convince him to let the holiday spirit into his heart. Light holiday fluff right this way!

The last "new" Peanuts special to air on CBS, over nine million households watched this—but it's also not as popular (or well-known) as the original 1960s Charlie Brown special. If you're hoping for more Peanuts content this holiday season and haven't watched this in a long time (or ever), this one's gonna hit you right in the feels.

All hail our queen Julie Andrews! This TV movie is making the correct choice by letting James Garner's character fall in love with her—the premise being that two strangers take shelter together during a winter storm. Corny, manufactured drama and romance ensue. If you happen to like Hallmark movies, this is an early draft of the romances you know and love.

This movie kinda requires you to watch the first films in the three-part series and also...is not a great movie. But John Travolta and Kirstie Alley are trying their very best to make it work—and if you ever wanted to listen to Diane Keaton and Danny DeVito do the voices for two strange dog characters, then do we have the movie for you.
