#6790. Phishing Threats Totaled 7.3 Billion in Q3 2026

E-mail phishing threats reached 7.3 billion in Q3 2026, with September activity increasing 41% from August, according to Microsoft Threat Intelligence.

According to a report from Microsoft Threat Intelligence and the Microsoft Defender Security Research Team, phishing detections reached nearly 3 billion in September alone.

The findings also highlighted changes in attacker techniques, including business-service impersonation, credential theft, and social engineering through Microsoft Teams.

The Redmond-based firm recognized approximately 129 million malicious messages spoofing the sender domains of tracked business services during Q3.

DocuSign was the most frequently spoofed brand in September, accounting for 29% of the month's tracked spoofing activity. Adobe, SurveyMonkey, and Barracuda also experienced increases toward the end of the quarter.

The research found that some malicious messages were delivered despite failing e-mail authentication checks and being identified as threats.

In September, tenant- or user-level security overrides applied to 63% of these messages with a recorded security outcome — most involved tenant-level exceptions.

Microsoft warned that overly broad exceptions intended to support legitimate business communications can weaken protection against impersonation attacks.

The company emphasized that these findings do not establish whether recipients opened the messages or whether accounts were compromised.

Microsoft also recorded approximately 141,000 malicious Teams call attempts during Q3.

Attackers increasingly used ordinary personal names instead of explicitly impersonating IT support personnel. Such display names accounted for 46% of an observed sample in July, rising to 88% in September.

Meanwhile, QR code phishing declined 67% compared to Q2, totaling roughly 12.1 million attacks.

CAPTCHA-gated phishing activity increased toward the end of the quarter, reaching 3.1 million detected attacks in September. SVG attachments played a significant role in the increase.

Credential theft remained the primary objective of malicious attachment campaigns, with approximately 94% to 96% of payload-based attacks directing users to phishing sites or fraudulent sign-in pages.

Microsoft recommended reviewing Exchange Online Protection and Defender for Office 365 configurations, enabling Safe Links and Safe Attachments, and strengthening authentication protections.

The company also advised organizations to review security exceptions and verify the identities of external Teams contacts before responding to suspicious requests.

For more information, go to the Microsoft blog post.

Cybersecurity company Flashpoint announced it has received U.S. Patent No. 12,705,360 for its Ransomware Risk model, a methodology designed to help security teams determine which newly disclosed vulnerabilities more closely resemble those historically used in ransomware attacks.

Cybercriminals are moving away from mass phishing scams and focusing on more targeted attacks, often using trusted websites and services to trick victims, according to a new report from KnowBe4.

District and state policies run the gamut from embracing to banning AI. This raises a key question: When does AI accelerate student learning and when does it interfere?

Ransomware attacks are becoming more automated, and AI could take that much further, according to cybersecurity company NCC Group's July 2026 threat intelligence report.

#6786. You Need a Funnel-Neck Coat This Winter

They’re cozy, polished, and way less fussy than a scarf.

If there’s a style that’s having its moment, it’s the funnel neck. Between sweater tops and coats, I’ve been seeing this trend all over my feed and I am quite obsessed. Especially as the winter months creep closer, to me, a funnel neck is a perfect style for the lazy-fashion girls. It’s not as restrictive as a turtleneck, but allows you the freedom that a scarf can’t while still keeping you warm.

Funnel necks are a balance between two necessary winter staples, while adding a little edge to your late fall and winter outfits. So, if you’ve also been seeing the funnel neck everywhere, I’ve gathered a few styling options in coat form below, so you can map out your own look next.

Contrary to the masses, I love a brown leather coat more than black. There’s something so chic about it, and with the added funnel neck it makes the whole look more interesting and even a bit mysterious.

A really good, thick coat is a necessity during the colder months. And as someone who always struggles to find a scarf that fits the vibe perfectly, rocking a coat like this does the job perfectly.

As I said, brown leather is my personal fave, but most people love a good black leather coat. It’s the easiest and sharpest monochromatic outfit you’ll be able to pull together. Pairing a good funnel-neck coat with a sleek pair of black trousers hits every time.

For the on-the-go Gen Z girlies, this feels as quintessential 20-something as it can get. not only are you on trend with the funnel-neck coat, but having it be belted with a pair of baggy jeans just reads as Cool Girl to me.

There’s nothing I love more than a monochromatic outfit, so if you’re feeling colorful this winter (to negate how gloomy and cold it is) leaning into a matching look like this is a trendy way into the funnel-neck style.

#6782. Is KATSEYE Following the Rules of K-Pop?

Fans are worried by Megan’s decision to perform in the face of a concussion, but maybe the debate is about more than one group, but about an entire industry (or two).

Online debates about celebrity work culture sparked when KATSEYE’s Megan Skindiel, who is recovering from a concussion, recently performed seated and in sunglasses during a show in Austin on the group’s WILDWORLD Tour. The next night in Dallas, video surfaced of the artist taking part in the group’s intense dance choreography, while wearing what many speculate to be a heart monitor.

Fans expressed grave concern for her well-being, questioning whether she should be performing at all. While it is important to note that we don’t actually know whether it was Megan’s own decision to perform, many still accused KATSEYE’s label, HYBE x Geffen Records, of potentially overworking their artists at the expense of their health. The label is a partnership between the South Korean entertainment company HYBE (home to groups like BTS, Illit, TXT, and Seventeen) and the American label Geffen Records (home to artists such as Olivia Rodrigo, Selena Gomez, Lady Gaga, and Lana Del Rey).

And there’s another relevant context: With Manon and Sophia already on hiatus, Megan’s absence would leave the group with just three members, only half their original formation of six, and for that reason the group had already postponed three shows. As of now, neither the label nor the group has publicly addressed the criticism.

For longtime K-pop fans, none of this is entirely shocking. Those who follow the industry have most likely already witnessed their idols push through panic attacks, fainting spells, extreme sleep deprivation, injuries from falls, and many other mental and physical struggles in order to give their fans the concert experience they were promised. But for many Western fans, this may be the first look at the grueling expectations that the K-pop world has for its artists, which helps explain the intense concern in their reactions.

KATSEYE is an especially interesting case for us to explore this friction. The group was formed through Dream Academy, a survival competition run by HYBE and Geffen Records, where the finalists trained mainly in Los Angeles, with trips to HYBE’s headquarters in Seoul. While KATSEYE’s music is mostly in English, the group promotes in both the U.S. and South Korea, exemplifying the group’s unique positioning between the two music industries, each with its own set of rules and ideas of what a pop career demands.

Commercially, that meeting point keeps getting closer, with the dramatic rise of K-pop’s popularity and its growing presence in mainstream Western media. And that cross-cultural exchange is reflected in the music itself: English words increasingly make up the majority of the lyrics in K-pop songs, and many labels are now intentionally debuting members who are proficient in English.

It also helps to compare how music careers get built, starting with how the artists are even first discovered by the world. Many of the West’s biggest stars began as those who were organically noticed: Justin Bieber was discovered through cover videos on YouTube, and Taylor Swift was spotted as a teenager playing Nashville’s Bluebird Cafe. K-pop runs on a completely different model: one where the company trains the individual into being an artist through a strict, meticulous formula within a larger system of strategic control.

Those who make it through the company’s insanely competitive rounds of auditions will then spend years as trainees with no guarantee of debuting. Those years typically involve regular evaluations, private lessons, as well as sometimes group living for management and surveillance purposes. Trainees often agree to be prescribed diet plans and sometimes even cosmetic surgery, as well as close monitoring of their private lives including harsh restrictions on dating and phone use to ensure that their status as trainees remains a secret. And what may be even more jarring for those new to this culture is that many of these trainees are often as young as 13, with more and more labels debuting their idols before they are even close to being legal adults.

In exchange comes a carefully engineered shot at success, with executives and experts calibrating the exact combination of members, visual concept, songs, and more to optimize audience appeal. Audiences got a glimpse of this process during Dream Academy, though in a more Westernized version. Whatever ethical questions this process raises, it works, at least commercially. All the biggest K-pop groups have come out of this exact system, and the labels continue to stay closely involved throughout their careers.

But the label isn’t the only relationship that heavily shapes a K-pop artist’s life. There’s also the one with the fans. Western audiences are no strangers to fan culture, from Beatlemania to Swifties, and plenty of domestic K-pop fandoms have a U.S. counterpart. However, one notable cultural difference is one of degree. Take whatever you’ve seen from American fandoms and multiply it by a hundred, and you start to approach the level of devotion an average K-pop stan extends to their bias, or favorite member. They follow idols to concert after concert and every public appearance in between, and they also work together, using step-by-step guides to stream songs in ways that send them up the charts, sometimes even outperforming many mainstream Western artists on global charts like the Billboard Hot 100.

And that kind of devotion comes with expectations. Many groups have dedicated fan-chatting apps, such as HYBE’s Weverse and the subscription-based Bubble, where artists can post and chat with fans almost directly, and fans come to expect regular contact through this service. Idols are also expected to keep up a cheerful image, to avoid canceling a show that fans paid for at all costs, and to immediately apologize when they fall short, even when the reason is an injury.

Public dating, meanwhile, has long been treated as a career-threatening betrayal for these artists. In 2024, after aespa’s Karina was revealed to be dating an actor, she faced a wave of backlash, causing her to post a handwritten apology to fans. Norms have loosened for established stars, but newcomers, or what the industry calls shin-ins, are discouraged, or often barred from it, by both their companies and their fans.

Because they’re still largely construed as Western artists, KATSEYE is, to a large degree, exempt from these rules. For example, members have been comparatively open about their dating lives—a luxury a Korea-based group would most likely not be afforded. But KATSEYE is still managed by a K-pop company, trained by a K-pop system. It wouldn’t be surprising that some of that ethos of always putting the fans first is internalized within the group’s own decision-making, shaping how much they feel they owe their fans in ways a Western artist might not.

From a Western perspective, it makes sense why all of this might feel like an oppressive system that needs reform, or even dismantling. And the criticism exists internally as well: On November 16, South Korea’s Culture Ministry officially announced the launch of a comprehensive survey to review concerns over young performers’ working conditions following the NewJeans controversy. However, one could argue that Western criticism can often be translated by domestic fans as a kind of white-savior complex, with “outsiders” interfering in the methods and systems that have existed without their attention for decades, while deciding it must assimilate to their terms and standards. Especially when many of these critics lack the necessary understanding of the complicated nuances of how K-pop’s cultural specificity largely reflects South Korea’s distinct historical, political, and socioeconomic landscape—one that dramatically differs from the U.S.

These aspects of K-pop are deeply normalized within the industry itself: Trainee systems are shown openly in documentaries and TV series, including ones the companies themselves help produce, and artists often talk about those years candidly, suggesting that many of them may not see these practices as the problem outsiders do. And maybe there is also a truth in the idea that K-pop’s impressive commercial success is partly a product of the very controls critics object to, including the symbiotic relationships between artists and their labels, and between artists and their fans. Without that culture, we would probably not have what we now know to be BLACKPINK or BTS.

None of this makes the overworking of artists acceptable, nor does it erase much of the valid concern so many people feel. We are allowed to worry when our favorite artist seems to be pushed too far, whether it’s by their own drive, their label’s instructions, or by the weight of fans’ expectations. And we’re allowed to question the very systems that make that possible—in K-pop, in Hollywood, or anywhere else.

But it’s also worth asking what it might mean for a system with decades of independent history—one that grew largely outside Western norms—to navigate a global spotlight (and the equally globalized standards that come with it). Where does cultural context end and basic safety begin? And who gets to decide what “better” looks like, if not the artists living it?

#6778. Naked Nails Are Already the Star Trend of Awards Season—How to Get Them at Home

Zendaya, Olivia Wilde, and Inde Navarrette all wore the barely there nail trend last weekend.

We may earn commission from links on this page, but we only recommend products we love. Promise.

On Sunday, the biggest stars in film walked the navy carpet at the 17th annual Governors Awards, kicking off awards season. While their gowns glittered and hair shined, one emerging beauty trend was noticeably, well, unnoticeable: naked nails. Instead of a shimmering manicure, classic red, or a simple nail design, the celebs—including Zendaya, Olivia Wilde, Inde Navarrette, and Florence Pugh—overwhelmingly opted for a bare nail look.

And I get the hype! Naked manicures are understated and whisper sophistication rather than shouting it. So, what exactly does a naked manicure entail, and how can you achieve it? Keep reading to learn everything about this timeless nail look.

The naked manicure is a barely there nail style that echoes the look of natural-looking nails. According to Julie Ventura, Orly’s global education manager, the trend stems from the need to give nails a break with a back-to-basics approach. “Consumers are more conscious than ever of nail health since so many have experienced damage from improper use of nail products,” Ventura says. “They’re opting for a more minimalistic look like this one,” she says. Think of a naked manicure like no-makeup makeup, but for the nails and hands.

The effortless-looking manicure, which is anything but boring, incorporates sheer and ultra-milky whites, pinks, creams, nudes, and beiges, or even a layer or two of glossy, clear polish. “By utilizing light, neutral shades of nail polish, the manicure mimics the look of clean, healthy nails for an understated finish that feels timeless,” says celebrity nail artist Erica De Los Santos. “It’s all about enhancing the natural beauty of the nails.”

Equally important as the nails is the condition of the skin on your hands, which should be well-hydrated and nourished to prevent dry, flaky, irritated, and peeling skin, as well as hangnails, which can distract from the manicure.

Nail length is also key for this “your-nails-but-better” mani. They should be short- to medium-length, boast blurred ridges, and have no signs of discoloration. De Los Santos says naked nails are most flattering on natural nails with a soft almond, square, round, or oval shape, for a sophisticated and elongated look.

The effortless-looking manicure may seem simple, but it involves multiple steps. For starters, the nails, nail beds, and cuticles must be meticulously groomed and trimmed since the manicure reveals nails at their healthiest and most refined state, according to Townhouse founder and creative director Juanita Huber-Millet. “Strong, well-cared-for nails are necessary, while hydrated hands and nourished cuticles elevate the overall effect.”

Ventura recommends first filing the nails into a uniform shape and length and then pushing back the cuticles to minimize dead skin on the nail plate. Next, clean underneath and around the nails to remove any dirt, debris, or oil, and then lightly buff the nails so that the polish adheres better. Applying a nail treatment, such as Epres EpHD, a strengthening base that also repairs the nails from within, is also a good idea.

Once the nails are prepped and primed, it’s time for polish. “Pick a sheer shade that complements your skin tone,” De Los Santos says. An all-in-one nail perfector like Orly Nail Retouch gives a soft-matte, blurred finish in one to two coats. Or, go the traditional nail polish route and layer on a base coat, one to two coats of sheer polish, and a glossy topcoat. Always finish with cuticle oil and a hand serum, once the nails are dry to the touch, for extra hydration.

Dazzle Dry Nail Lacquer in Mind Your Mani

Manucurist Active Glow Raspberry Jelly Nail Polish

To keep your naked mani looking clean and fresh, regularly hydrating your hands with a rich cream is a must. Our pick: Prada Hand Cream. Ventura suggests applying nail oil frequently to help keep the nails flexible so that the polish doesn’t chip. “This also helps prevent hangnails and dry skin around the nails.”

There are ways to dress up a naked manicure while still staying true to its clean girl roots. Huber-Millet likes adding a chrome finish on top for a luminous sheen. You can also add a layer of micro shimmer polish for a soft, glazed look or consider a milky jelly polish for a high-shine, translucent look.

The goal of a naked manicure is perfectly groomed nails that boast the slightest hint of bare color. Perfect for wearing year-round, naked-looking nails are like the equivalent of a basic white t-shirt, making them a classic, versatile, must-have staple manicure.

Perry previously shared photos with Trudeau to mark her 42nd birthday, revealing they went on a trip together. “Climbed to level 42 this week!” she wrote on October 29. “Was feeling indifferent about the inbetweeness of age 42…Then it was explained to me that 42 is actually the answer to everything. Though I still don’t understand, I’m ok with turning 42 as long as I can turn 42 with you ♥️ back to living…”

Perry and Trudeau have been dating for more than a year. In September, the singer called him the love of her life in an interview with People.

She looked back on her past year of healing, telling the outlet, “I learned how to step back into my purpose, and I got the greatest gift from this [Lifetimes] Tour: I got to meet the love of my life.”

Reflecting on her feelings just before meeting the former Canadian prime minister, she said, “I always wanted this epic, legendary love, and I was talking to my therapist about it: Everything in my life is epic, but this is kind of the missing puzzle piece—then it showed up.”

She also opened up about her boyfriend’s support of her music career, saying, “He knows the words, he’s supportive, and he’s in awe; it’s super healing. He is really heart-centered, and I think that we align in that way. I’m so grateful.”

#6775. At the Frick Collection, Louis Vuitton Finds Itself Among the Masters

The French house’s sponsorship of the Frick includes a fashion show and a landmark exhibition of Italian bronzes.

Above: Louis Vuitton kicked off a three-year partnership with New York’s Frick Museum with its cruise show in May.

Bright lights go up, Peaches’ “Boys Wanna Be Her” starts pounding, and a girl wearing layers of denim begins strutting past such luminaries as Zendaya, Chloë Sevigny, and Ava DuVernay. In many ways a normal New York fashion event—except the rooms are adorned with Renaissance paintings, Qing Dynasty vases, and 19th-century gilded French furniture.

The exalted surroundings are in fact the galleries of the Frick Collection, the Gilded Age treasure trove that was recently reenvisioned with the help of Elle Decor A-List architect Annabelle Selldorf. The fashion, music, and glamour are courtesy of Louis Vuitton, which has made a tradition of working with cultural institutions and heritage sites. The French house kicked off a three-year sponsorship of the Frick with this show in May, and now the first exhibition with the company’s support is open: a landmark show of Italian bronze sculptural masterpieces.

The reliefs, figurines, medals, and candelabra were drawn from collections as wide-ranging as Dresden, London, Washington, and Siena, the focus of the show. Donatello’s tomb of the Bishop of Grosseto, a life-size traffic stopper of a slab, timeworn yet still lyrical, is worth a visit alone, as is the miniature, gilded zinc brass relief of Bellerophon and the Chimera by Francesco di Giorgio. In an era of endless swiping, the lesson of the Chimera—and of these timeless bronzes—endures: be wary of desire’s fast fulfillment. Instead, wander into the rooms and stay a while.

This story originally appeared in the November 2026 issue of ELLE Decor.

#6774. All the Times Robert Pattinson Basically Manifested Becoming the Next James Bond

Robert Pattinson has officially received his license to kill. As James Bond, that is. Hollywood’s favorite leading man was announced as the next 007 on Monday, November 16, after Puck News reported that he screen-tested for the role in the eleventh hour.

“James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honor of a lifetime,” Robert wrote in a statement, per ABC News. “To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement. I couldn’t be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team.”

As it turns out, Robert has unknowingly manifested the role of a lifetime throughout his banger-after-banger career. No, seriously—R-Patz locked into Ariana Grande as Galinda-levels of manifesting here, whether he believes it or not.

Even after all these years as a Twihard, I’m genuinely shocked at how much this man was asked about potentially playing the famous spy. So, for the sake of your scrolling time, I’ve rounded up all the times Robert Pattinson manifested his role as James Bond, right here.

All roads lead back to Twilight. Robert got his big break playing swoonworthy sparkly vampire Edward Cullen in the film franchise, and the first movie lowkey predicted his current role as 007. Don’t believe me? Check out this scene.

When Bella’s friend group discusses the school’s upcoming Monte Carlo prom theme, Eric says, “Gambling, tuxedos, and Bond, James Bond,” before the camera cuts to Edward and Bella stepping out of his car.

Robert starred alongside another Bond, Pierce Brosnan, in 2010’s Remember Me. While doing press for the movie, he was constantly asked whether he’d want to take on the iconic role at some point.

During an interview with Fandango, he admitted that he would “quite like to play a villain in a Bond film.”

“That would be fun,” he continued. “Or maybe a male, like, Bond girl. A Bond boy.”

The BBC separately asked if he’d be into the role, to which he sheepishly responded, “Oh, I don’t know. That’s quite big shoes to fill. If I did it right now, it’d probably be pretty bad. Pretty embarrassing.”

He remained humble at the time, but fast forward 16 years, and he’s officially been cast as 007 himself!

The Bond questions kept coming after Remember Me, though Daniel Craig had led the franchise since 2005.

During an interview with Shortlist, Rob said he was open to taking on the role in the future.

“Yeah definitely, but more like 20 years,” he said. “I think there’d be nothing worse than, like, ‘Let’s get a fresh-faced Bond!’ That would be the worst idea in the world. After Daniel Craig, you have to have some baggage. It would be ridiculous to reinvent [him] as some young posh kid. Or, if [he] was, I’d have to get so tortured in the first few scenes. I’d have to do the first film with one arm or something.”

In a separate conversation with the BBC, Rob was asked about the role again, responding, “Why do you keep asking me this? There already is a James Bond. I don’t know. I mean, I love James Bond. So, I don’t know.”

Okay, so this technically wasn’t spoken prophecy from R-Patz, but someone previously tied to another Bond project expressed interest in seeing the actor take on the famous role.

Danny Boyle, who was originally tapped to direct the last Bond movie, No Time to Die, told The Guardian that while he watched Robert’s flick High Life, “I was sitting there thinking: ‘Oh my God, they should get him to be the next Bond.’”

#6773. A Kitchen in Bloom: How Tiffany Howell and Miele Reimagine the Heart of the Home

Eschewing conventional design for an moody, romantic kitchen, this wildly glamorous space proves that high-tech convenience can foster intimacy, slowness, and the art of living well.

When Tiffany Howell of Night Palm Interiors designs a home, her vision transcends conventional norms, veering into an ethereal realm—an approach she calls “the poetry of place.” In Howell’s mind, film, fashion, and music are as essential as decorative art, and she uses these inspirations to create theatrical spaces that ignite all the senses—layering texture, sound, scent, light, and form to evoke deep emotion. When executed with this level of intention, a room becomes an environment you don't merely look at but fundamentally feel.

When Miele partnered with Howell to create a dream kitchen for an installation at Art Basel, she seized the opportunity to reimagine what a kitchen can be. The result is the interactive 360-degree rendering seen here—a wildly imaginative digital environment that inspired the brand’s upcoming physical installation at Miami’s premier art fair. “I wanted an undeniable sexiness, a beautiful, sensory experience,” she says. “I created the space with characters in mind that I’d invite to a dinner party in this kitchen.” After all, the kitchen is a home’s heartbeat, an interactive space with multiple purposes.

“I do think the kitchen is really one of the most tender rooms in the house,” Howell says. She leaned into that romance by installing black cabinetry with blossoming branches and birds in iridescent greens and pinks. The cabinets are an homage to her love of 1920s chinoiserie furniture and fashion, seen through a very glamorous, Los Angeles lens. That California focus also meant bringing the outdoors in. The grand conservatory space harnesses diffused, natural light with the promise of the scent of jasmine wafting into the room. Howell’s ideal playlist sets the tone with jazz greats and ambient synth-pop.

“I wanted to create a kitchen that’s a completely sensory experience,” Howell explains. “The sound of a crackling warm fireplace, the aroma of a meal cooked for loved ones, or of making coffee in the morning.” For Howell, these aren't incidental details; they are the sensory architecture that turns raw space into lived emotion. In Howell’s view, this kitchen is “also a place where you can take a nap, read a book, or write in your journal. Every moment in this room can become a ritualistic experience of living well.”

When it came to the practical needs of a kitchen, Howell used Miele as a muse, an invitation to eschew the pale minimalism so common in luxury kitchens. “The appliances are so elegant, they kind of act as the jewelry of the room,” she says. “And their functionality and ease of operation give you back time to live better, relax with a drink, hang out with family and friends, and create the stories that make up a life.”

Consider the Miele Built-In Coffee System and wine cooler in matching dark finishes which are nearly camouflaged so the technology reads more as furniture than appliance. That tension between heirloom design and high-tech styling becomes a unified part of a lived-in, well-collected home. Accent pieces, including a vintage Fortuny pendant lamp over the kitchen island, and upholstered chairs in the conservatory with detailing reminiscent of antique lingerie, create a moody environment well suited to Miele's black-finished lines that resemble rich obsidian.

The 36” Full Surface Induction Cooktop features a frameless, flush design that disappears into a dark-veined countertop. Transforming the entire glass surface into one expansive cooking area, it fits up to six pots or pans at once and with Intelligent Pan Recognition and SmartSelect White controls seamlessly transfer power settings wherever pans are moved. On the same wall is the 30” Handleless Combi-Steam Oven XXL, with DualSteam technology that emanates ASMR sounds of steam cooking, and a black glass façade that resembles a framed panel or window. From the cool, flush glide of the induction cooktop to the whisper-quiet hum of precision steam, the technology engages the senses rather than interrupting them, turning modern convenience into an intuitive, tactile ritual. Rather than breaking up the wall with a stack of conspicuous appliances, these seamless integrations keep the architecture artful. And for added convenience, Miele’s elegant touch controls are enhanced with Wi-Fi connectivity for an easier user experience.

Howell’s concealment of technology is exhibited in her use of the 42” French Door Refrigerator with its elongated custom handles and a dark lacquered paneled front that echoes the floral chinoiserie motifs—an unconventional solution that turns a mundane appliance into a piece of decorative art. Once the refrigerator doors are open, the Brilliant Light Pro illumination makes it easy to survey the food inside the large capacity interior.

“How do you nurture yourself and others in the kitchen?” Howell asks. Her answer: a design that creates a restorative space evoking intimacy and slowness, where technology can encourage a lightness and give us back more time. By composing every sight, surface, scent, and sound into a single harmonious narrative, Howell proves that a kitchen shouldn't just be an aesthetic statement—it should be something you feel in your bones. “What excites me is building a new world with more possibilities,” Howell says. “I don’t think I could design any other way.”

Kate brought a colorful wardrobe for the mini trip with her husband. She made her first public appearance this morning in a fresh pistachio-green blazer from Veronica Beard, and then changed into a bright cobalt-blue dress from Roksanda.

#6763. Daydream’s New AI Agent Can Shop for You While You Sleep

Daydream wants to become a personal stylist in your pocket. The AI-powered fashion discovery platform, launched in 2025 by former Stitch Fix executive Julie Bornstein, is introducing a 24/7 AI shopping agent that can learn consumers’ tastes, assemble outfits and purchase products on their behalf — even while they sleep.

The new agent, which shoppers can chat with through Daydream’s app or by texting it directly via SMS, marks an evolution from the conversational fashion search engine the company launched just over a year ago. It can remember previous exchanges, put together complete outfits, offer virtual try-ons using an uploaded photograph and handle the steps leading up to checkout.

During an exclusive preview, co-founder and chief brand officer Lisa Yamner asks the agent to resume shopping for an upcoming trip to Mexico. Remembering her plans, it asks a few questions before assembling looks for beachfront dinners, complete with dresses, shoes and bags. Yamner swaps between pieces, tries them on using a virtual version of herself and uploads an influencer’s Instagram image to find similar items.

“Once you express a need or an interest, it can shop while you sleep,” Yamner explains. Shoppers can leave the agent to monitor products for price drops or continue working on a shopping request in the background, rather than repeatedly checking themselves. Any purchase still requires their approval. “We firmly believe that shopping doesn’t have to be a task, but there are parts of it that become that.” The aim is to take the drudgery out of shopping without losing the pleasure of discovery, she says.

At launch, the agent can shop across Daydream’s existing network of roughly 350 brand and retail partners, spanning more than 10,000 brands and three million products. Shoppers can ask it to purchase an item on their behalf, or check out directly with the retailer.

It comes as OpenAI, Instinct and Meta double down on shopping as a core use case and revenue stream for their newly launched ‘always on’ agents, and fashion retailers are now racing to build their own agents. Last week, Zalando announced plans for an AI agent that will purchase products on customers’ behalf from other retailers as well as its own catalog, from 2027. Meanwhile, brands including Ralph Lauren and J.Crew are building out their own branded AI shopping assistants, with J.Crew partnering with Anthropic on its new AI “Style Advisor”. Last month, Prada became the first luxury brand to launch an official plugin within OpenAI’s ChatGPT.

Daydream's answer is to sell its fashion expertise. The company has developed an internal “fashion knowledge graph” to enrich the information attached to products in its catalog, while human stylists help shape the agent’s recommendations. It recently appointed Francesca Sully as its first “stylist in residence”, tasked with teaching the technology to think more like a stylist and keep pace with trends.

Daydream recently appointed Francesca Sully as its first “stylist in residence”, tasked with teaching the AI agent to think more like a human stylist and keep pace with trends. Photo: Courtesy of Daydream.

Its founders believe a general-purpose AI agent, however sophisticated, will struggle to replicate the nuances of personal style. It comes back to the central question haunting fashion AI: can it mimic taste?

“We feel like a generalized agent is just not going to get fashion right,” Bornstein tells Vogue Business in an exclusive interview alongside co-founder Lisa Yamner. “Style is so nuanced. It relates to some very specific things that matter. So we need to know the right questions to ask, but also understand the product catalog of every brand out there — not just the price points, but also what the aesthetic of a brand world is, and how to connect that to other brands that align with that aesthetic and may be of interest.”

That expertise is also intended to help shoppers discover unfamiliar labels: approximately 97% of searches on Daydream contain no brand name, according to Bornstein. But in an increasingly crowded market, can that fashion expertise stand up as an independent AI shopping offering against the mass convenience of frontier AI agents and trusted retailers’ owned product catalogs?

When Daydream debuted last year, its proposition was to solve one of fashion e-commerce’s enduring frustrations: finding the right product across a fragmented universe of brands and retailers. Its conversational search engine allowed shoppers to describe what they wanted in natural language, rather than relying on conventional keywords and filters, encouraging users to “say more” about what they sought.

Although Daydream had already positioned itself around the idea of an AI agent, what it lacked was the ability to deliver the more involved, personalized service its founders envisaged — agents in their current form didn’t actually exist.

“We’ve been wanting to build from day one, but it took us a while to get there for a couple of reasons: one was that the agentic technology wasn’t yet there, and two is that the first version of the platform helped us really understand what consumers were looking for and what they wanted from an AI shopping assistant,” Bornstein says, explaining that Daydream was finding its original product couldn’t deliver the level of assistance shoppers wanted. Shoppers were asking very specific questions to find products for a need that included an occasion and their body type, and Daydream was showing them a page of search results, “when what they really wanted was more tailored help,” Bornstein adds. Conversational search might make finding fashion products easier, but it doesn’t necessarily solve the more subjective problem of deciding what to wear.

Bornstein recalls a similar challenge at her previous company, The Yes, where shoppers struggled to move beyond the conventions of traditional search. “We tried to get people to search by telling us a need and they would say, ‘Oh, I need a red dress for a Valentine’s Day party. I want to look sexy, but age-appropriate.’ And then you’d say, ‘Great, go ahead and type it into the search part.’ But then they would type in ‘red dress’, because their trust in search working was so low, and there was no mental model of being able to give a more detailed prompt.”

ChatGPT helped change that behavior, she says, making consumers more comfortable describing their needs in detail — and helping users understand how to use a product like Daydream. “Consumer expectations have started to change and people now understand what an agent is in a way they definitely didn’t two years ago when we started and no one understood what we were talking about,” Bornstein says.

The platform says it has amassed more than 2 million users since its June 2025 launch, with millennial women its largest audience, followed by Gen X and Gen Z. Bornstein describes two overlapping groups: fashion-savvy shoppers who appreciate having thousands of brands in one place, and time-poor consumers seeking more direction. But Daydream won’t disclose how many of its 2 million shoppers return or make purchases, making it difficult to gauge whether initial curiosity is translating into increased sales.

It comes just a week after Zalando announced an adjacent offering — a new AI agent feature, Zalando Extended, that will allow shoppers to discover and buy products from other third-party retailers without leaving the Zalando app, available from 2027. The European multibrand platform has 63 million active customers, extensive brand relationships and years of purchase and sizing data — assets that a much younger shopping platform like Daydream can’t easily replicate. Yet Bornstein argues the two companies are targeting different markets — Zalando solely operates in Europe, while Daydream is focused solely on the US. She also says the US retail landscape’s department stores and multibrand retailers generally have “more curated assortments”.

“The fact Zalando is going outside its own catalog makes a lot of sense because they’ve always tried to be extremely broad and like the higher-end ‘Amazon of fashion’ in Europe,” Bornstein argues.

But geography offers only a partial defence in a market where frontier AI models like ChatGPT and Claude are developing shopping capabilities that could eventually reach consumers across multiple countries, and gain more sophisticated fashion knowledge, via direct brand plugins like ChatGPT’s recently launched Prada plugin.

Asked what Daydream can offer that a much larger retailer can’t, Bornstein points to its first-mover advantage as the first cross-brand conversational search tool that’s “properly entrenched in fashion”, and the two years of data and prompts it’s collected from fashion-savvy consumers in that time. “I would also say we are solely focused on this,” she adds. “Having worked for other larger companies before in my past, I know how hard it is to build something like this on the side.”

There is also competition from fashion brands themselves. Ralph Lauren’s Ask Ralph and the launch of J.Crew’s new AI stylist last week suggest that brands increasingly want to provide personalized guidance within their own shopping environments.

Yet Bornstein says these brand-owned stylists can sit alongside Daydream’s ambitions. “When we launched originally, many brands asked us if we could build this AI agent for their sites,” she says. “And what we said to them is our initial goal is to have one place for consumers to go and see all brands — without having 10 tabs open.”

Daydream has also expanded into providing its technology to brands. Around eight brand sites are currently using its conversational search technology, Yamner says, and the company plans to bring some of its new agentic capabilities to those partners.

“Our feeling is if you know the brand and you go straight to the brand, there’s no reason why you wouldn’t want tools to help you shop that brand as effectively as you can,” Bornstein says. “So we’ll evolve the agentic product that we provide to brand sites to map to our core product, as it’s very portable to single brands too. But we are fundamentally focused on the B2C experience — it just also happens to work for B2B.”

One of Daydream’s potentially most valuable assets is the information it gathers from the way consumers describe their shopping needs. Traditional e-commerce search data might tell a brand that shoppers are searching for dresses or shoes. Conversational search can reveal the occasion, aesthetic and practical requirements behind those searches, as well as details like whether shoppers are searching for particular past collaborations or archive pieces — valuable data for brands’ product development and merchandising decisions, Bornstein says.

“That’s been the single best thing I think we’ve done for the industry over the last year — being able to surface really valuable and different insights for them, especially catalog intent,” she says, adding that they’ve found the same shopper tends to be entering complex conversational queries on Daydream but still be searching ‘red dress’ on brands’ own DTC sites. For brands, that information could can offer a more granular understanding of what customers want and why. For Daydream, it also creates a potential advantage over competitors that lack the same volume of detailed fashion-related prompts.

But the next stage of its personalization strategy requires shoppers to share considerably more. Daydream is developing integrations with Gmail and Google Calendar so its new AI agent can access this customer data and allow it to identify upcoming occasions and learn about previous purchases and marketing email subscriptions. Shoppers will soon also be able to share Pinterest boards with the agent to communicate their style preferences.

Users can set Daydream’s new AI agent tasks, like price comparison and stock checks, that it can carry out 24/7, even while they sleep. Photo: Courtesy of Daydream.

Daydream also operates on a commission model, yet Bornstein insists that commercial relationships won’t influence what the agent recommends — and it’s not pursuing advertising within the agent, at least for now. “There are no commercial incentives that go into what shows up for the customer,” she says. “Whatever they buy, we receive the same level of commission. So we are completely agnostic in what we’re showing and it’s about the customer’s preferences.” Brands will continue to receive customer information when purchases are completed through Daydream.

While Daydream is investing in a more complex and personalized experience, it’s not disclosed the conversion or retention figures needed to assess how effectively that experience translates into repeat purchasing. But Bornstein and Yamner remain convinced that fashion requires a different approach from the general-purpose agents increasingly being developed to manage everyday tasks.

“We’re watching the direction that the tech and customers are moving in, and we’re trying to get out ahead of it,” Yamner says. “We’re trying to say we get it. We get that this is what the customer’s expectations are going to become.”

After posting the breakup announcement, Ty spoke with People about the split—and admitted it’s been “tough” watching SLOMW: OC knowing they’re no longer a couple.

#6760. Robert Pattinson Is the James Bond Millennials Deserve

The 40-year-old actor has been chosen to become the seventh James Bond in film, following in the footsteps of Daniel Craig

The news is finally out: Robert Pattinson is the next James Bond. After weeks of speculation and an almost algorithmic audition process that played out on our social feeds, Pattinson has triumphed over a list of peers that reportedly included Nicholas Hoult, Callum Turner, and Josh O’Connor.

For the last few weeks, I’ve watched the rolling news coverage of the casting process with trepidation, because the concept of a machismo-fueled, womanizing killing machine feels tired and outdated in 2026. But that’s exactly why the choice of Pattinson made me breathe a sigh of relief. Since breaking out in the 2000s,Pattinson’s career has been defined by his willingness to subvert traditional masculine archetypes, crafting them instead into slightly twisted leading-man roles. From his starring role in 2022’s The Batman to the 2026 rom-com The Drama and most recently the disturbing Oscar-tipped biopic Primetime, he has often looked for ways to subvert our expectations of the classic leading man. If there’s one actor who just might be able to make 007 feel aspirational and relevant again, it’s him.

From the beginning, Pattinson, who first emerged as a teen icon in the Twilight movies, has represented a counter-argument to traditional, protein-based masculinity. “Team Edward” and “Team Jacob,” the franchise’s central romantic rivalry (and marketing ploy), offered two very different visions of male desirability. Jacob, played by Taylor Lautner, was part man, part wolf, and was muscular, physically imposing, and (thankfully) almost always shirtless, which today draws more of a visual parallel with the sort of hypermasculinity that has flourished in online gym-bro culture and the so-called “manosphere.” And then there was Edward, Pattinson’s pale, brooding vampire who was more sensitive and emotionally tortured. With the selection of a new Bond, it feels like we’re once again seeing this masculine power struggle play out—and again, it’s Pattinson who has come out on top.

In the packed field of chiseled, handsome, talented actors who were vying for this role, whoever snagged it was always going to have his work cut out. As an archetype, 007 is a relic of generations gone by. The flashy gadgets, the signature martini, the expensive cars, and the ability to charm almost any woman belong to a very particular, nostalgic vision of masculinity. Through a more contemporary lens, Bond is the ultimate masculine drag act: an exaggerated, prop-heavy performance that is just as likely to be viewed as regressive and cliché.

We see the same trend in Bond’s dwindling romantic appeal. In our grandparents’ generation, when the character was at peak aspiration, a man arriving in a nice suit, carrying flowers, and driving a flashy car was considered a catch. But today, the dynamics have changed. I recently read The Project, the debut novel by British Vogue columnist Annie Lord, where she makes the observation that many of the most common dating “icks” now stem from men trying too hard: putting themselves out there too much, making an overt display of their interest, or seeming too confident. Lord notes that we’ve become accustomed to viewing these qualities as undesirable or embarrassing, which draws clear parallels with Bond, whose entire appeal has rested on this sort of performance. The spy’s extravagance and his carefully cultivated image were once what made him attractive, but can you imagine going on a date with a guy who seriously asks for his martini to be “shaken, not stirred”? You’d probably tell your group chat about it and endlessly mock him.

Looking more widely, there is also the question of whether the Bond franchise’s particular type of escapism can still work in the fraught world we’re currently living in. The franchise once offered a fantastical vision of evil, with megalomaniacs plotting world domination in ways that felt almost comically removed from reality. (Remember Bond’s “invisible” car in 2002’s Die Another Day?) But now, the real world feels uncomfortably close to that fantasy. Billionaires wield the kind of influence once reserved for nation-states, and the increasingly overt relationship between money and power makes it harder to distinguish the Bond villain caricature from what we’re encountering in day-to-day life.

Part of the reason Pattinson landed this role, I suspect, is that he already has experience in navigating nostalgic expectations and present-day anxieties. In The Batman, for example, he proved his ability to bring new dimensions to an old-school character with his tortured take on Bruce Wayne. And as a versatile actor who can move between action blockbusters, rom-coms, and critically acclaimed projects like Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, he has the star power and the credibility to give Bond a millennial makeover.

It’s worth saying that during Daniel Craig’s tenure as Bond, considerable effort was made to turn Bond into a deeper, more considered character. Craig’s films explored Bond’s childhood trauma and alcohol dependence, and they also introduced female characters who were more than just a sidekick or a throwaway romantic interest. But in the five years since Craig departed, a loud and unrepentant misogyny has taken hold in corners of the internet. And from the Epstein files to the Cornell University rape allegations and, most recently, the conviction of Russell Brand, so many stories come back to the central issue of toxic masculinity.

The wider conversation about male behavior has made casting the next Bond feel strangely high-stakes, which is probably why every screen test seemed to be leaked and endlessly dissected online. And it’s also why I’m relieved that they’ve picked an actor who might be able to make Bond a little more strange. Pattinson presents the opportunity to take Bond in a different direction—one that finally frees the character from the fantasies of the past.

#6759. Is Zalando’s New AI Agent a Blueprint for the Future of Retail?

What happens when a multibrand fashion retailer starts selling products it doesn’t stock? European e-commerce giant Zalando is joining the AI shopping agent race with plans to let shoppers buy from other retailers through its platform. Its new offering, Zalando Extended, will use AI agents to complete purchases on customers’ behalf, potentially transforming Zalando into a shopping gateway beyond its own catalog.

Zalando is testing the service with premium home and living retailer Westwing. Its products already appear in Zalando’s search and browsing results, but shoppers currently have to click through to Westwing’s website to buy them. From 2027, Zalando’s AI agent will handle those purchases on customers’ behalf, allowing them to check out without leaving the Zalando app.

Retailers can join through a relatively simple integration, providing something similar to an affiliate product feed and entering into an additional agreement with Zalando. The company has not disclosed what commission or fee, if any, it will earn from these transactions. It's a notable move for a retailer that has spent years building its own assortment and relationships with thousands of brands, from Gucci to Burberry and Jacquemus. But as the likes of OpenAI, Google and Meta race to make general-purpose personal AI agents, the battle is increasingly over who controls the customer relationship, rather than simply who stocks the product.

Zalando’s AI assistant currently helps shoppers purchase from the multibrand retailer’s product catalogue. Photo: Courtesy of Zalando.

Zalando’s response is to position itself on both sides of that coin. Its three-pronged strategy aims to make its own platform the first stop for fashion discovery, expand its assortment through external retailers and also reach shoppers through third-party AI agents. It plans to offer checkout within Google’s AI Mode and Gemini app when its agentic commerce launches in Europe, and has tested advertising inside ChatGPT in the UK.

This also places Zalando in competition with specialist AI shopping platforms such as Daydream, which also launched a new AI shopping agent this week. Both are betting that fashion requires expertise beyond that of general-purpose AI agents. While Daydream operates in the US and Zalando in Europe, the latter enters the race with a significant advantage in scale.

But for rival luxury and multibrand fashion retailers, Zalando’s AI strategy raises a bigger question: is the future of fashion e-commerce about selling your own assortment, or becoming the gateway to everyone else’s?

At the Web Summit conference in Lisbon, Vogue Business sat down with chief technology officer Graeme Smith to discuss the company’s ambitions and who stands to own the customer relationship in the age of AI agents.

Vogue: Why allow Zalando customers to buy products from other retailers through Zalando Extended?

Smith: We’ve got over 63 million active customers at Zalando, and through our Lifestyle AI [Zalando’s umbrella term for its AI-powered personalization technology], we’ve really got to know their preferences — the brands they like, the price points they shop at, the brand values like sustainability they look for, and how their needs change over time. We can use all this to create a personalized experience that can even become proactive.

So we thought, why limit ourselves? We already have our wholesale and partner platforms, but with AI agents, we’ve found a really lightweight way to bring in other retailers whose products you wouldn’t normally find on Zalando.

Our first partner is Westwing. Today, you can discover its products on Zalando and click through to buy them on Westwing. But early next year, you’ll be able to buy that sofa or lamp directly on Zalando, using your existing account and payment details, without leaving the app. We’ll buy it on your behalf.

Imagine how much more assortment across fashion and lifestyle we could offer this way, without stocking it ourselves. We can then build that into our personalization, learning more about customers’ interests beyond our existing catalog and helping them discover more products.

Vogue: With general-purpose AI agents increasingly capable of shopping on consumers’ behalf, are you competing directly with the likes of OpenAI, Google and Meta? Why would shoppers choose Zalando instead?

People are going to use a variety of agents, but our mission is always to make Zalando the best place to start the fashion and lifestyle shopping journey. That comes down to the customer experience we can provide that others can’t, which starts with data.

We’ve been using AI for over 15 years, including for personalized shopping recommendations, and we’ve invested heavily in size and fit. We get tens of thousands of body measurements a week, and we have so much data from customer returns about which items run small or large. So we’ve got over 10,000 size charts, and we’ve put AI on top of that. No third-party agent has got that. So if you care about getting the fit right the first time, Zalando’s agent will be the place to come.

We’ve also invested in recommending whole outfits based on our understanding of trends, how people shop for different occasions and years of customer behavior at scale.

Vogue: How quickly do you expect Zalando Extended to grow? Are you planning to onboard lots more retailers in the coming months, or is this more of a test-and-learn phase?

It’s a little bit of both. We’re testing and learning, but it’s not a particularly complex thing we’re doing, and we’re very excited by what we’ve seen so far. Assuming it’s successful, this has the potential to scale very fast because the integration is so lightweight.

Most of these retailers already produce an affiliate feed, which is essentially what we need. We can make the sign-up and operations very simple for them, and it’s very light for us too. So there’s potential to scale this massively.

Vogue: Trust is fundamental to AI agent adoption, and attitudes vary between markets. Why would consumers trust Zalando Assistant more than a general-purpose AI agent?

Zalando is a brand that people trust, and we’ve worked very hard to earn that trust. The company has just turned 18, and we’ve built that trust through how we look after the customer experience, including how we handle their data. We’re a European company, so the data we hold is subject to high European standards for data protection.

We’ve seen customers enthusiastically adopt Zalando Assistant. Interestingly, questions about what we know about them haven’t been a big part of the conversation — people have just started using it. We’ve had 22 million customers engage with Zalando Assistant this year, including 13 million in the last quarter.

Customers are twice as likely to buy something in a session where they use Zalando Assistant compared with one where they don’t. And of course, we have all the consent mechanisms required in Europe. Customers can also request that their data be deleted.

Graeme Smith, Zalando’s CTO. Photo: Courtesy of Zalando.

Vogue: Is there a risk that Zalando could lose its direct relationship with customers by bringing other retailers onto its platform?

No, we don’t think of it like that. We want people to come to Zalando more and more, and for it to be the place where they start their shopping journey. We’ve got 70% organic traffic, which is very high, and we work hard to maintain that.

We think we can do that by building really great experiences tailored to fashion and lifestyle shopping. Bringing in more retailers actually gives people more reasons to come to Zalando, because they know they can access a wider variety of products. They can buy a sofa on Zalando, as well as everything else. So we think this could actually drive more traffic.

Now, could someone go directly to Westwing to buy their next sofa? Of course, and that’s fine. We don’t sell sofas on Zalando. What matters is that we’re the best place to discover fashion and lifestyle products, wherever they come from.

Vogue: You’re also piloting advertising in ChatGPT and preparing to participate in Google’s Universal Commerce Protocol. How does that fit with your ambition to make Zalando the starting point for shopping?

There are three strands to our strategy. The first is getting people to keep coming back to Zalando as the best place to start their shopping journey. The second is what we call inbound agentic commerce, and the third is Zalando Extended, which allows us to massively expand the assortment available through outbound agentic commerce.

Inbound agentic commerce is what most people talk about when they discuss AI shopping agents. People are using ChatGPT, Google’s AI-powered search and other platforms. We had to decide early on how we felt about that, and we saw it as an opportunity. Our customers are going to use these services anyway, so we want Zalando to be there and meet them where they are. We also want to reach new customers.

We’ve become very good at generative engine optimisation (GEO) — we’re the number one fashion destination in Europe referred to by AI agents. But we haven’t stopped at organic visibility. We’ve also piloted advertising inside ChatGPT in the UK, and we’re now looking at the results and deciding where to go next.

With Google, it’s even more interesting. When Google launches agentic commerce in Europe, Zalando will be there from the start. Customers will be able to discover Zalando products and even check out within Google if they want to.

But they’ll still need a Zalando account. That’s very important to us. We want to engage with these AI platforms on our own terms and maintain the customer relationship.

Vogue: Fashion shopping is often emotional and highly considered. Do you think consumers will really want to complete purchases through AI agents, rather than visiting a retailer’s website?

We don’t know how this is going to play out. I’m very excited by it, but fashion is very personal and emotional.

What we see is that when customers arrive at Zalando from another channel, whether that’s an AI agent, Instagram or TikTok, they often don’t buy the item they landed on. They explore three or four more products, look at similar items and browse around before making a purchase.

It’s another signal that fashion is different, it’s a high-consideration purchase. So if I had to bet — and it’s always difficult to make predictions — I think people will use agents to research products, but they’ll still want to click through to the retailer, like Zalando, to ask: is this item quite right for me? What more can I learn about it? What similar products are available? And then maybe they’ll buy from there, but let’s see.

#6755. Florence Pugh Shimmers in a Sculpted Blue Gown at ELLE's Women in Hollywood Event

ELLE Women in Hollywood honoree Florence Pugh chose a stunning, timeless look for ELLE’s Women in Hollywood event at the Four Seasons Hotel in Beverly Hills this evening. The Dune: Part Three actress wore a sculpted Ralph Lauren gown, accessorizing with Bulgari jewelry, including a gold statement choker.

When Pugh’s cover story dropped last week, she expressed her delight at being recognized alongside such incredible actresses.

“This has been a true honor being selected by ELLE for their ‘Women in Hollywood,’” she wrote on Instagram. “I heard who else was a part of the lineup and gasped. I have watched and studied and practiced their lines. I have appreciated their words on and offscreen. To be in line with THESE INCREDIBLE TALENTS IS MAKING ME SQUEAL—Samantha Morton, Carrie Coon, Elizabeth Debicki, Penélope Cruz, Rosalind Eleazar, Julianne Moore, [and] Inde Navarrette. Congratulations, ladies! What a nice present 2026 gave us.”

In her interview, Pugh reflected on the lessons she’s learned over time working in the industry. “The thing that I’m getting better and better at is protecting myself,” she said. “Every time I work on a movie, I get more confident in the way that I can protect myself and the way that I can lead a film set, and just not stand for bullshit anymore. I’m not doing it. I’m not standing for bullshit behavior. I’m not standing for bullshit attitude. I’m not allowing for people to be rude to the crew. You just get bolder and bigger and more confident with time, and you want to be around and work with the right people. And the moment someone is making that vibe feel off, everybody feels it. I don’t want to deal with messy. It’s just about surrounding yourself with professionals who have the same way of working in mind: Show up on time, don’t be rude, don’t be a misogynist.”

#6754. What’s It Like to Be Tennis’s World Number One? Daniil Medvedev Lets Us Into the Club

The ATP Finals—the most important men’s tournament on the tennis calendar outside of the Grand Slams—kicked off on Sunday in Torino. Founded in 1970 as a season-ending competition pitting the highest-ranked players against each other, the current iteration features the world’s top eight men—Alexander Zverev, Carlos Alcaraz, Ben Shelton, Daniil Medvedev, Flavio Cobolli, Arthur Fils, Frances Tiafoe, and Rafael Jodar—facing each other first in a round-robin group format and then in elimination stages. (It’s similar in format to the women’s WTA Finals, which concluded Sunday in Indian Wells, with Mirra Andreeva taking home the big trophy.)

Ranking, of course, is everything—it’s what gets you invited to the finals—and the summa achievement of the world’s top ranking is the subject of a new book, ATP No. 1 Club: Icons of Men’s Tennis, just out from Phaidon. It features iconic photos of each number-one player since 1973—the men’s game has seen only 30, including Alcaraz, Zverev, and Medvedev—along with text by the late award-winning tennis writer Mark Hodgkinson.

We sat down with one of those iconic players—Medvedev, one of the five current or former number-ones still competing—to ask him, you know, what it’s like to do something better than anyone else in the world.

Vogue: Do you remember, from your earliest years playing tennis, who was number one at the time?

Daniil Medvedev: I started playing tennis when I was six, in 2002, but I was not yet a tennis fan, let’s say. By the time I started to understand tennis a bit more, Roger [Federer] was there already, and I think for most of my childhood it was Roger at number one, and then Rafa, who from time to time took the top spot. And then came Novak—who, as we know now, took the leading spot for a longer period of time. One time, years later, I made a game of it—I think I named, not all of them, probably 27 of them.

Did you have a tennis hero when you were a kid?

So I have to be honest here: I’m still probably a bit like this, but when I was young, whoever was winning too much—doesn’t matter which sport—I stopped liking them. I’m like, Okay, he’s only winning. So at one point I was supporting anyone against Roger—I don’t say it in a bad way, it’s just how I am. At one moment it was Barcelona with [their former coach] Pep Guardiola and they were beating everyone, and I was like, Okay—give us something new.

But it changed from tournament to tournament: I supported Marat [Safin in 2005] when he won the Australian Open. This was incredible—we, as kids in Russia, were waking up early in the morning to watch his matches. Andy Roddick—I loved his serve; sometimes I was copying it. Novak as well, when he just came in, before he started beating everyone and I was cheering for the underdog. I never had one hero.

When you were dreaming kid dreams, was it about winning Wimbledon or another tournament? Was being the world number one ever part of that?

I never was thinking about number one or a Grand Slam. Of course, when I grew up and started playing better tennis, those kind of goals came into place. But when I was really young, I remember hitting against the wall, and because the wall never misses, I was thinking that I’m playing against Roger, Rafa, Novak. I was trying to beat them, but of course you cannot beat the wall. Those were fun memories—and I think, probably, in the back of my mind, I knew that if I’m playing them, it means that I’m somewhere in the top rankings.

My dream was to become a great tennis player, and I feel like I achieved it. I’m happy about it: Every day you go to practice, you work hard, you fight for the matches, and you don’t think about it. But when I talk to someone like you and put myself back there, I’m like, I actually achieved my dream. It’s just that the dream constantly changes, because you want more.

Did you feel different when you first became the ATP number one player in 2022?

Yes and no. Maybe there’s a tiny bit more pressure and attention paid to you, but it’s also just such a nice feeling. I mean, you are the best in the whole world, and everyone else is just trying. And it was not easy, but I made it. [Medvedev became the first player outside the so-called Big Four—Djokovic, Federer, Nadal, and Murray—to hold the top ranking in 18 years.]

Did that put a kind of target on you that hadn’t been there before?

For sure, especially in the world we live in now, that happens. Whenever you lose: “Oh, he’s not good enough to be world number one.” But I didn’t care, because I’m like, “I’m number one,” and it felt so good. People would ask me after a loss, “Maybe the ranking put more pressure on you? Maybe that’s why you didn’t perform.” I’d just say, “Maybe yes,” but I didn’t care. It was such a good feeling. Anyone who has been there, I think, will tell you the same: It’s a nice feeling. I want to try to be there again, of course—it’s going to be super tough, especially with Carlos and Jannik [Sinner] winning so much.

Did people—either inside or outside of tennis—treat you differently when you were number one? Did things come to you more easily?

For sure, when I was the world number one—I was on a big stretch of winning the 2021 US Open, playing some Masters finals, winning some Masters—I got some, whatever you call it, invitations. I remember going to Los Angeles before Indian Wells after I became world number one, and I went to some restaurants and I would ask for the bill and they’re like, “Yes—someone took care of it.” So stuff like this—when you are world number one, people talk a bit more about you; you’re on TV more. These are things which come with, let’s call it fame, which also can have a downside: Some people do this kind of thing just for pleasure, but maybe someone else pays and thinks that you’re going to sit and talk to him for 30 minutes. And I don’t want to be obliged to do something because someone did something for me—that’s just how I live. Especially if I’m rushing somewhere, you know: I’m okay to pay, man. As I say, there are some upsides, some downsides. If you get invited to a football match and you meet some players, or a baseball match: fun.

Ah, game. Okay. I didn’t know this. In any case: I just enjoy life. I’m number one, I enjoy life. I’m number 10, I enjoy life.

This conversation has been edited and condensed.

#6750. The 8 Best Salicylic Acid Cleansers for Acne, According to Dermatologists

These sudsy picks are the first step to clearer skin.

We may earn commission from links on this page, but we only recommend products we love. Promise.

Oh, hi, hello! I'm assuming you've stumbled upon this page because (a) you'd do anything to cure your acne, and (b) there's an equally good chance you've f*cked with your face (see: red, inflamed skin) while trying to do so in the past. Well, allow me to introduce you to salicylic acid—the powerhouse chemical exfoliant that effectively clears out blackheads, whiteheads, and excess oil. The best and easiest way to start incorporating the ingredient into your skincare routine is with a salicylic acid cleanser.

Listen, as easy as it is to go to the drugstore and pick up a new salicylic acid cleanser, I encourage you to take a beat. While the ingredient is gentler than other acne remedies—like benzoyl peroxide—salicylic acid can still cause dryness and irritation for those with sensitive skin. It also comes in many different concentrations and formulas, so finding the right product for you and your skin type is important. That’s where I come in. I spent the last year testing the top salicylic acid cleansers to see how they reacted on my own skin, and consulted the pros on all the need-to-knows. (Hi, board-certified dermatologists Annie Chiu, MD, Lucy Chen, MD, Cheryl Burgess, MD, and Loren Krueger, MD!)

Keep reading for the full breakdown of the best salicylic acid cleansers—according to team Cosmo’s testing—along with tips from dermatologists on choosing the best salicylic acid cleansers, how to incorporate one into your skincare routine, and what to look for before you buy.

Why we love it: Sometimes simple is better—and that’s one of the many reasons why we fell in love with this daily acne cleanser. (It just won a Cosmopolitan Acne Award, FYI!) We especially appreciate that it addresses multiple types of breakouts, including stubborn cystic and hormonal acne, with 1 percent salicylic acid, making it gentle yet extremely effective.

One Cosmo editor says: “On the rare days I wash my face in the morning, I like a no-frills cleanser that’ll degrease whatever oils spewed onto my face overnight. This one, with 1 percent salicylic acid and anti-inflammatory zinc, does this flawlessly without making my skin feel tight.”—BETH GILLETTE, BEAUTY EDITOR

Why we love it: Alix Earle has been real AF about her acne journey, and we know she took the time to develop a line that truly works to address breakouts. All of team Cosmo is obsessed with Reale Actives, but especially this cleanser. This gets allllll the gunk out of pores for a deep clean that doesn’t feel stripping. It utilizes salicylic acid naturally found in willow bark extract, along with caprylol salicylic acid, an LHA, to gently refine texture. We noticed enhanced glow from the first use, and quickly added this to our permanent acne-fighting lineup.

One Cosmo editor says: “I’m familiar with BHA (aka salicylic acid), but LHA is new for me, and based on this cleanser, I think I love it. It chemically sloughs away dead skin to reduce clogged pores and bumpy texture, but it’s not too strong or intense for sensitive skin.”—BG

Why we love it: If you're new to chemical exfoliants or are sensitivity-prone and don't want to irritate your skin, this cleanser is a great starting point because it has a lower salicylic acid concentration. It still manages to clear out clogged pores without much effort, helping them look smaller in the long run. Dr. Chen recommends this three-in-one cleanser, saying it improves uneven skin tone, dullness, and helps prevent acne breakouts. "It is formulated with a soothing gel that calms and refreshes your skin, and it effectively cleanses without irritation," she says.

One Cosmo editor says: "This was my go-to cleanser for years (particularly immediately post-college). It really helps calm down and eliminate my acne, and it lasts a very long time."—BG

Why we love it: Although this cleanser smells like yummy, fresh pear juice, it's pretty damn tough on breakouts. The gel-to-foam formula is packed with 2 percent salicylic acid and lactic acid (which also happens to be brightening), as well as moisturizing lactobacillus ferment and soothing witch hazel. Consider it a triple threat that exfoliates, brightens, and moisturizes for happier, glowing skin.

One Cosmo editor says: "I've been a Sunday Riley fan since day one, and have been loyal to the acne line since it launched. There are four pieces in the collection—a mist, a serum, a retinol, and a cleanser, but the cleanser is by far my favorite. The jelly texture transforms into a fluffy foam to get rid of oil, makeup, and sunscreen, and the salicylic acid breaks down debris and dead skin cells. It's so good at keeping skin clear without causing irritation or dryness." —LAUREN BALSAMO, BEAUTY DIRECTOR

Why we love it: Salicylic acid may have a reputation for drying out skin, but this unique formula is one of the most hydrating exfoliating cleansers we’ve ever used. One Cosmo editor says: “I thought cleansers could either be moisturizing and soothing, or exfoliating and clarifying. Not both. But this fully proved me wrong—it foams up to a lovely lather that doesn’t dry out my skin yet definitely helps break down oil.” —BG

Why we love it: Almost every single dermatologist recommends this cleanser. A Cosmo expert says: “This cleanser is effective for those who struggle with blackheads and whiteheads, thanks to the 2 percent salicylic acid in the formula, which helps target excess oil and unclogs pores. One Cosmo editor says: "This probably my favorite face wash of all time, which is really saying a lot considering I’ve literally tested hundreds in my 10-year career as a beauty editor. The exfoliation comes from salicylic acid, but it’s honestly really gentle, you don’t need to worry about overdoing it, IMO. I love it for removing makeup, giving my skin a deep clean, and smoothing any bumpy, uneven texture."—LB

Why we love it: If you haven't heard of The Inkey List, you're seriously missing out. Not only are the products gaining an increasing amount of popularity, but they're also incredibly inexpensive.
