#6744. 8 Great Airbnbs in Marfa to Book for a Design-Forward Vacation

If you’re a design and art lover, Marfa is one of those places you need to see at least once. With about 1,800 residents, it’s a blink-and-you’ll-miss-it town in the high desert of West Texas, put on the map by the minimalist artist Donald Judd. Judd left New York for Marfa in the 1970s, bought buildings downtown, and later took over a decommissioned army post outside of town. He filled it with permanent installations, turning the town into a creative hub that continues to attract a steady stream of art-devoted acolytes.

But even those who aren’t chasing the museums or the Prada Marfa store will get something out of the town to love; the nature-driven traveler, for example, can find some of the best stargazing in the country. So whether your itinerary is packed with gallery visits or you plan on doing little more than watching the sun set from a porch, kick things off by booking an Airbnb in Marfa.

These eight spots offer just as much inspirational design as the town itself; here’s where to stay in Marfa for a memorable desert getaway.

Quite naturally, this home takes its cues from Donald Judd, with clean lines and furniture that leaves plenty of space around it. It’s laid out as three separate studios, each with its own entrance, bath, and walled patio, so a group of friends can come together but still have a quiet place to retreat. The main studio is anchored by a fireplace with a low sofa and two lounge chairs—ideal for cozy nights in—while the library studio has a vintage wood-burning stove and worktable. Judd’s work at the Chinati Foundation is minutes away and the Marfa Lights viewing area is a short drive.

Amenities: Private soaking pool, fireplace, wood-burning stove, full kitchen plus two kitchenettes, Starlink WiFi, pet friendly

In this beautiful two-bedroom rental, a large tumbleweed hangs from the ceiling of the sunroom and the floor-to-ceiling glass doors open onto Southwestern-style gardens. The desert theme is not subtle, but it is done in an elevated, tasteful way—right down to the limewashed walls that echo the tones and textures of the West Texas landscape.

Head outside to the private courtyard to discover an oversized chiminea; stay inside, and you’ll find a fireplace and a hi-fi record player. It sleeps a small group or a couple of friends, and the detached casita next door can be booked for bigger groups.

Amenities: Fireplace, outdoor chiminea,WiFi, flat top grill and smoker, AC, dog friendly

Built in 1937 and carefully restored, this Spanish Revival home keeps its original wood beams and plaster walls, but has been warmed up with textiles and Western artwork. From the pink kitchen to the blue tile that outlines the television, this is definitely a house where style leads.

In fact, each of the four bedrooms in the main house has its own flavor: the Library Suite is lined with books, the Treetop Suite looks out over the desert. A detached casita with its own king bed and kitchen sits across the property with an expansive outdoor area. The whole place sleeps 10 adults, which makes it great for a group trip. The living room, with its fireplace and roomy sofa, is where everyone is likely to end up after a day at the galleries, which are a short walk away.

Amenities: Fireplace, detached casita with kitchen, WiFi, dedicated workspace, AC, outdoor backyard

This solar-powered house sits alone across 1,000 acres of ranch land, with the Rio Grande at the edge of the property and Mexico on the horizon. There is a modern wood-burning stove inside which heats the living room, and both bedrooms have their own tiled baths and windows framing the view. It’s a true escape for two couples; or perhaps a writer who needs a distraction-free setting from which to work (especially since there’s no cell service, only a landline and internet). Chinati Hot Springs is 20 minutes away for a soak, and Big Bend Ranch State Park is about an hour off for mountain biking.

Amenities: Solar powered, wood-burning stove, chef’s kitchen with gas stove, outdoor grill, washer, internet and landline, outdoor TV

Few houses in Marfa get photographed as often as this 320-square-foot box on the edge of town. It looks like one of Donald Judd’s sculptures turned into a place to live—to see the real things, Judd’s concrete and aluminum works at the Chinati Foundation are a short walk away.

Downstairs is an open kitchen with a dining area and a walk-in shower; two doors open from the kitchen straight onto a shaded patio with outdoor dining. A steep staircase leads up to the bedroom, which juts out over the first floor and faces the desert. You can watch the sunrise from the queen bed, and a heated mattress pad helps on cold fall nights.

Amenities: Fire pit, shaded patio with outdoor dining and loungers, heated bed pad, full kitchen, walk-in shower

Attention, green thumbs: The garden here is so stunning, it’s been featured in four books. The hosts co-wrote a field guide to Chihuahuan Desert plants and have filled all 1.25 acres of the property with native plantings and walking trails. The outdoors is very much the focus here: This casita is a 500-square-foot room, with a kitchenette and large covered porches that look out to the garden and mountains. Its al fresco appeal extends after hours, too. McDonald Observatory has certified the property as night-sky friendly, so after dark you can see even the Milky Way from the porch.

Amenities: Covered porch, native garden with walking trails, kitchenette (induction cooktop, convection toaster oven, microwave)

Most of the action at this Marfa adobe happens out back, under a big pergola with climbing vines, two long outdoor sofas, and many areas to sit and gather. Indoors, rooms are filled with bold paintings and modern furnishings like a low curved sofa in chocolate brown, worn leather armchairs, an iron chandelier that hangs over a white brick fireplace, and a cute checkerboard floor kitchen. Downtown is within walking distance, so you can stroll to galleries and dinner and come back to a fire.

Amenities: Fireplace, covered pergola patio with outdoor lounge and dining, dedicated workspace, WiFi, AC

If you’re coming to Marfa for a milestone birthday or special event, book this place for the barn alone. It’s a historic 1,250-square-foot space with room for a large dinner or party. The home itself was newly renovated to include a cook’s kitchen, a gym, and two king bedrooms—all set under 10-foot ceilings. Best of all, you’ll be just a short walk from downtown, and since dogs are welcome, you can extend the guest list to the whole family.

Amenities: AC, dedicated workspace, barn for events, gym, WiFi, pet-friendly

#6743. GQ’s Men of the Year Dinner May Have Found the Next James Bond

Cocktail hour was drawing to a close; the traditional pre-party dinner for the 31st edition of GQ’s legendary Men of the Year event, presented by Johnnie Walker Blue Label, was about to kick off. GQ’s Designer of the Year, Celine’s Michael Rider, and our Director of the Year, Denis Villeneuve, were already posted up inside the Chateau Marmont’s lobby lounge; the guests lingering just past the entrance included Odysseus himself, Matt Damon, building with his Ocean’s partner-in-crime Don Cheadle before pivoting to greet Chris Rock—like Damon, one of GQ’s three Men of the Year issue cover stars. (Andrew Garfield, subject of that third cover, had rolled in a few minutes earlier, resplendently coiffed, immediately gathering his After the Hunt co-star Ayo Edebiri and director Luca Guadagnino into a reunion hug.)

But among the Men of the Year veterans in attendance—like Rock, who scored his first MOTY cover in 1999, circa Bigger and Blacker—there were also plenty of first-timers from the new class of news-makers and paradigm-shakers celebrated in GQ’s 2026 Breakouts portfolio. And that varied mix—of longtime icons and undeniable up-and-comers, from Owen Thiele and Inde Navarette to I Play Rocky’s Anthony Ippolito and electro-rock duo Fcukers—made for a veritable particle accelerator of improbable collisions.

Chicken Shop Date’s Amelia Dimoldenberg in deep confab with Tinashe. Tony’s Stavros Halkias in an across-the-table comedy summit with Chris Rock. Journalist Pablo Torre, whose reporting on Kawhi Leonard and the LA Clippers salary-cap shenanigans shook the NBA, engrossed in conversation with GQ’s own Zach Baron and Villeneuve, who’d just signed off on the prints—for real this time—for his third and final Dune movie, soon to shake the walls of nearly every IMAX theater on Earth.

And Villeneuve wasn’t the only auteur on hand: Between the Dune mastermind, Misty Green writer/director/star Rock, Club Kid’s similarly slashed Jordan Firstman, the La Bola Negra writer-directors jointly known as Los Javis (Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrosi) and Guadagnino, who upon arriving had almost immediately located a cinematically moody lamplit corner to hold court in, the Chateau’s lobby was, quipped GQ Global Editorial Director Adam Baidawi, “an incredible room to be an out-of-work actor in.”

Because journalism doesn’t take a night off—not even GQ’s biggest night—Baidawi also tried, during his opening remarks, to pry some info regarding the identity of the new James Bond (off the record, just between us) out of Villeneuve.

As the director politely demurred—hey, we had to try—another guest piped up from across the table. “Wait,” said Matt Damon, as Baidawi passed the former superspy the mic. “I have a question. Just a thought experiment. What if James Bond were older? And American?” (In the unlikely event that Damon just booked a second iconic-superspy role, you heard it here first.)

Toast time was upon us: Rosalind Eleazar, raising a glass to Chris Rock, recalled her Zoom audition with Rock for Misty Green, which was followed in short order by a missed call from an American number and the two-word text message that would change her life: “Chris Rock.” (That’s right—when Chris Rock calls you from an unknown number and gets your voice mail, he follows up with a text that just says “Chris Rock,” an absolute power-move that is, unfortunately, hard to replicate by the rest of us.)

“Thinking I was being rather witty, I replied, ‘Rosalind Eleazar,’” Eleazar said. “I waited eagerly for his response and—not so much as a laughing emoji. And I quickly realized that I am communicating with one of the funniest people on the planet and I should probably just leave the funny to him.”

Eleazar recalled Rock telling her on set, My movie—your character, giving her the freedom to discover Misty on her own. “And that’s a rare gift,” she said, “and one that I will always be grateful for.”

“Thank you, Rosalind,” Rock said. “The check will be there in the morning.”

Ayo Edebiri began by saluting “my dear friend, one of my favorite people in the world, one of the best actors ever, and a little bit of a role model to me if I’m being honest: Robert Pattinson.” She paused as the crowd fell out laughing. “Andrew! Andrew Garfield. I’m so sorry. This is a different speech for a different guy.”

“You never know what you’re going to get when you work with somebody,” Edebiri noted, but said the resolutely “normal” Garfield had put her immediately at ease on After the Hunt, making it “safe to be unsafe” in difficult scenes. “And, on that movie especially, we had tough stuff to do,” she said. “We were not nice to each other. Some of the boys these days, on Method, you never know.”

“If you ever see him in public,” Edebiri continued, “don't try any small talk with this man. Just don't do it. He's medically allergic to small talk. You get very deep, very fast. You will end up talking about esoteric poetry or the nature of masculinity in the modern world or just water, like the power and the mystery of water.” (This we can confirm.)

“I just love you so, so dearly,” Garfield responded, “and I hope we can be in each other's lives forever.”

And with that moment of open-hearted sincerity out of the way, it was time for Damon to hear from frenemy Jimmy Kimmel, who fired off weapons-grade roast jokes. “I fought for the First Amendment this year,” Kimmel said. “You fought a puppet cyclops.”

Damon, in response, mostly took the high road, offering up praise (for Edebiri’s speech) before getting the last word. “In closing, I would just like to repeat that I did not invite Jimmy Kimmel to this place. I’ve never invited him anywhere, and I never will. He is a horrible human being. And I thank you all for being here.” ✦

#6741. Kate Middleton’s Awkward Moment as a Fan Encourages Her to Break Protocol Ahead of the Earthshot Awards

The royal had to stick to her guns and wouldn’t back down.

The Princess of Wales, best known as Kate Middleton, had a slightly awkward moment on her tour of India this week (where she’s raising awareness for her husband Prince William’s Earthshot Prize Awards, which reward innovative environmental solutions). While greeting an excited crowd gathered in Mumbai, the Princess sadly had to disappoint a cluster of children who were hoping to get her autograph.

Speaking to one child who had a pen and paper in hand for the Princess, Catherine reportedly had to say, “Sorry, I can’t!” as to sign her name would be a severe breach of royal protocol.

None of the royal family are allowed to give out autographs, owing to fears that their signature could be replicated and forged, or that they’ll simply be sold on for monetary gain.

In recent years, they have become more amenable to people requesting selfies, which previously was not common practice.

It’s far from the first time the Princess has had to navigate this type of delicate situation with a member of the public; earlier this year while on a visit to Wales, she was also asked to sign her name and had to offer up a consolatory handshake instead.

The trip to India is Kate’s first international visit since her cancer diagnosis in 2024, and her attendance was somewhat unexpected. She has missed the last three Earthshot Prize ceremonies, but given she’s traveled all the way to Mumbai, it’s not a surprise that she showed up alongside William for this year’s event, wearing a stunning Anarkali by Indian designer Mahima Mahajan.

The 2026 Earthshot Prize ceremony will not air live but will be available to watch on Amazon Prime from November 30.

#6738. Buying Your First Pair of Selvedge Jeans? Start Here

We’ve got bad news for white couches: Crunchy, indigo-dyed, raw selvedge jeans are back. People might say they never left, but as someone who literally edited a daily web series about denim fades from 2015 to 2018, I can assure you that across the almost-decade since, the category has taken something of a back seat as jeans with interesting washes and nostalgic cuts (Our Legacy’s Third Cut, GAP’s 90s Loose) surged in popularity.

But while it, ahem, faded from the public eye, the raw denim market was still tended to by the true believers among us. And we owe them a great debt, because their stewardship means we’re not just picking up where the last trend left off. Instead, we’re jumping into an elevated timeline. The best makers in the world have only gotten better, the cuts have gotten more diverse, and a whole bunch of stuff that was once incredibly hard to find in the United States is now readily available.

So available, in fact, that the selection can be overwhelming. Which is where I come in! Because while there are now thousands of pairs of raw denim jeans to choose from, I can tell you that only a precious few specific cuts have consistently dominated Subreddits, YouTube roundups, and my text message history for the best part of this century. Ten of them are below, starting with five approachable icons, and moving through to five more legendary deeper cuts. Let’s get faded.

The company behind Sugar Cane, Toyo Enterprise, has been making hard-wearing garments since the mid-’60s, but Sugar Cane didn’t come around until 1975. Ever since, they’ve been making some of the most considered, sturdy and timeless jeans and workwear on the planet in Japan, all of it aging more beautifully than a fancy barolo.

If you’re looking to dip your toes into the Sugar Cane pool, the 1947 model brilliantly recreates one of the most well-loved iterations of the most well-worn model on the planet (we won’t name names, but they’re in here too), and comes in a four-season, 14.25oz. selvedge denim fabric that will produce some preposterously good fades.

For anyone who’s fallen in love with a pair of old old vintage jeans, and wondered what they felt like when they came off the production line, it’s hard to get closer than a pair of Fullcounts. The brand was started in 1993 in Osaka, Japan, with the express purpose of reverse engineering the wonder of those vintage pairs, down to the all-cotton threads and long-staple cotton.

They sure figured it out, and still make everything in Japan. And while the classic 0105 is an absolute knockout, the Wide Straight iteration gives you a little more comfort with the same break-in potential. And if you’re just getting yourself into the raw selvedge game, a little comfort never hurts.

The only Canadian entrant on this list—partly because Henry’s hasn’t restocked yet—Naked & Famous has been around since 2008. And as you might expect from a brand whose hallmark fit is called the Weird Guy, they’re a little quirky. In a good way! For not only are they rigorously dedicated to sourcing the sickest raw denim on the planet, but that denim often has some funky detailing as well, like a green weft or some galaxy-like imperfections.

The True Guy cut is technically a relaxed straight (don’t confuse that for baggy) and this particular pair has kevlar woven into the fabric, for those into literal bulletproof denim.

If you’ve ever spent time on denim message boards, you’ve probably seen the name “Iron Heart” associated with some of the heaviest denim known to man. (If you’ve never been, steel yourself before entering.) And while it is true that the Japanese brand pushes the definition of heavyweight to its absolute limit, it also makes a damn good pair of regular jeans.

In fact, the mid-weight fare is as good as any on the market, will produce some HOF-worthy fades, and won’t require a title fight to soften up. Within that weight class, the straight leg of the 634S-142 is the kind of timeless silhouette that should outlast most trend cycles. (Also, for the record, “mid-weight” is a relative term. This is the lightest-weight denim that Iron Heart will entertain.)

While the US quite literally invented jeans as we understand them (denim as a fabric is another story, for those keeping very detailed score), you’d be forgiven for thinking otherwise, considering the lack of US-made options on this list. But thankfully, 3Sixteen is doing the work of like six companies at this point, sourcing the world’s finest denim—we don’t really make that here anymore—and stitching the 5-pockets up back home in the USA.

Every cut they make has a legion of fans, but the semi-recent, semi-baggy RS is the one tearing up the charts at the moment. And for great reasons. It’s got the aforementioned room, has a top block (re: the area that houses the waistband, fly and pockets) that doesn’t get all bunched up and funky, and a higher rise that’s flattering on just about everyone. As a result, it’s a pair that both denimheads and denim rookies appreciate with the same kind of zeal.

When it comes to details that will turn a denimhead into a living meme—Vince McMahon Progression, Guy Turning Around, you pick—few brands can execute them like Oni can. From the denim itself, which is milled in Japan and feels more handmade than small-batch sourdough, to the period-accurate details like flat-felled seams and linear bar tacks, every pair starts as a work of art and develops into a wholly separate work of art as they’re worn.

The only issue, really, is finding them, because hand-making just about everything isn’t exactly a scalable process. When they’re around, (and they currently are!) they’re worth more than just a gander, particularly the Wide Straight, which has a loose, straight leg and a healthy, fairly forgiving rise. This pair in particular is made with lighter-weight 12oz. denim, but don’t mistake that for lightweight denim—it’ll hold up year round, and could always handle some longjohns during a cold-snap, if you feel so inclined.

Those familiar with the Osaka 5—the loose collection of denim brands that sprouted up in Osaka in the ‘70s, ‘80s and ‘90s and redefined the very notion of raw denim specifically and the idea of what “jeans” could be, more broadly—will know that Warehouse was the fifth and final member, founded by two alums from a different member, Evisu. And for roughly 30 years the brand’s pumped out intricately detailed, vintage-indebted jeans that some of the pickiest people on the planet have sworn by, even going so far as sourcing American cotton to keep the look and feel as close to the source material as possible.

This pair in particular is based on one of the most popular pairs of 501s Levi’s ever made, the 1966 model, which had a straight leg and a high rise and a slightly twisted seam after a few washes, giving it a slow-developing signature—all present and accounted for here in 2026 via Warehouse.

These aren’t for the faint of heart. Let’s get that out of the way. 21oz. denim is almost armor, especially if your previous denim reference point is something with a wash, a rinse or some stretch. But for anyone looking for a challenge, absolutely electric fades and a pair of jeans that might outlast horseshoe crabs, look no further.

That’s because Samurai, another Osaka-based brand (but not part of the Osaka 5, for whatever it’s worth), makes some of the hardest-fading, hardest-wearing, most-revered jeans anywhere, and that includes the ultra-heavyweight numbers. And who knows, all that extra (fabric) weight might be nice with winter incoming.

Levi’s offers some great raw selvedge 501s at a pretty reasonable price, a pair that will age well and (with proper care of course) last for years. The 501, however, isn’t a standardized cut. In fact, it’s tweaked every few years to reflect the prevailing sentiment of the time a little bit better. And as a result, different eras have different hallmarks—for instance, the 1947 is a bit slimmer, the 1954 is the first pair with a zipper and the 1901 is the first pair with two back pockets.

Levi’s Vintage Clothing, a sub-label under the broader umbrella, still makes a bunch of these pairs and while the aforementioned are killer, the 1933 feels paradoxically relevant to 2026: it’s got a healthy, wide leg, a healthy rise and a couple cheeky details to differentiate it from the rest of the pack, like a back cinch and suspender buttons.

We couldn’t make this list without including a pair from the first member of the Osaka 5, in part because it’s hard to imagine any of this would be possible without Studio D’Artisan and in part because the brand still makes some of the best jeans in the world. Founded in 1979, Studio D’Artisan kicked off the obsession surrounding raw selvedge denim and bygone detailing, doubling down on craftsmanship and material quality in an era defined by synthetics and acid-washing. And they never really strayed, ultimately adding some more timeless staples to the denim assortment, all of it made in Japan with commensurate care. The SD-801 is a classic straight leg fit, made in Japan from a rope-dyed natural indigo 15oz. denim fabric and armed with a host of cheeky details, like a selvedge hit at the coin pocket and a goat leather patch at the back.

Of course, trying out any new look comes with the eternal question: How do I style these things?

Well, one of the best things about raw selvedge denim is that it wears well with pretty much everything. With that in mind, don’t overthink it. But if you do grab yourself a pair of elite-tier jeans and feel like upgrading the supporting cast around it, we have some recommendations for you. For instance, a pair of sturdy leather shoes—whether some Tyroleans, a work boot, or the like—has a multiplying effect beneath some rope-dyed indigo. The same goes for a vintage-inspired, well-proportioned t-shirt or hardy flannel. Of course, as is the case with the jeans above, not all of these items are created equal. The below eight, however, have the GQ seal of approval.

#6737. The Fashion Lover’s 2026 IYKYK Gift Guide

It’s about that time again. For the fourth year running, we’re tackling gifts for one of the most challenging groups to shop for: fashion obsessives. We get it—and we speak from experience.

Here, we’ve compiled a list of “if you know, you know” fashion, beauty, and lifestyle gifts that won’t just satisfy, but impress the fashion lover in your life. Some are practical; others are simply beautiful; all are things Vogue editors can’t get enough of.

Below, Vogue’s 2026 IYKYK gift guide. Happy shopping!

It’s nearly impossible to get ahold of Emily Dawn Long’s small-batch “Spoiled Boys” T-shirts, but the downtown designer has plenty of colorful knit bucket hats to go around. One notable fan? Zoë Kravitz.

Speaking of Kravitz…she’s one of many celebrities who adore this cooler-than-cool sunglasses brand. (Other notable fans include Jennifer Lawrence, Kendall Jenner—oh—and Kravitz’s fiancé, Harry Styles.) While Thistles offers any shape your heart desires, we’re partial to the sporty Als.

Yes, this Vogue beauty editor favorite is a failsafe option for dry lips (especially in the winter!), but this is no medicinal lip balm. Le Chouchou’s broad color range will leave you with a lovely tint, from warm espresso to frosty Y2K pink.

This LA designer’s shoes are her claim to fame, spanning candy-colored pumps to unisex sneakers. But it’s her ultra-comfy, something-for-everyone penny loafers that earned Haller, a 2026 CFDA/Vogue Fashion Fund finalist, her IYKYK status. They were inspired by her grandfather—the ultimate influencer.

If you’re going the socks route, they might as well be cashmere—and from the buzziest collab of the season.

Add a touch of glamour to your dreary winter wardrobe, or throw it around your waist and try out the burgeoning cummerbund trend. Holiday party dressing just got a whole lot more interesting.

Whether they’re after an eclectic charm necklace à la the Celine runway, or they prefer a more curated jewelryscape, Celine’s novelty charms promise a dose of whimsy in any fashion lover’s wardrobe. Play it safe with their initial or swing for the fences with a petite artichoke, domino, or a trumpet—if you’re feeling crazy.

Former Vogue editor Laia Garcia-Furtado’s passion for Prada jumps off the pages of this illustrated guide to the Milanese label’s rise from fashion underdog to luxury behemoth. Equal parts charming and knowledgeable, this makes a great gift for any fashion obsessive.

For the biohacker who wishes their wearable tech wasn’t so…well, hideous.

The perfect stocking stuffer, this sheet mask is a sure-fire hit for all skin types, focusing on skin hydration and elasticity. Everyone can get behind that.

There’s nothing more thoughtful than a handwritten note, and there’s nothing chicer than some understated, customized stationery. Become that person who sends a handwritten thank-you note!

For the person who already has a red light mask, up the ante with this handheld, portable device. With hot and cold settings, this TheraBody wand tackles depuffing and dark circles.

Polish designers Karmena and Dominika of Forge Objects created something truly precious with this sterling silver fan inlaid with carnelian cabochons. It’s definitely not the fan you throw in your tote on a sweltering day—this is an heirloom in the making.

This New York brand isn’t new, but its spring 2027 show was an industry favorite. What better way to hop aboard the 6397 train than with a seasonally appropriate Fair Isle sweater?

Revisit the last decade in Grace Coddington’s storied career in fashion editorials, sketches, and commentary. Pairs well with Grace: A Memoir.

This is no classic gourmand. Notes of white chocolate, grapefruit, and cardamom are balanced out with warm sandalwood and amber, plus floral jasmine and lilies. A funky bottle doesn’t hurt either!

#6736. King Charles Had the Most Unexpected Response to Robert Pattinson Being Announced as James Bond

The royals have long been fans of the franchise.

King Charles and Queen Camilla had the best response to the long-awaited news that Twilight and Batman legend Robert Pattinson is set to become the new James Bond.

The royal family has long been associated with the iconic British spy series, with the King and Queen—along with Prince William and Catherine, Princess of Wales—attending the No Time to Die premiere at London’s Royal Albert Hall in September 2021 (the last film that was released in the long-running franchise).

In response to the official James Bond X account sharing the news about Pattinson, the royal family's account (which acts as a news source for the King and Queen), re-shared the post along with the comment: “Welcome to His Majesty’s Secret Service, Mr Bond.”

So far, the quip has been liked over 250,000 times.

Prior to the 2021 premiere, the King had attended plenty of other screenings of the Bond series—dating as far back as 1981 for the launch of For Your Eyes Only, which had Roger Moore starring as the fictional MI6 agent.

The late Princess Diana and Princess Margaret also turned out for that particular premiere.

Commenting on his major career leap, Robert Pattinson said in a statement, “James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honor of a lifetime.”

He continued, “I’m deeply grateful to Denis, Amy, David, Tanya, and everyone at Amazon MGM Studios for their belief in me. To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement. I couldn’t be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team.”

Filming is expected to begin early next year, with an unspecified release date slated for sometime in 2028.

It will be the first James Bond movie produced by Amazon MGM, after the Broccoli family unexpectedly sold the rights in 2025.

#6734. Lights, Camera, Action! An Exclusive Look Inside ELLE’s 2026 Women in Hollywood Celebration

Florence Pugh, Julianne Moore, Penélope Cruz, and more were honored at our annual event.

Los Angeles has no shortage of awards shows, but ELLE’s annual Women in Hollywood event has always been about something more: putting the spotlight on the women whose work makes the industry worth watching. On Monday night, eight of film and television’s most talked-about talents came together to celebrate their collective achievements, with plenty of oohs, aahs, and well-deserved gushes along the way.

This year’s honorees—Carrie Coon, Elizabeth Debicki, Rosalind Eleazar, Julianne Moore, Samantha Morton, Inde Navarrette, Florence Pugh, and Penélope Cruz—gathered at the Four Seasons Hotel Los Angeles at Beverly Hills for an evening hosted by ELLE editor-in-chief Nina Garcia.

Presented in partnership with Ralph Lauren and Bulgari, with support from Evian, the soirée drew familiar faces from across Tinseltown. Matt Damon, Seth Rogen, Bryce Dallas Howard, Alexander Skarsgård, and Louisa Jacobson were among those who took the stage to present the honors, while Morton accepted hers remotely from her home in London, where she was sick with the flu.

Beyond the eight honorees, the guest list included Lily James, Ashley Park, Elsa Hosk, Madison Beer, Jackie Tohn, Molly Sims, and more.

Champagne and yuzu mocktails flowed as guests mingled before making their way into the ballroom, where a three-course dinner awaited: beet salad, Chilean sea bass, and chocolate tortino.

Garcia kicked things off by celebrating a banner year for moviegoing, while reminding the room that there’s still work to be done when it comes to creating opportunities for women. “We need roles for women that are messy, complicated, funny, and real—and sometimes even older than 50!” she said.

#6732. On the Podcast: How Richard Avedon Redefined Fashion Photography

Richard Avedon spent decades shooting for magazines like Vogue, Harper’s Bazaar, and The New Yorker before his death in 2004. Now his life and work are the subjects of a new documentary, Avedon, directed by Ron Howard.

To learn more about Avedon’s legacy—and to hear what it was like to work with him as both a model and a fashion editor—Nicole Phelps invited Tonne Goodman on to The Run-Through.

Goodman was still in high school when she entered the world of fashion. “I was in 10th grade and I wanted a summer intern job,” she explains. What she got, through her friendship with Diana Vreeland’s grandson, was modeling work for Vogue. “I think that the fact that she sent me to Avedon and to Penn and to the best photographers that the magazine had at that point was really a gesture of kindness to her grandson,” Goodman says.

Her first photograph in Vogue, taken by Avedon, was published in 1971. Decades later, she would collaborate with him as an editor on a commercial shoot for Neiman Marcus starring model Nadja Auermann. “Dick was a sponge. He captured every single kind of example of a fashion photograph that you could possibly take,” she says. “I’m sure that there is not a photographer today who has not referenced his work in some way or another.”

Later in the episode, after the break, Chloe Malle sits down with the film’s director, Ron Howard. At first, he says, the Avedon Foundation was reluctant to open its archives to a documentary crew, but Howard’s 2024 film Jim Henson Idea Man persuaded them that the material would be in safe hands.

As he began the research, Howard says, “I think they could just see that I was pretty blown away. I related to him a lot more than I thought I would. I began to understand that these weren’t snapshots. He wasn’t ever counting on luck—he really was a storyteller.”

The two also discuss Avedon’s motivations, and some of the unflattering reviews he received during his career. “A lot of interesting people are paradoxes, right? He had that anger that was pushing him,” Howard posits. “We talk about how he was frustrated by the critics. And of course, they were devastating to him in a way, but I think he used that as fuel.”

In the end, Tonne believes that Avedon would have appreciated what Avedon has to say about him. “I think Ron got him,” she says, “and I think he would’ve gotten it totally.”

#6729. Is This the Greatest Fashion Auction of All Time?

3,000 fashion items from a personal collection are up for sale at Maurice Auction in Paris.

Who owns four vintage Dior Maasai necklaces? Not very many people, except for, of course, one of Paris’s most mysterious women and deeply devoted collectors of fashion. The anonymous French clotheshorse is now the subject of an upcoming multipart, 3,000-piece sale at Maurice Auction. “It’s not someone who is known by the industry, it’s just someone who was very wealthy and that could afford such a collection as a true and passionate collector for more than 30 years,” Salomé Pirson, co-founder of Maurice Auction, tells ELLE.

Dubbed the Infinite Wardrobe, the multipart auction contains haute couture, ready-to-wear, handbags, and accessories from the likes of Chanel, Dior, Hermès, Valentino, Roberto Cavalli, Fendi, and Ungaro. The Infinite Wardrobe will kick off with a live auction on November 18 in Paris, followed by eight different online-only auctions sorted by brand or subject (Chanel, Italian fashion, Dior, bags, for instance). Even with the growing interest in auctions recently spurred by a younger demographic, it’s certainly one of the most extensive fashion auctions that has happened in recent years. Earlier this year, Maurice Auction broke records when it sold rare haute couture from the collection of couture queen Mouna Ayoub.

Much of the Infinite Wardrobe is unworn or only worn once, pristinely preserved like a time capsule for decades in one closet. Some of it even still has tags attached. “What’s unusual is the volume,” says Marie-Laurence Tixier, co-founder of Maurice Auction. “The client was really someone who collected, and when she liked a look or a pair of shoes, she would buy all the colors.” For the auction, that means Hermès Oran sandals in every shade of the rainbow and every iteration of vintage Chanel Gripoix necklaces. Some of the items will be sold in more than a dozen variations.

When the duo first encountered the collection, it was stored in a single Parisian apartment, all exhibited by color, type of accessory, and brand. “I’ve heard that people, when they went to have dinner at her place, they visited the closet, because it was a piece of art itself,” adds Tixier. It’s by far the biggest auction the company has ever done since it was founded in 2022, and also the biggest undertaking of their careers in terms of cataloging, researching, and organizing all of the pieces. “It’s like going into a fantasy closet where you realize it’s not gonna be a dream, it’s gonna be a real job for three months,” says Tixier. The rarest items were researched in collaboration with Kerry Taylor, fashion’s favorite London auctioneer.

If you love designer fashion, it’s a great opportunity to pick up a vintage luxury just before the holidays. But for the real fashion freaks, there are some ultra-rare gems that rarely come to market, too. Think: Jean Paul Gaultier-designed Hermès crocodile jackets, Emanuel Ungaro haute couture, and incredible, lightweight vintage Fendi furs. “She had exquisite taste, it’s very elegant, very, very refined,” says Tixier. “There are no logos.”

Roberto Cavalli beaded trousers, Christian Dior by Gianfranco Ferré mini bustle dresses, and Gianni Versace embroidered jackets are just a few of the treasures available in the first part of the auction. In other words: the dream closet is real, and soon, it will be up for grabs.

#6726. GQ’s 2026 Men of the Year Party Brought Everyone Out

There’s no party quite like a GQ party. Who else could bring together Andrew Garfield, Robby Hoffman, Future, and Angel Reese under one roof? But that’s exactly what we did on Thursday night at Los Angeles’s famed Chateau Marmont for our 31st Men of the Year party, presented by Johnnie Walker Blue Label, with special thanks to the 1 Hotel West Hollywood.

Following a dinner honoring our trio of cover stars—Matt Damon, Chris Rock, and Garfield—the real fun began when all three of them, along with nearly every other celebrity in town, descended on the Chateau’s garden to mix it up to the sounds of DJ Yung Tada (plus a late-night set from GQ Breakouts electro-pop duo Fcukers).

I caught Damon at the entrance to the party looking to continue our conversation from his cover story, but our reunion was cut short when Inde Navarette pulled up to say hi and exchange contacts. If the 25-year-old Obsession newcomer was starstruck by the 56-year-old Hollywood hero, the feeling seemed mutual.

Future and Travis Scott rolled up nearly at the same time; Travis, who performed the end-credits track for The Odyssey, told me he was ready to hit the Oscars campaign trail.

In every corner was a cluster of stars from different Hollywood galaxies. Abbott Elementary’s Tyler James Williams and Chris Perfetti made the rounds together, looking nothing like the harried teachers they play on TV. GQ Breakout Owen Thiele and his longtime friend Cazzie David (who gave Owen his first acting gig on her web series years ago) ignored our red carpet instructions to bless us with photogenic poses they’d pre-planned long in advance. When I asked broadcaster Taylor Rooks for an on-the-fly NBA Cup prediction, she gushed about the Celtics and the Lakers. And there was something fun about seeing Anderson .Paak and Diplo chop it up, too.

The friendly embrace shared by Austin Abrams and Skyler Gisondo, noted Good Dudes, is the unscripted team-up the internet goes nuts for. The Resident Evil and Primetime actors later shared that they’d just been on the phone together while getting ready for the party, neither realizing they’d be seeing each other shortly. When I brought up James Gunn and his recent departure from DC Studios, Gisondo called it a “bummer”—he just wrapped the “Jimmy Olsen vs. Gorilla Grodd” series, he said, and hopes that it’ll still come out (and that Gunn continues to write and direct even if he’s not in executive mode anymore).

In other unlikely but endearing encounters: Ayo Edebiri and Thiele excitedly nabbed IShowSpeed for a photo, and Lamorne Morris stopped Anthony Ippolito to give him props for I Play Rocky, counseling him to take it all in. Ippolito told me he’s headed off to Europe soon to continue promoting the film; a certified foodie, he was hunting for Paris recs (I had to put him on to HolyBelly, for the pancakes). I also caught GQ’s Director of the Year Denis Villeneuve, whose eyes lit up when I mentioned his woefully underrated Jake Gyllenhaal thriller Enemy.

Midway through the night I spotted Andrew Garfield and Monica Barbaro, who were considering an Irish exit. Garfield’s forthcoming Artificial (out December 25) is the movie on everybody’s lips, but he told me he’s looking forward to spending the holidays in New York and taking a brief break before what will probably be a busy campaign season for the Man of the Year.

No one captured the evening as succinctly as Robby Hoffman, who described her upcoming TV show as “Curb [Your Enthusiasm] for poor people.” When the conversation turned back to GQ, Hoffman rued the decline of magazine paper quality. But this latest issue got her seal of approval: appropriately glossy, well-considered, and elite to the touch. Though she might have just been describing the party’s guest list.

But even if you didn’t make the cut, you can see how GQ’s Men of the Year 2026 party looked from the inside. ✦

#6725. Joan Jett and Hannah Martin Are Bringing a “Bad Reputation” to Fine Jewelry

You’d never imagine being asked to pierce the ears of one of your teenage idols, but five years ago, renegade London jeweler Hannah Martin found herself in that exact, heart-racing predicament.

Pitched up at the Sunset Marquis hotel in West Hollywood—Martin’s self-described “home from home in Los Angeles”—she received a call from her close friend Maryam Malakpour, the stylist to rock legend Joan Jett, who just so happened to be staying at the same hotel. “I headed over to her villa feeling vaguely anxious because she’s my total hero,” Martin says, with a laugh. “In the end, it was more a case of forcefully pushing an earring through an existing piercing, rather than a totally new one…” (So far, so punk!)

Following that first encounter, Martin began loaning the “Bad Reputation” singer pieces of jewelry—her suitably subversive designs include hoop earrings punctured with malachite safety pins, rings resembling kinky harnesses, and razor-blade dog tags—before the pair decided to collaborate on something to mark the 45th anniversary of Jett’s version of “I Love Rock ’n’ Roll.” “The conversation was really organic,” Martin says. “We began talking about creating one piece, but there was such a wealth of inspiration that I got very overexcited.”

The resulting Hannah Martin London x Joan Jett collection comprises 14 pieces of jewelry and precious accessories, rendered in sterling silver, white, and yellow gold, that riff on the iconography of Jett’s legendary rock-star style. Think: high-waisted denim with zips secured by safety pins, battered leather jackets, Ramones tees, and a tangle of leather cords and chains strung with pendants.

“Hannah is the designer and I was really the muse,” Jett explains, “so a lot of it started with conversations about things I’ve worn, symbols that mean something to me, and pieces from my own jewelry and closet.”

The first piece—a pacifier pendant inspired by one Jett wore religiously in the ’80s, and her favorite of the collection—has been reimagined as a sculptural, geometric orb. “There’s something very punk about taking an object like that and turning it into fine jewelry. It has an edge to it, but Hannah made it feel elevated and beautiful,” Jett says. Elsewhere, DIY concert badges are reimagined in hand-painted enamel, leather lighter cases dangle from roadie-style lanyards, and leather cuffs are fastened with smooth sterling-silver buckles. The safety pin is reduced to its purest form, as a sculptural link in a chain, while Martin’s signature teardrop motif becomes a sleek heart, studded with spiky, reverse-set diamonds.

“It was really about stripping everything back,” Martin explains of her approach to the collection. “My design language is always about focusing on elemental forms.” And so, alongside pin-ups of Jett, Martin’s mood board also featured sculptures by Constantin Brancusi and works by Austrian designer and metalworker Carl Auböck. “It was a real mix of punk imagery and refined artistic forms.”

Martin can’t quite remember when she first heard Jett’s music, but suspects she absorbed it by osmosis from her dad’s record collection while growing up in the ’90s. “It was such a male-dominated universe and people like Joan, Courtney Love, and Patti Smith became part of my musical world,” she says. Now, one of her teenage heroines has made it into her fine-jewelry hall of fame.

#6720. Was This the Biggest Week in Sneakers of 2026?

As we inch towards the end of the year, there’s always a massive holiday rush in the sneaker industry (in addition to, well, everywhere else). Annual seasonal drops like the reliable Black Friday and Holiday XI launches from Jordan Brand, plus every major label trying to end the year on the highest note possible, make November and December some of the most exciting times to be a sneakerhead. To be fair, 2026 certainly still has some gas in the tank—plenty of us are already looking ahead to the return of the “Space Jam” Air Jordan 11 next month. Still, this week stands out even in an already crowded release calendar—in fact, I’m inclined to say it’s the biggest and best week of sneaker releases this year has had to offer so far.

Nike and Adidas lead the way with collaborations from massive designers and some up-and-comers alike, including one release that makes a strong argument for being the best sneaker of the year. Reebok’s gradual revitalization takes a massive step in a fun, innovative new direction. And over at Converse, one of the most reliable celebrity designers in the footwear world is dropping some of his best work yet. Start drafting an apology letter to your credit card for everything you’re about to do with it—these are just a few highlights from the biggest, boldest week of sneakers in 2026 yet.

Who said anything about Samba fatigue? Turns out all it takes to make one of the most gen-pop shoes of the last decade feel brand new is a take like the one offered this week by Adidas Consortium collaborator Invincible, a Taiwanese brand that’s quickly establishing itself as a can’t-miss partner for the Three Stripes. Alongside a stellar line of apparel the brand has savvily outmaneuvered any semblance of cultural exhaustion with one of Adidas’s signature silhouettes by keeping it simple: They’ve outfitted the silhouette in a premium black unstructured leather and, bafflingly, a dress shoe sole rather than the Samba’s traditional gum rubber. With perforated Stripes and detailing that mimics those found on dressy leather brogues, it’s an instant contender for sneaker of the year…even if it just barely qualifies as one. This one goes on sale on November13, but with a catch—it’s an Asia exclusive. Pray to the resale market gods.

Nike has been struggling to find their next big-name collaborator, but in the meantime, some old favorites are still holding strong. One of those names is Union, the Los Angeles-based boutique founded by streetwear giant Chris Gibbs. This week, the brand is offering a buzzy iteration on the classic Nike Dunk that comes in a luxe brown suede and a heel-less mule silhouette. Like the Invincible Samba, the MO here is that all it takes to make an old shoe feel new again is a left-of-center take. These are dropping via SNKRS and Union on November 13, for $130 a pop.

Through Reebok’s ups and downs over the last decade, there has been one shining constant: Allen Iverson, the greatest athlete they’ve ever had on their roster. AI’s shoes are always in style, so if the brand simply brought back the original Question Mid silhouette for the shoe’s 30th anniversary, it’d be noteworthy enough. This year, though, they’ve taken the shoe to a new and fairly innovative space, refitting it with modern performance enhancements, making it court-worthy for the first time in decades. Sure, you can still wear them with oversized tees and baggy shorts. But for the first time in ages, the Question could also make it back onto an NBA court (or at least the pavement at your local park). It’s priced at $170 and is available now via Reebok and select retailers.

Ever since he first inked a deal with Converse in 2017, Tyler, the Creator has been one of the best celebrity collaborators in the sneaker biz. This has only become more true since the launch of the 1908 Project last year. The endeavor has seen the pair diving deep into Converse’s archive to revive everything from classic nautical boating shoes, to a jogging silhouette that hadn’t seen the light of day in decades. Ahead of Tyler’s annual Camp Flog Gnaw festival last year, he and Converse launched their best work at the time: the Bronco Boot, a canvas and rubber-toed banger of a sneaker-boot. This year, they’re running it back on a low-top Bronco Boot silhouette—once again ahead of the festival, where we’ll likely see Tyler wearing them. Think of it as the Doc Martens 1461 to the original Bronco Boot’s Doc Martens 1460. Coming your way in four earthy colorways, these are on sale now via Converse.

Speaking of Converse and boots: One of the biggest sneaker stories of the year has been Rick Owens’s return to Adidas after a fruitful stint over at Converse. The designer’s much-anticipated return collection launched this week, with these stunners at the center of the capsule. Debuting on the runway at Paris Fashion Week this past summer, Owens’s Springblade boots are a showstopper of a return. The shoe’s upper is made from a loose textile that fits up over the ankle and a leather toe cap, but the real heat comes in the return of the Springblade sole Owens and Adidas first debuted over ten years ago. They retail for a crazy $850, and can be purchased via the Adidas Confirmed app. Rick’s gonna Rick!

#6719. Netflix’s ‘The Body’ Is The Most Fun Teen Drama We’ve Had In Years

The following article contains minor spoilers for The Body.

It’s been a big few years for the teen drama, from Off Campus and Sterling Point to The Summer I Turned Pretty and Heartstopper. Nothing ever truly bad happens, but emotionally there’s always something at stake.

Quinn Shephard’s The Body, which came out on Netflix this month, is also a teen drama—but don’t confuse the latter with other iterations of the genre. The Body is winking, sapphic, and totally deranged. It has more in common with Mean Girls and Cruel Intentions, by way of Carrie and The Crucible, than the gentle high school stories of late. (Already there’s a Christian petition to cancel it that has gathered 90,000 signatures, so you know it’s good.)

Our story begins on Halloween in 2004, at a Catholic high school in a small town (we’re not told where, though filming took place around Ontario, Canada). Everyone’s in Juicy Couture, lips glossed to the nines, Chloé Paddingtons and Balenciaga Le City bags slung over their shoulders (never mind that the former was released in 2005; you’ll discover that The Body plays fast and loose with historical accuracy). In the opening episode, the school’s dance troupe, the Lions, throws a big party at an abandoned convent and everyone’s invited: even the weird outcast, Lisbeth (Geena Meszaros). But when they all take ecstasy and engage in a Satanic initiation ritual—leaving one of the dancers, Grace (Sofia Wylie) unconscious—the balance of the group is thrown into disarray.

What happens next is part mass psychogenic hysteria (when some of the girls’ hands start shaking, followed by seizures and visions, it brings to mind the 2011 story out of LeRoy, New York, in which 20 girls at a high school developed “conversion disorder”), part possible supernatural occurrence; we’re left hanging in the balance. What’s more interesting, though, is the idea of repression and religious guilt, compounded by the attitudes of the era (everything lame is described as “gay,” so extra points for accuracy there). Sapphic thoughts and feelings bubble beneath the surface, threatening to spill over. Burgeoning sexuality fizzes throughout these high schoolers’ lives. The series is an excellent portrait of girlhood; more times than once I was transported back to being 15 or 16 and acting like a girl possessed.

Yet while plenty of the themes are gritty (religious trauma, crystal meth addiction, internalized homophobia), this isn’t a serious show. The humor is dark and a little twisted (at one point, the girls are all screaming their confessions, which range from “I’m not a natural blond” to “my brother killed seven people in Afghanistan”). The fashion is a sort of Gen Z-ified version of millennial style (all J’adore Dior tank tops and bejewelled XXL shades, rather than, like, greasy side-bangs and knit hats with flames on them). The latter is fun rather than annoying or erroneous; much like in Mean Girls and Cruel Intentions, we’re given a slick and sexy version of high school. In many ways, that’s the most 2004 thing of all.

Of course, the eight-episode series is not completely flawless. There are moments when the pace sags a little, and a few plot points arise that are either hard to make sense of, or that disappear into the ether. Even so, in this era of mild-mannered and overly earnest YA shows, The Body stands out as deliciously knowing and mischievous—even a little off-color. (In the opening minutes, as the teen girls stretch each other in the grass, the brilliantly wry Elise, played by Sara Boustany, comments, “Holy fuck, you guys look like a bunch of dykes.” Again, historically accurate.) In fact, I haven’t had this much fun watching a teen drama since the first season of Yellowjackets, or early episodes of Riverdale.

As is often the case with Netflix, the ending leaves room for a second season, without there being any indication as of yet that there will be one. Reddit threads are already alight with fans stressing out over whether they’ll axe the show (my instinct is that a second season is a no-brainer, though that doesn’t really mean anything). Regardless, it’s been a truly addictive first outing. And the streamer would be possessed—nay, demonic—not to green-light another.

#6716. How to Reset Your Skin Care Routine After 40

Dermatologists break down the ingredients, steps, and treatments that matter most for skin over 40.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

As we age, there’s seemingly always something new to think about, including adjusting your skin care routine to meet your skin’s evolving needs. You may not need to add a bunch of new products to your current regimen, but increased dryness, changes in texture, fine lines, and enlarged pores may require ingredient swaps that your current lineup can’t deliver. The skin care products you used in your 20s and 30s may have worked then, but once you hit 40, your skin may start to need something different. Experts share how to reset your routine for 40+ skin, including the non-negotiables, new ingredients that can have the greatest impact, and what to avoid to keep your maturing skin looking and feeling its best.

Over 40, skin has already started to thin, at both the epidermis and dermis levels, explains Dr. Suzan Obagi, a board-certified dermatologist, associate professor of dermatology and plastic surgery, and director of the UPMC Cosmetic Surgery & Skin Health Center. “This means that skin will start to appear more fragile, fine lines will start to show, and skin becomes drier. For these reasons, a good skin care regimen should include a retinoid (retinol, retinaldehyde, or tretinoin) to help improve skin thickness, increase extracellular matrix proteins (collagen, elastin, and glycosaminoglycans (GAGs)), and encourage fibroblasts to make more of our Natural Moisturizing Factor (NMF),” Obagi tells ELLE.

Most skin over 40 also has some sun damage, which Obagi says can present as freckles and sun spots. Well before 40 and certainly after, there’s one daily non-negotiable for skin of any age: sunscreen. If the spots have already shown up, Obagi recommends a skin-brightening serum with tranexamic acid (TXA), antioxidants, and peptides to help correct the hyperpigmentation.

Additionally, Dr. Chris Tomassian, a California-based, board-certified dermatologist and founder of The Dermatology Collective, says a retinol at night will go a long way, as will vitamin C in the morning and aggressive moisturization.

As for ingredients, Tomassian says the key players in the post-40 reset will be retinol, SPF, and vitamin C, as already noted, along with PDRN, ectoin, ceramides, and occasionally estradiol.

If you’re not already on a daytime and nighttime routine, now’s the time to start.

Morning: Use a gentle cleanser if your skin is oily or if you didn’t get to a proper wash the night before. Tomassian suggests skipping the cleanse if your skin feels dry when you wake up. Follow with a good antioxidant like an L-ascorbic acid (vitamin C) serum or one with tetrahexyldecyl ascorbate (THD), silymarin, or phloretin. Layer on a PDRN moisturizer and SPF before any makeup.

Night: Before bed, cleanse thoroughly to remove makeup and sunscreen. Layer on a copper peptide serum, ptiox treatment, tretinoin (retinol), and a PDRN moisturizer. Obagi also suggests combining a pigment-correcting serum with a retinoid to help build the dermis extracellular matrix and target hyperpigmentation.

Bonus steps: Exfoliate one to two times each week with a combination peel pad, alpha hydroxy or beta hydroxy acids depending on your skin’s dryness level or if you’re experiencing any breakout. Tomassian warns, though, that post-40 skin should avoid over-exfoliating. “Skin gets drier with age, and breaking down your skin barrier by scrubbing or peeling too aggressively or too often can leave skin vulnerable to drying out,” he explains.

At any age, consistency is key. Even if you’re lucky enough to have minimal signs of aging, both experts agree that these steps will go a long way. “It is still important to incorporate a retinoid, an antioxidant, and a good moisturizer into your daily routine,” says Obagi.

There’s plenty you can do at home to care for your skin after 40, including adding LED light therapy to your lineup to help with fine lines and wrinkles and stimulate collagen—but Tomassian notes these are only beneficial if you use them consistently. An even greater investment is pairing your home routine with regular visits to a professional for in-office procedures like microneedling or ablative and nonablative lasers. These treatments can jump-start your skin to start producing more collagen. For chronic sun damage like redness and dark spots, Tomassian recommends Intense Pulsed Light (IPL), Picosure, or DermaV/Fraxel/CO2 lasers. These devices target pigmentation concerns that skin care does little to improve.

Obagi adds that pro visits are important since collagen production peaks at age 18 and, with each passing year, our skin makes 1 percent less collagen, elastin, and GAGs. “By our mid-30s and early 40s, we would benefit from devices that boost collagen production periodically. These can be noninvasive lasers, microneedling, and radiofrequency devices. These will boost collagen for a short time, but when combined with a well-thought-out skin care regimen, the results can be prolonged,” says Obagi.

You’ve lived with your skin for 40+ years, so you can tell when things start to change. Obagi says you have to listen to your own skin. “If you are on the dry side or have fragile skin, avoid harsh ingredients such as glycolic or lactic acid, strong retinoids, or over-exfoliating with scrubs. These can irritate the skin and drive sensitivity,” she highlights. If you have thicker skin or are oilier, she suggests exfoliating fruit acids and says your skin can tolerate stronger retinoids.

Tomassian’s rule of thumb is that after age 30, use as many ingredients as possible to bank collagen and focus on thicker moisturizers as you get older, since we produce less oil.

Key ingredients: oat-derived surfactants, plant-derived humectants, polyhydroxy acids

Key ingredients: liposomal tranexamic acid (TXA), oligopeptide-68, THD, and hydrolyzed algin to help target the various pathways driving pigmentation

Key ingredients: stabilized vitamin C, hyaluronic acid, panthenol, soothing allantoin, and green tea extract

Key ingredients: collagen, copper peptides, smoothing and brightening niacinamide, retinal, rice PDRN

Key ingredients: low-molecular PDRN, moisturizing squalane, panthenol, and ceramide, brightening niacinamide, firming rose peptide

Key ingredients: glycolic acid, lactic acid, malic acid, antioxidant-rich resveratrol, and green tea extract

Key ingredients: 10 percent Homosalate, 5 percent Octisalate, 3 percent Avobenzone, brightening niacinamide and ethyl ascorbic acid; moisturizing argan oil, squalane, and bisabolol

#6713. LuxExperience Reports 8.5% Sales Growth Amid Turnaround

LuxExperience — owner of Mytheresa, Net-a-Porter, Mr Porter, and Yoox — grew net sales 8.5% on a constant currency basis in the first quarter of fiscal 2027, generating €604.7 million. This marked the fourth consecutive quarter of growth since the group formed in April 2025 following Mytheresa’s acquisition of Yoox Net-a-Porter (YNAP) Group.

“[It was a] super quarter considering that it’s still a mixed picture out there for luxury,” group CEO Michael Kliger tells Vogue Business. “It shows there is demand in multi-brand and digital.

The group’s adjusted EBITDA improved year-on-year, climbing 590 basis points to 2.1%, up from -3.9%. LuxExperience also honed its outlook for fiscal 2027 to 6-9% growth, up from a mid-single-digit to high-single-digit range. The company increased its adjusted EBITDA margin to 2.5-3.5%, up from 2-3%.

Kliger described the quarter as the group’s strongest so far since the LuxExperience inception. “We are ahead of plan with these numbers. That’s why we upped the guidance,” he says.

By brand, Mytheresa’s sales grew 10%, generating €250.8 million, bolstered by a 9% climb in the US. Net-a-Porter and Mr Porter together grew 7.2%, generating €231 million, attributing this to a 24.3% jump in the US. Carried by strong performance in Europe (excluding the UK), Yoox — the group’s off-price retailer — also grew 8.2%, reporting €128.6 million in net sales.

Despite the group’s online foundation, each business invested in IRL events during the quarter. Mytheresa delivered 18 premium customer activations across Europe, the US, and Asia, continuing its one-of-a-kind VIC clienteling strategy. Net-a-Porter and Mr Porter also executed seven and 10 “extremely important person” (EIP) experiences, respectively, across the US and Europe. Yoox continued its focus in Europe, unveiling 14 community events in the region.

“This customer on the luxury side [Mytheresa and the Porter brands] is resilient,” says Kliger. “On the Yoox side, we see that in the lower and middle class, people prefer good offers, having not so much discretionary spend and still loving luxury. Whereas on the Mytheresa and the Net-a-Porter and Mr Porter side, we really speak to those that have the means to buy the latest [product] as soon as it hits the market.”

Mytheresa increased its adjusted EBITDA by 128.1%, while Net-a-Porter and Mr Porter upped theirs to 0.3%, marking the second quarter of profitability post-acquisition. Yoox remained unprofitable; however, it reduced its quarterly loss from €-19.1 million to €-6 million, taking adjusted EBITDA margin from -16.1% to -4.6%

Kliger says that Mytheresa is leveling out its marketing investment, shifting focus from digital to premium physical events, citing the two-week yacht voyage across Monte Carlo and St. Tropez, as well as upcoming pop-ups in the French Alps and Florida.

Both Net-a-Porter and Mytheresa will keep their focus on top spenders, Kliger affirms. What distinguishes Mytheresa and the Porter brands? “Mytheresa is very focused on the womenswear side,” Kliger says, noting that it only offers around 220 brands. “Net-a-Porter [offering around 500 brands] is broader and is for the customer that looks for editorial advice and brand discovery.”

For Net-a-Porter and Mr. Porter, the company is investing more in marketing and ramping up the editorial output and video production. “So we invest more to really inject energy into these brands,” Kliger adds.

Between Net-a-Porter and Mytheresa, customer overlap remained at 12%. (The figure has not changed in the last 18 months.) “The brands themselves have really carved out different personalities,” says Kliger. “If anything, we want that to become even sharper. The growth both businesses show does not come at the expense of one of the other. They’re growing into the market.”

Kliger attributes LuxExperience’s continued growth to a handful of core factors. First, the company is digital, and the digital market is expanding. Second, the group is positioned on both sides of the market, offering high-end and off-price. Lastly, the business isn’t heavily exposed to the luxury slowdown in China. “Our China business — we have good representation in APAC — but it was never oversized, and therefore we don’t suffer overly from the sluggish demand.”

Looking ahead, Kliger doesn’t foresee any major obstacles to the continued growth and predicted return to profit for Yoox, which he expects to realize between the last quarter of fiscal 2027 and the first quarter of 2028.

#6712. Florence Pugh Credits the ‘Thousands of People’ Who Made Her Career Possible

Florence Pugh is making sure every person who helped make her career possible gets their due. In her Women in Hollywood speech, the Dune: Part Three star reflected on what a “bonkers ride” it is to be a woman in the industry. “Being bold and powerful and opinionated—always opinionated—and then vulnerable whenever the cameras need, is a skill I’m still in awe of all of us being able to do,” she said. “Thank you, ELLE, for honoring all of these powerhouse women.”

She went on to acknowledge the “thousands of people” who helped make her career possible. Being an actress was a childhood dream. “When I was child, I was asked what I wanted to be when I grew up, and it was this,” she recalled. “But I didn’t know what ‘this’ was, though. I just saw the women and men on my TV and would feel supremely jittery and thrilled watching them. I would get close to the screen, so close I could feel the warmth and static and study all of their faces. I would mainly get jealous of men actually, and weirdly, he’s in my speech, Matt Damon, I was just always jealous of him. And I don’t know why! I don’t! He’s got it all!

“I knew I wanted to do that,” she continued. “All of it, the bells, the whistles. The ability to be free and perform and live in make-believe. The thing is, I wasn’t aware that the biggest and best thing about working in this industry was yet to come. Yes, the explosions and close-ups and locations and free breakfast, lunch, and dinner is cool, but when I truly sit and think about how I got here, it’s down to the thousands of people who have been a part of my career all the way through. They made the path smooth so I could climb to the top of the mountain and wave my flag, which is what I am doing right now. My career and existence in this job is down to thousands of people.

“I think of the crews I’ve been lucky enough to work with, who create the space and the stage so I can do what I do comfortably. I think of the casting directors at the beginning of my career, who took a risk arguing for me, claiming that it didn’t matter that I had no qualifications and only one film credit. Or for the dressers, who would fib and say there was a costume malfunction when they could see I hadn’t had enough time to eat my lunch—this was pre-SAG membership. So don’t panic, SAG. Or to the glam teams all over the world who join because they believe in you and what you do. The makeup artists and hair stylists who wash and clean brushes well into the night just for you, tomorrow at 5 A.M.”

“I think of all of these people who protected me on my journey,” she said. “And it would not have been possible without every single one of them. Just in case you’re listening now and you’re not aware how grateful we are and how important you are, I just received an ELLE Women of the Year honor, and I didn’t get here on my own. I only took stock in myself because I could see you doing it for me first.”

Watch Pugh’s full speech above and read her Women in Hollywood cover story here.

#6711. These Holiday Perfumes Smell Like the Most Wonderful Time of the Year

‘Tis the season... to smell really freaking good.

We may earn commission from links on this page, but we only recommend products we love. Promise.

Call me Buddy the Elf, but IMO, there’s no such thing as getting too in the holiday spirit. I’ve been known to display multiple Christmas trees, I love putting together holiday cards, and cooking Christmas dinner for friends and family is one of my great joys in life. And of course, all of this is happening while I’m blasting Mariah Carey and all my other favorite holiday songs.

But don’t think I’ve forgotten about the beauty side of things! As a faithful beauty editor, I also get excited to change up my fragrance this time of year and embrace some holiday scents. Do I want to smell just like a Christmas tree? No, not really. But I do want to spritz something that’ll help get me in the holiday spirit. Think about all the best scents of the season—gingerbread, pine, cinnamon spice, vanilla... These make for perfect holiday perfumes. So, in the name of very important holiday beauty research, I’ve rounded up the best festive fragrances worth adding to your rotation this season. From cozy gourmand perfumes to fresh woodsy notes and everything in between, one spritz of any of these will instantly get you in the holiday spirit.

Nest’s famous holiday candle is a staple in my home, and now, I can wear the scent on my skin too. It bottles up that festive feeling with fir balsam, winter cranberry, and grapefruit for a perfume that’s equal parts fresh, fruity, and woodsy. Think wandering through a Christmas tree farm with a little tart cranberry cocktail. It’s festive without smelling like you’re hiding pine branches up your sleeves.

Holiday parties call for a little spiked eggnog, and Dior Spice Blend brings that same boozy, spicy energy to your fragrance wardrobe. Rich rum notes, fiery black pepper, and zesty ginger blend together for a warm, intoxicating, and spirited scent. I love that it’s bold, sophisticated, and much less sugary than a typical holiday gourmand.

You don’t actually have to know how to ski to appreciate a good après ski moment (bring on the hot chocolate and jacuzzi, please). Ellis Brooklyn’s wintry scent captures that exact winter getaway feeling, thanks to seasonal notes of juniper berries, cardamom, soft suede, and musk. It’s woodsy, a little romantic, and pretty much begging to be worn at a chic mountain lodge.

Hot chocolate is a holiday must-have for me, but let’s be real: The best part is the mountain of whipped cream on top. Philosophy Fresh Cream bottles up that sweet, fluffy deliciousness with notes of whipped cream, tonka bean, heliotrope, and sugar. It’s soft, milky, and comforting without any heaviness or spice. And at under $60, it’s a pretty sweet addition to your holiday fragrance wardrobe.

Dreaming of a white Christmas? Future Society Snow Beginnings can make that happen. It smells like the magic of a fresh snowfall, but with a surprisingly fruity, floral twist. Cool Japanese mint and sparkling pink grapefruit deliver that feeling of crisp winter air, while lychee, crystallized rose, and sake add a sweet warmth. It’s a winter wonderland in a bottle, no freezing temperatures or shoveling required.

Who says you have to spend a fortune to smell festive? Dove’s Holiday Treats Frosted Plum Berry Body Mist delivers a juicy, fruity take on holiday fragrance for just about the same price as your seasonal latte. The sweet, bright, and surprising plum feels playful and is a refreshing departure from the usual dessert-heavy holiday scents. Plus, it’s easy to layer with your favorite body lotion, scrub, or perfume for a little extra festive flair.

Catharine Malzahn is a contributing beauty writer at Cosmo who covers all things beauty, including fragrance.

Catharine Malzahn is a contributing beauty writer at Cosmopolitan and was previously the beauty assistant at Good Housekeeping, Woman's Day, and Prevention.
