#6698. The Best Hostess Gifts to Bring to a Holiday Party

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Over 75 ideas to carry you throughout the season

It’s an established social etiquette rule that showing up to a party empty-handed is a bit of a faux pas. Of course, there are more intimate gatherings where a simple bottle of wine or an extra cheese for the board will suffice, but the holiday season runs on a different track. Homes are dressed to the nines, menus are calibrated to merrier flavors, and the stakes somehow feel higher. Arriving with a gift for the hostess not only signals your appreciation, but also adds to the evening’s celebratory air. But what to bring?

There’s zero shame in going the traditional route—no one is going to turn their nose up at a Le Labo candle, after all. If your host is a hardcore holiday enthusiast, why not bring a handcrafted ornament to dress their tree with? Or a fresh stack of illustrated Christmas cards? Something pretty for the pantry will always go to great use, and if you have a strong sense of their taste in interiors, a sleek vase or decorative tray will surely make your host feel extra special.

This year, rather than scrambling to secure the best hostess gifts in the 11th hour, save yourself the stress and stock up ahead of time. Below, shop over 75 picks (starting at just $12) to bring along to all your upcoming holiday fêtes.

For the serial hosts who regularly throw dinner parties, gift them a beautiful tablecloth for the season, or an artisanal set of napkin rings. If you’re hoping they might use your gift the same night of the party, Gohar’s clever crumb catcher could easily be placed on the table for pre-dessert tidying.

Carolina Irving & Daughters Avignon Tablecloth

La DoubleJ Tyrrhenia Tulyps Set of 2 Dessert Plates

Gohar World Silver Plated Mini Crumb Catcher

Attersee Frames A-Jour Placemat and Napkin Set

This gift falls squarely into the category of something the host would probably never buy for themselves, but would love to receive. An elegant soap—bar or liquid—or hand lotion transforms their powder room into a mini spa moment, and will make them think of you each time they visit the sink.

Cabana Marbled Ceramic Soap Dish & Soap Gift Set

Claus Porto Deco Mini Soaps & Soap Dish Gift Set

Rather than pouring snacks into an ordinary bowl or repurposing a mug, these sleek snacking vessels will make your host proud to display their assorted nuts and olives. And because they’re crafted in versatile glass, ceramic, and steel, they can be used all throughout the year.

Noon & Moon Isabella Artisan Rose Duad Dish

Mark & Graham Celebration Beaded Serving Bowls, Set of 2

For hosts who have been known to deck the halls aplenty, get into the spirit of the season with a festive gift. If they celebrate Christmas, an ornament is a winning choice. You could also give them a fresh, handmade wreath to bring their door to life.

Lulu and Georgia Fresh Handmade Olive Leaf Wreath

Zara Home Oval Glass Christmas Tree Ornament

Moda Domus Set-of-Three Glass Candy Ornaments

One of the safest gifts you can bring to a party is food (just check for allergies). Perhaps a tin of artisanal hot cocoa to keep your host cozy throughout the coldest months? Or a limited-run panettone for the dessert-obsessed? If it’s an especially momentous celebration, Flamingo Estate’s manchego cheese wheel is downright impressive.

Charbonnel et Walker Sea Salt Caramel Batons

Savannah Bee Company Honeycomb Gift Set, 5.6 Oz.

Bateel Palm Luxury Stuffed Dates Gift Set

Sant Ambroeus Panettone Limited Production

If your host is all about setting the vibes—dim lights, flickering candles, burning incense—bring them a gift that complements their home’s curation of cozy accoutrements.

FoundRae Strong HeartsLove Link Candle Holder SetBrass

Diptyque Feu de Bois (Wood Fire) Medium Candle

Astier De Villatte Palais d'Hiver Incense

They can whip up a beef Wellington with great finesse and waltz around with a tea towel permanently attached to their shoulder—the hosts who can cook are simply the best. Bring them a gift that befits the kitchen, like a solid-wood cutting board, or something more playful, like a holiday apron.

For a sentimental gift, bring something to help capture memories. A picture frame is always a thoughtful gesture. Or, if you want to give your host something they can use right away, give them an instant camera that can be passed around the party throughout the evening.

L’Objet Deco Twist Platinum-Plated Picture Frame, 4 x 6

Kodak Ektar H35 Half Frame Film Camera, 35mm, Reusable

For the caffeine addicts in your life, a gift centered around coffee or tea will be well appreciated. #6697. Robert Pattinson’s James Bond Announcement Is Already Brewing Some Watch Drama

Throughout the years-long process of casting the new James Bond, I tried to follow the watches to an answer. When Aaron Taylor-Johnson joined the Omega family in May 2025, it felt like watching the 007 Vatican spit white smoke from its steeple. Just this past weekend, fans were still pinning red strings on their bulletin boards between Jack Lowden and the MI6 superspy when images resurfaced of the Slow Horses star wearing Omega. Since 1995’s Goldeneye, Bond has been an Omega man—a relationship later canonized in one of cinema’s most iconic line readings, when Daniel Craig confirmed his brand of choice in three stretched-out syllables: Oh-Mee-Guh.

If, like me, you were only basing your predictions on what the reported pool of potential Bonds wore on their wrists, Robert Pattinson would have been an easy name to cross off. The newly announced 007 only signed on as an ambassador for the Swiss luxury brand Jaeger-LeCoultre two short months ago! When I interviewed Pattinson about the appointment over the summer, he was effusive about his new partner: “I very rarely even wear watches, but when I tried it on, I was like, ‘That’s my favorite watch.’ I wanted to just buy it.”

Now, in addition to juggling his other iconic role as Batman, Pattinson will presumably need to balance his existing commitment to JLC with his new gig’s long-held ties to Omega. (Reps for both brands did not immediately respond to requests for comment, though JLC conspicuously posted a photo of Pattinson on Instagram a few hours after the announcement.)

During our conversation earlier this summer, Pattinson revealed what he looks for in a watch. He caught the collecting bug in March, when he wore JLC’s Master Control Chronometre Perpetual Calendar to the Oscars afterparties. “All these other actors with their fancy watches on asked me, ‘Hey, what are you wearing?’” Pattinson recalls. “It was one of those moments where I’m like, ‘It’s kind of badass having this thing on.’”

If it’s attention-grabbing badass watches Pattinson is after, he’s in good hands with Omega. The brand is best known for supplying the watches Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin wore when they landed on the moon in 1969. Omega has been happy to create special versions of the Speedmaster for its current partners to dial up its profile. And, of course, the Swiss house continues to expand its Bond-inspired offerings: The maker recently added a “Spectre” version of the Seamaster, 007’s preferred model, to the lineup. And whenever Omega needs to drum up buzz around soon-to-be-released models, they tend to show up on former Bond Craig’s wrists during public appearances.

Speculators trying to pin down the next Bond would have had better luck if they’d read some less recent watch tea leaves. Back in 2020, Christopher Nolan released Tenet, his inscrutable but enthralling time-warp thriller in which Pattinson plays a mysterious, dapper, and charming spy involved in a high-stakes mission to save the world—about as good a preview of what the 40-year-old actor will look like as 007 as you’ll find in his filmography. And the watch on his wrist in that flick? An Omega.

India had sat at the top of Kate Middleton’s bucket list ever since she married into the royal family in 2011. First came an Alexander McQueen dress, its paisley print drawing on the textile traditions of India and Persia, followed by a pink-and-pistachio tunic dress by Mumbai-based designer Anita Dongre, worn to play cricket at the Oval Maidan with children supported by local charities. Then along came a Jenny Packham gown, hand-beaded by Indian artisans, to a Bollywood gala, and a blue-and-white embroidered sheath dress by Cumballa Hill-born designer Naeem Khan for a visit to the Taj Mahal. Catherine, the Princess of Wales, wearing Alexander McQueen at the Taj Hotel in Mumbai, 2016.

Catherine, the Princess of Wales, at the Oval Maidan in Mumbai, 2016.

A decade on, the couple returned to India on Monday morning, where Prince William is set to host the sixth Earthshot Prize summit and awards ceremony in Mumbai. The annual Earthshot Prize gives £1 million ($1.3 million) each to five winners tackling some of the world’s most pressing environmental problems, and India has produced more finalists than any other country since its founding in 2020. It will be Catherine’s first appearance at the event since Boston in 2022, while the inaugural Children’s Earthshot Awards should provide familiar territory for the princess, whose charitable work has long focused on the next generation.

#6694. How to Maintain Long, Healthy Hair Over 50, According to Experts

From top treatments to when to plan your next trim, here’s everything to know

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

There’s something undeniably chic about a head of long, luscious hair. Think glossy, waist-skimming, bouncy, voluminous lengths that make extensions an option rather than a long-term commitment. What’s more, long hair provides the ultimate canvas for experimentation, with styling possibilities that feel limitless.

As hair matures, however, maintaining the same level of shine, strength, and vitality can require more attention. As texture changes and dryness increases, the key is to adapt your routine to give your longer lengths the care they deserve. “Long hair can look beautiful at any age, but keeping mature hair glossy and healthy-looking is all about replenishing moisture and maintaining shine,” says celebrity hairstylist Naomi Brooks. “I always recommend prioritising hydrating products that help smooth the hair cuticle, improve softness, and enhance shine, alongside regular trims to keep the lengths and ends looking healthy.”

If you’re considering making the transition and letting your bob grow out, look to a host of celebrities for inspiration. From Demi Moore and Naomi Campbell to Andie MacDowell and Claudia Schiffer, countless iterations are proving just how effortless long hair can look on women over 50. As Brooks explains: “Demi Moore is a fantastic example of how beautiful long hair can look at any age. Her hair is consistently glossy, healthy-looking, and full of movement.”

While genetics certainly play a role, Moore’s glossy lengths are also the result of great care and strategic products. Her hairstylist, Dimitris Giannetos, revealed on social media that he often relies on Kérastase’s Gloss Absolu Glaze Drops Anti-Frizz Hair Oil to reduce frizz, boost shine, and ensure hair remains sleek without looking too heavy. Indeed, experts recommend investing in a high-quality hydrating treatment to ensure mature hair is treated with extra care. “Mature hair can become drier, finer or more fragile over time, so maintaining moisture and shine is important,” says Warren Edwards, creative director at Warren & the Hare.

Additionally, for those with gray or silver hair, session stylist Danilo Giangreco recommends incorporating a clear gloss into your routine to enhance shine. This can also help counteract any unwanted brassiness, ensuring hair appears brighter and healthier.

Another expert-approved tip is to keep heat styling to a minimum where possible. If you do rely on hot tools, applying heat protectant can help shield strands from damage while preserving moisture, strength, and shine.

Finally, contrary to popular belief, long hair thrives on regular maintenance. Though it may seem counterintuitive when trying to grow your hair, routine appointments are essential to keep split ends at bay and prevent the ends from looking too thin or tired. In turn, this helps keep long, mature hair looking fuller, healthier, and overall more glossy.

#6693. David Duchovny on Books, Band and ‘The X-Files’

David Duchovny has been famous for as long as I have been alive. From 1993 to 2002, The X-Files made government conspiracies a staple of primetime television. Duchovny’s FBI special agent Fox Mulder, with his skeptical counterpart, Gillian Anderson’s agent Dana Scully, personified the imminent breakdown of consensus reality in the coming century, delivering the paranoid fringe into 20 million American living rooms. The show belongs to a world of monoculture that no longer exists, and it launched Duchovny into a realm of visibility that’s hard to imagine now, when famous people are produced and consumed at an industrial rate. A few weeks ago, as my boyfriend shopped for a suit jacket at Crowley Vintage in Brooklyn and I edited this story on my phone, I watched a college-age boy put on a long, gray trench coat and announce to his girlfriend: “Mulder mode.”

Duchovny went on to star in Californication, a raunchy dramedy about a divorced novelist navigating the sexually and professionally parasitic Hollywood studio system of the 2000s. Many viewers interpreted Californication as a kind of autofiction, although Duchovny did not write for the show. The actor has written a number of novels, but it’s apparent to anyone who has spent 30 seconds with him that this soft-spoken, reluctant celebrity has nothing to do with the character Hank Moody. Still, Californication did anticipate something about art, celebrity, and self-commodification: Anybody who writes today must contend with marketing an artistic persona for a public that does not, as a rule, read.

In addition to his six books, Duchovny has released four records, and written and directed a number of feature films. He greets the degraded state of American arts with a charming blend of rigor and self-deprecation. “I’m not Jonathan Franzen,” he says of his fiction-writing process. “But if I work on something every day, it deepens. And eventually, hopefully, I can achieve one tenth of what Jonathan Franzen achieves.” But he has an aversion to the sort of publicity that might make his various artistic ventures more lucrative. He tells me he finds it “spiritually impoverishing.”

I meet Duchovny with his band—millennial slackers half his age—at their practice space in Carroll Gardens, where they’re preparing to tour their fourth LP, Prince of Pieces. He wears a white Hanes T-shirt, tight underneath his athletic arms, and he has a tattoo on his ankle—a compass pointing west, something he got when his daughter, West, was hospitalized as an infant. (She’s 27 now, an accomplished actor. “She wanted to be a doctor,” he says. “I was so happy when she told me she was going to pursue acting. Thank God.”)

The albums are composed of subdued, easy-to-listen-to folk-rock tracks, not dissimilar from early Kurt Vile. It’s the band’s first rehearsal in ages, and one of their only chances to prepare in advance of a European tour. In person, they play the songs harder and heavier, sprinkling in crowd-pleasing covers: “Godzilla” by Blue Öyster Cult, “The One I Love” by REM, and—“sadly only one time,” Duchovny says—“Hotline Bling.” The energy in the room is high. These men like one another. Duchovny’s manager offers me a beer from the cooler I’m perched on. I gesture to the tallboy in my purse. He looks disappointed. “You didn’t trust us,” he says. Duchovny steps aside to take a sip of water and picks up the microphone.

“You can sing along,” his keyboardist, Colin Lee, says.

At 66, David Duchovny remains a sex symbol. He’s in better shape than he was on The X-Files. He’s in better shape than the boys in the band. The night after practice, during a Q&A for a screening of his 2023 film Reverse the Curse, he mentions that the wardrobe department had to fashion a “BDSM harness” for him to wear under his clothes to remind him to hunch like an old man. He plays a Red Sox fan who bonds with his estranged son over baseball, marijuana, and their shared lust for a beautiful, young death doula. Duchovny’s character has terminal cancer. “I’m in my dying era,” he tells the crowd. “I die in every film. ”

For the most part, the audience at Westchester County’s Irvington Theater is old enough to have watched The X-Files as it aired. At least two esoteric-looking old men carry David’s poetry collection like a prayer book. There are a handful of young people. A college-aged girl in a KN95 mask raises her hand to ask about Bucky Fucking Dent, the novel adaptation of the Reverse the Curse screenplay, which Duchovny wrote while the movie was in production purgatory. “In the book, Ted and Marty’s last name is Fullilove. In the movie you change it to Fullaker. Why did you do that?”

“Good question,” Duchovny says, stalling. “Full of love. Full of shit. It’s all the same.”

Inevitably, someone asks about the new X-Files. Ryan Coogler is rebooting the show for Hulu. Duchovny will later suggest to me that Chris Carter, the show’s original writer, has designs on a reboot of his own—“He has plans, and wants to end with the original show.” As for Coogler’s version, he says, “I know he said he wants me to come do something, but we haven’t figured out what yet.” During the audience Q&A, Duchovny seems to have misheard the question, and spoils the ending for The Exiles, his forthcoming Taiwanese crime film: “I die in that one too.”

Duchovny’s latest book, About Time, a collection of poems published last year by Akashic, is also largely about dying: the death of his father, the death of his first marriage, the ambient death that hung in the air at the beginning of the decade. He started writing the poems when his therapist encouraged him to talk to dead people. “He was talking about Rudolph Steiner’s belief that you can talk to the dead. And he said: You can talk to your father and you should. My dad and I didn’t connect like we might have,” Duchovny says. “When you’re younger, you think you have all the time in the world to get the relationship you want. But the relationship doesn’t end.” In conversation, he is cerebral without being annoying. “There’s a power struggle when you read a really good novel,” he says. “Somebody’s mind is taking over your mind. I think about language a lot and how we take it for granted as being an accurate signifier. When I was younger I thought communication was possible. I’m not so sure now. But it’s fun to try.”

Duchovny’s humility complicates the sexual charisma that still lives at the center of his public persona. His introduction to About Time begins, “I know what you’re thinking: Just what the world needs now—a bunch of poems from an actor.” There’s a sense that he wants to get ahead of the reader’s skepticism. But there’s also plenty of perceptive lines in the poems themselves: “You dreamt you wrote something so good, / so ambivalent and destructive, so creative, / so lacking in morals, decency, or instruction, / so sad and so funny, / so useless and old, / so familiar and new, / so full of theft and power / that they had to name a god after it.” I ask him if good writing is necessarily amoral. He says, “Probably. Which is why any politically correct work of art is usually super successful and really bad. Usually artists are difficult people, and I have no problem separating the art from the artist. But people do now.”

In college, Duchovny wanted to be a poet. “I thought it was an actual occupation you could have,” he says. When an underclassman turned up in his workshop who was better than him, he quit writing poems on the spot. “It was actually Walter Kirn,” he says. “He showed up at 16-years-old. He was a genius. I was like okay—I’m not a poet.”

The two men have become close in the last decade. Kirn, who wrote Up in the Air and founded the newspaper County Highway, tells me what Duchovny was like at Princeton: “He was golden. He had an aura. I was a little starstruck by him.” Duchovny has agreed to play a character inspired by paranormal radio host Art Bell in American Nights, a film that Kirn is developing alongside director Alex Lee Moyer. Bell’s Coast to Coast, a cult AM show during the ’80s and ’90s, was beloved by long-haul truckers and compound preppers alike, who called in to report UFO sightings, cattle mutilations, and crop circles. “I, like the rest of my generation, grew up on The X-Files,” Moyer tells me. “It made a massive impression on me, and I’ve been a fan of David ever since. The synchronicity of him being a part of this is not lost on me.”

I ask Duchovny if he always needed to be the best. “I at least needed to be the best in my class,” he says.

In LA, I meet Duchovny in a quiet restaurant to talk about his books. He describes his first novel as “an act of cowardice.” Holy Cow is narrated by an anthropomorphized barnyard animal who uncovers the conspiracy theory that is factory farming. “I thought: Well, they’re not gonna cut me off at the knees on this. Because I’m clearly not that serious. It was calculated. I didn’t want to try for the great American novel the first time as an actor.” The books that followed are more ambitious, each one better than the last. By the time he was promoting his fourth book, 2021’s Truly Like Lightning, he made his ambition plain. “I want to be taken seriously,” he said on Marc Maron’s podcast. “That’s my weakness. I want that book to be taken seriously.”

“You don’t want people to be like the guy from The X-Files wrote a book,” Maron said.

“That’s what they’re gonna say,” Duchovny said, “but I hope and I believe that eventually people will see that I mean business.”

Truly Like Lightning centers on a Mormon polygamist family forced to enter the godless world of Los Angeles when their homestead is upended. “When I started to read about Mormonism, it struck me as super optimistic. Everyone’s gonna get their own planet and everyone’s gonna be able to propagate souls. As opposed to a European perspective, which was always about the end of something, being 2,000 years removed from this thing. The Mormons said no, this is still happening.” The novel takes cues from the literary critic Harold Bloom, who wrote that Mormonism was an “American original” and called its founder a “religious genius.” Duchovny studied under Bloom at Yale, where he earned some of an English PhD. “Everything goes back to Bloom,” he says. “And you never really leave grad school. I’m not sure I’ve left grad school. They might still be waiting for my dissertation.”

But Duchovny did leave grad school. He signed with a talent agent one summer to try to earn some money acting in commercials. His agent told him that if he wanted to go out for theater or film roles, he’d have to get into an acting class. “I said: I’m not doing anything. When I stepped into acting class, something happened. I wasn’t a demonstrative person—I was an intellectual person. So it was like: Yeah, be unreasonable. Be irrational. It opened up a different world, a world of fiction, a world without consequences. I’m doing a scene, and I’m yelling at this person and I’m going to murder them, but I don’t have to go to jail.”

For someone with half a dozen good books and an enormous public profile, it’s surprising there haven’t been more reviews. Johnny Temple, who published Duchovny’s two most recent books on Akashic, tells me, “It’s certainly frustrating that there hasn't been more review coverage of David’s books. For any well-known actor, musician, or other type of public figure, there’s always going to be obstacles to being taken seriously in a different medium.” Kirn tells me, “That makes writing fiction a much purer achievement in my mind. You’re doing this because you love it, and you know that two thirds of your fans will only remember you as a TV character. It’s a brilliant, Sisyphean task. Also, he’s a superb writer.”

I ask Duchovny whether he still thinks about being the best. “I think now I can acknowledge that it’s a hollow designation,” he says. “Especially in the arts. Even though we give awards, which is silly. Holy Cow made the Times bestseller list. Ever since, everything I write sells less and less.”

“It’s hard for someone to champion it,” he adds. “If I wrote a memoir, I’m sure it would get reviewed in the Times.”

Talking to Duchovny, one is reminded that wanting to be taken seriously and being in on the joke aren’t mutually exclusive. As band practice winds down in Brooklyn, the guys are excited to cover Lou Reed’s “Perfect Day.” Duchovny crosses his arms in front of his lap like a schoolboy as he sings. To my ear it sounds just fine, but Lee, the keyboardist, asks the mixer to lower the reverb on David’s voice.

“Maybe lower David’s mic in general?” the bassist, Mitchell Stewart asks.

“Lower than zero,” Duchovny says. “Less than zero.”

A few days later, he texts me. He just screened an early cut of Soapbox, a Hollywood satire he wrote and stars in opposite Laverne Cox. At first, he’s bummed that the test audience has decided that his character shouldn’t get killed in the final moments of the movie. But a couple hours later, he writes me again: “People don’t want me to die. I guess I should be flattered.”

#6692. Explore the year 1 final projects created by our 2025/26 CondéFuture students

In October 2025, 12 students joined the CondéFuture programme where they gained an exclusive insight into the media industry from Condé Nast professionals who then, through various workshops, encouraged them to explore their passions in photography, video, social media, fashion, digital design, and more. This cohort of CondéFuture students split into three teams, each one building a full magazine issue the way a real editorial team would. Each team picked one or more Condé Nast titles to design an issue around. They developed a theme, then tackled every part of getting an issue out into the world — from finalising layouts, reporting, conducting photo shoots, building a social strategy, to creating both short and long-form videos.

After months of ideating, designing, shooting, and writing content, then weeks spent rehearsing their presentations, the three teams were ready for the showcase. It opened with a student Q&A before each team walked the audience through their magazine, cover to cover, explaining specific choices along the way. Let’s take a look at what they created!

The Allure x Wired team, consisting of Creative Director Ava Gholson, Design Director Amalia Pena, Features Editor Camilla Spillmann and Digital Director Ian Kim, took on one of the more unresolved questions in beauty media right now: what happens to beauty standards when the images shaping them are increasingly AI-generated? The cover carried that concept through the visual of a model's face broken into panels with dotted facial-recognition-style scan lines laid over a beauty shot. The cover story, "We Can't Take Our Eyes Off Iyan Moon Yang," profiled a model through that same lens of tech, beauty, and representation, written by Camilla.

The team chose this theme to highlight a new wave of white supremacy ideology embedded into AI algorithms. Databases are fed the idea that beauty standards should align with white, Eurocentric features, thus perpetuating a harmful cycle in both the beauty industry and the social fabric of America. The Allure x Wired team “find it important to shine a light on this issue, as Gen Z and Gen Alpha have unprecedented access to technology and can be easily influenced. [They are] sometimes made to feel insecure by a system designed to manipulate how they see themselves without even knowing it”.

Inside, the issue is the "Sea to Skin" advertisement, a fictional sustainable skincare brand created by the students, as well as "Is It AI?”, a quiz-style spread testing whether a reader can tell AI-generated beauty content from human-made. "Authenticity in the Age of AI," also by Camilla, was a reported piece on AI beauty influencers.

"I Like Girls With Fair Skin", written by Ava, took on colorism and Eurocentric beauty standards directly. When describing her reason for writing this piece, Ava described the article as her “experience with colorism within society”, “this essay argues that Eurocentric beauty standards are a legacy of colonialism and capitalism, designed to enforce oppression and homogeneity. It calls for a critical examination of these standards and their impact on self-perception, culture, and society”.

On this same theme, they created a video that took the form of a Wired-style autocomplete piece, with young people responding on camera to search-bar prompts about modern beauty standards and AI's impact on creativity and trends.

"Our team decided on combining the two magazines because we liked the idea of "traveling through Bon Appétit" and exploring different cultures in NYC through food, especially immigrant-owned businesses” explained Jerniya Jones, Digital Director of this project. Jerniya, along with teammates Elaina Klein, Design Director, Kevin Lin, Creative Director and Alice Popovych, Features Editor, “wanted to show that New York City has more to offer than just the touristy side of Manhattan."

The cover story, "Traveling Through the Boroughs," explored the city's ethnic communities through food, profiling spots like Veselka, 5 Boro Cafe, New Asha Sri Lankan Restaurant, and Fish 'N' Ting. Two articles ran alongside it: "Locals Know Best," highlighting fifteen spots recommended by actual New Yorkers, and "Affordable + Healthy," promoting ten specific healthy restaurants that don't cost a fortune, including Happy Zoe Vegan Bakery in Greenpoint and Motley Kitchen in the South Bronx.

"The City of Art and Culture" paired an interview with two working PhotoVogue photographers, Chiemeka Offor and Andrew Kung, on how New York City shapes their work and their sense of identity and place.

"A Local's Tale", written by Alice Popovych, profiled Tai Garcia, Community Program Manager at CondéFuture. It followed her into the penthouse of the Brooklyn Museum of Art's director, whose walls happened to be covered in work by the artist Kehinde Wiley, who she unexpectedly got to meet in person! "Turns out that we walked into the home of the man that runs the entire Brooklyn Museum of Art," Garcia said. "There was the most beautiful artwork, paintings, sculptures, all on his walls, and you could get so close to them, closer than you could get in a regular museum."

Other spreads included "A Day in the Life," a Polaroid-style photo collage of what the students describe as the real New York experience, and "Afterschool Activities," a guide to where city kids actually go to eat or hang out after 9th period (though for this cohort, that's sometimes the Condé Nast office at the World Trade Center). One spread was a parody ad, a riff on the city's old Dunkin' campaign reading "NYC Runs on Dunkin'." Their video was an interview with the owner of one of the city's legendary frozen dessert stands — Delicioso Coco Helado — who told the story of how her father got the idea after seeing similar stands in Puerto Rico, and how they've since become a quintessential piece of New York City childhood, bringing people together across different neighborhoods.

Dawn, the senior copy editor who worked with several teams on their drafts, had high praise for this project. "I'm a lifelong New Yorker, and one of the pieces I loved so much was a story about getting to know New York, all the different boroughs, through food and the authenticity of food as culture. Not only did I get a list of restaurants to check out, I felt like the flavor of that story jumped off the page. They were teaching me about a city I've loved for decades." She'd read it as an early draft and saw it through many edits. "It started strong and ended stronger," she said, pointing to how the team tied in Veselka and the way that community has rallied around the restaurant since Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

Creative Director Olivia DiGennaro, Digital Director Ryan Martinez, Design Director Jasmeryn Reynoso and Features Editor Sydney Liu built this special edition around the theme "Everlasting, Evergreen." Their own mission statement opened the issue: Vanity Fair has covered culture, fashion, and current affairs since 1913, and the team wanted to explore how style today continually draws on and reimagines the eras before it, while pushing back on the idea that only certain kinds of faces belong in a magazine.

Ryan explains the group’s interest in this particular theme: “late 1900s Hollywood celebrity culture has left us with a cycle that is visible and present in today's youth in the form of their interests, inspirations, and most importantly, styles. Our Vanity Fair special edition covers exactly how this evolution takes shape, noticeably in our present society. Just like the brand's heritage, it explores the shift in culture, fashion, and current affairs within our generations (and especially Gen Z) in the past few decades”.

Beyond this, the issue included a story on how modern pop stars like Sabrina Carpenter and Olivia Dean have drawn on old Hollywood fashion and style ("The Golden Age: Luxurious, Tragic, Longing, the New Sound of Old Hollywood"). The cover story itself interviewed seven NYC teens about how they see their own fashion choices in relation to the eras before them, drawing a line between 20th-century style and how their generation reinterprets it now. The piece was careful to note the difference between influence and imitation: their inspirations, while important, stay that way – just inspirations, not guidelines. The issue closed with a spotlight on Alexandra Dautel, a Paris-based photographer whose work the team said shaped their own photo direction.

The students’ work over year 1 culminated in an end of year showcase. Their work was presented in a gallery format, with their covers and spreads laid out for guests to browse through. Amongst these guests were alumni from CondéFuture's earlier cohorts who came back to see what the new group had accomplished.

Students were also able to present their work to the guests, talking them through their journey. Walter Doyle, Senior Education Manager, explained that “the CondéFuture showcase highlights all that the students have absorbed in such a short time. The presentations were incredible, with each capturing the spirit of the brand they were representing”.

As students head into their second year, they are faced with a different kind of project ahead of them: rather than working in teams, each will be paired one-to-one with a mentor for an individual capstone project, applying what this year taught them about how a media career actually works.

#6690. Robert Pattinson Might Be the Most Fashion-Forward Bond Yet

From Sean Connery’s immaculately tailored suits in Dr. No to Daniel Craig’s thigh-bearing trunks in Casino Royale, each man who has played James Bond has brought a new aesthetic sensibility to the role. For Connery, this meant soft-shouldered Savile Row tailoring, polo shirts, and knit ties to suit the era of Ivy Style, while Roger Moore’s wardrobe of safari jackets and nylon ski suits embodied the sporty hedonism of the 1970s. In the 21st century, Daniel Craig’s Bond was built around a timely blend of Brioni, Tom Ford, and stalwart British brands that complemented the contemporary #menswear scene. Today’s news that Robert Pattinson—a longtime Dior ambassador and one of the most consistently thrilling dressers in Hollywood—has been cast as 007 suggests Bond’s most fashionable era may be yet to come.

Daniel Craig is no slouch in the clothing department, but before donning the tux for Casino Royale, he was primarily known as a stage actor with a penchant for distressed jeans and Chuck Taylor high-tops. Pattinson, meanwhile, has been the face of Dior’s menswear for a decade, during which he’s established his impeccable taste and a willingness to take big swings with his outfits—not to mention a reputation for wearing the absolute heck out of a gray suit. Now, with fellow Brit Jonathan Anderson (who cast Craig in Loewe’s quirked-up fall 2024 campaign and posted this heartwarming pic today) running the show at Dior, the stage is set for a Bond with a taste for capital-F fashion.

Tradition dictates a vibe shift whenever a new Bond is chosen, but whatever James Bond wears has an outsized impact on menswear. Pierce Brosnan’s era had structured Brioni suits and made the Omega Seamaster a star, while Daniel Craig helped cement Tom Ford’s tailoring as a red-carpet staple and juiced sales of N.Peal ribbed Army sweaters and Drake’s suede chukkas. As GQ’s Cam Wolf noted in a 2018 article about Skyfall, Daniel Craig’s Barbour jacket, sweater, jeans, and brogue boots from that film—a classic but fairly unremarkable outfit—became the aspirational template for untold numbers of men on r/malefashionadvice. A few years later, when Craig wore a Rag & Bone slim-fit henley in No Time to Die, the brand sold out of the unassuming undershirt in a matter of days.

It’s been five years since No Time to Die’s release, and it will likely be at least a couple more before Pattinson’s first outing as 007 hits screens. That’s a long wait to see how the next Bond era aesthetic comes together, but given Pattinson’s distinctive approach to fashion, it should be well worth it for the clothes alone.

Marvel has filled most of the seats for its new X-Men film. Sadie Sink is Jean Grey, Kit Connor is Cyclops, Christopher Abbott is Professor X, Samara Weaving is Emma Frost, Inde Navarrette is Rogue, and Maya Boyd is Storm. But there’s still one grizzly gap in the line-up: Wolverine.

Earlier this month, Jeremy Allen White was linked with the role after insider Jeff Sneider reported that he had met with Marvel about a small part that could become much bigger later on. Nobody has confirmed that the part is Wolverine (and Sneider has since stressed that White isn’t officially in talks) but the internet did the math pretty quickly. And now there’s a smoking gun: facial hair.

While walking around the Studio City Farmers Market over the weekend (because, of course), The Social Reckoning star was spotted carrying a bouquet of flowers bigger than his torso and wearing some extremely Wolverine-y mutton chops. Normally, growing out your sideburns wouldn’t count as casting news. But when you’ve just been linked with Logan and suddenly look ready to join the X-Men, people are going to ask questions.

White would make a lot of sense. He’s 5’7”, which puts him much closer to the comic book Wolverine’s famously stocky 5’3” frame than Hugh Jackman ever was. He also spent months getting absolutely massive for The Iron Claw, so the muscle is already there. And after years of watching him play Carmy in The Bear, we know he can do angry and exhausted and permanently one minor inconvenience away from losing it. That’s basically three quarters of the Wolverine job description.

Jackman has owned the role since the first X-Men film landed in 2000. He’s played Wolverine across 10 movies, most recently returning for 2024’s Deadpool & Wolverine. His version became so definitive that it’s difficult to picture anyone else with the claws (other than the time Troye Sivan briefly had them in 2009’s X-Men Origins: Wolverine), even though the 6’2" actor looked very different from the shorter character drawn in the OG comics.

Maybe White just fancied some giant sideburns. Maybe the flowers are covering three adamantium claws. Either way, Marvel should probably give him a call—assuming it hasn’t already.

#6684. Why Everything New Looks a Little Vintage Right Now

Designers are adding depth to their ensembles by mixing and matching eras with irreverence

Backstage at the Spring 2027 Chanel show in Paris, after a parade of elegantly skirt-suited women strolled beneath an extravagant set of birds suspended midflight, Matthieu Blazy told a story of picking his teenage nephew up from school. Observing the students, he was struck by the irreverent way they dressed. “They wear a lot of vintage. They are not dictated by a decade—they are a lot more free,” he told Bazaar. “They wear something from the ’30s, ’50s, ’70s. I wanted to expand on that.”

One look in particular felt more akin to how someone would dress to attend the Chanel show rather than to walk it—an old-school Chanel jacket worn with new Chanel shoes, a pair of black trousers, eclectic jewelry and an old belt. It wasn’t an anomalous look; the vintagey vibes loomed large. Knee-length skirt suits were styled with heaps of necklaces. Men’s shirting was mixed with relaxed tailoring and leather separates; tiny white tank tops peeked from beneath tweed jackets festooned with oversized, floral brooches.

Loving and collecting vintage (or better yet, holding onto pieces until they became vintage) was once the domain of fashion insiders. But today, young people are growing up native to the secondhand market. (According to ThredUp’s 2026 Resale Report, 62 percent of Gen Z shopped secondhand last year.) As they age, dressing from a closet that contains clothing from multiple style eras has become inevitable. And designers are taking notice.

Just as the Dolce & Gabbana show was about to start in Milan a week before the Chanel show, the loudspeaker turned on to regale the audience on “the wardrobes of Sicily’s grand houses. Clothes once worn by great-grandmothers, grandmothers, mothers, aunts and daughters. A slip dress is worn over a jacket, antique lace meets contemporary pieces, lingerie and eveningwear coexist, and the precious and the everyday merge in an unexpected balance.” The styling made it feel as if a young woman pilfered grandma’s closet, mixing an antique, pussy bow blouse with embellished and ripped jeans or pairing a D&G baby tee with a leopard-trimmed, tweedy jacket.

At Gucci, Demna dissected the archetypes of the bourgeoisie, including “the rebellious aristocrat.” A series of looks paired variations of rugby shirts, pleated tartan skirts, puff-shaped bomber jackets with oversized belts adorned with horsebits and heaps of jewelry piled onto necklines. It’s what a “blue-blooded child of an aristocrat might wear to the private school that she hates,” Demna mused after the show. Within that layered ensemble, he defined a character: Her kilt is part of her school uniform; her rugby polo and leather jacket were mined from a thrift store or her dad’s closet. She wore all these pieces together with no regard for where or what era they came from.

The idea of dressing “vintage” on a runway is inherently contradictory. The runways are a place of new; vintage is, by definition, old. But the concept is more about adding depth and texture to an ensemble than it is about the age of the garment itself. It’s not about, as in seasons past, garments that are distressed to look worn and weathered. It’s about achieving a kind of idiosyncrasy in a landscape that had become samey and polished and “quiet luxury.” It’s about a desire for irreverence.

The Row is a spectacular case study here, particularly as it was one of the brands that ushered in the minimalist look of the early 2020s. So how to evolve without alienating your customer? For Spring 2027, the Olsen twins draped and knotted antique linens, lace, and doilies over their typical rotation of sleek, black trousers and perfectly mussed trench coats. Models wore layers of dainty beads or single chunky necklaces that nodded subtly towards eclecticism or bohemian.

Fashion must contend and engage with vintage; increasingly, it is just a part of how people shop. As the secondhand market gains traction, it presents new challenges; houses are in constant competition with their own archives. Just look at the resurgences of secondhand Pucci and Etro from the early 2000s. Many have embraced reissues: Chloé’s Maxime wedge or the McQueen skull scarf, for example, shown tucked into contemporary collections of recent years. Of course, creative directors at legacy houses have always had to find ways to be in conversation with their archives and predecessors. The greatest designers, however, manage to use this formula to their advantage.

Take Blazy at Chanel, for instance. He must contend with Gabrielle “Coco” Chanel’s founding legacy of the early and mid-1900s in addition to Karl Lagerfeld’s from the ’80s through the 2010s. The idea of a knee-length skirt suit in nubby fabric could seem retro, but Blazy leaned into it instead of pushing against it. He didn’t rewrite the idea entirely, but shifted our perception with subtle tweaks in materials, textures, and styling. He even sent Gabrielle’s original 2.55 bag down the runway, paired with a gauzy white cocktail dress and then again later with a black skirt suit.

Ralph Lauren mined his own greatest hits for a spring collection that was a glorious mishmash of old and new, clashing Americana Westernwear and prep with tropes of the English aristocracy, and even utilitarian workwear. He strung models’ waistcoats with pocket watches, paired brocade evening jackets with distressed denim, and matched ruffled-collar blouses with metallic skirts.

It’s that dialogue between items that conjures the feel of someone who wears vintage, someone who curates their closet with stylistic depth, nuance, and contrast. What young people achieve with aplomb is decidedly difficult to manufacture. But that’s what makes it so desirable. It turns runway models from mannequins into characters and makes you want to learn their stories.

#6683. Applications for the 2027 LVMH Prize Are Now Open

Each year in Paris, promising young designers present their work to industry legends, hoping to distinguish themselves as part of fashion’s rising new guard—and to secure a cash prize of €400,000. Today, applications for the 14th edition of the LVMH Prize are now open.

Over the length of the Prize, the event has served as an invaluable launchpad for independent designers, including two former contestants who are both set to make historic debuts. Grace Wales Bonner (winner, 2016) will present her first collection for Hermès men’s in January, 2027, and just last week, Martine Rose (semifinalist, 2017) was confirmed for the top job at Balenciaga following Pierpaolo Piccioli’s departure. Meanwhile, this year’s Karl Lagerfeld prize winner, Zane Li of Lii, also snagged the top prize at the 2026 CFDA/Vogue Fashion Fund.

Jury members, who this year included newbies Michael Rider of Celine and Louis Vuitton CEO Pietro Beccari, are interested in fostering designers with promising businesses. “The jury this time around was very focused on where people produce, where they distribute, and who the final client is,” said Delphine Arnault in an interview following Julie Kegel’s 2026 win. “They were interested in designers who [could talk about] who their [customers] are.”

Designers can submit their application on lvmhprize.com from now through April 4, 2027. Winners of the Karl Lagerfeld Prize and Savoir-Faire Prize, will each take home €200,000, while the three winners of the LVMH Prize for Young Graduates will join the creative studios of the Group’s Houses on one-year contracts. Both the graduate winners and their schools will also receive a €10,000 allocation. Applicants must be between the ages of 18-40 and have created at least two ready-to-wear collections. The semifinals will take place in Paris on March 3 and 4, 2027.

#6682. 3 Ways To Defrost Chicken Without Spreading Salmonella, According To An Expert

Your dinner plans aren't ruined just yet.

Forgetting to take chicken out of the freezer is an all-too-common occurrence that can bring your dinner plans to a screeching halt. To get things back on track, your gut instinct may be to thaw it as quickly as possible. But there are more important things to worry about than a delayed dinner.

Raw poultry can carry Salmonella, so how you handle it matters. Nothing is less appetizing than giving your whole family a foodborne illness.

But before you give up and order takeout, we’re here to help. We chatted with Ellen Steinberg, PhD, RD, LD, and food safety specialist, to find the best (and safest) methods to thaw chicken. Whether you plan ahead or need to defrost it fast, here’s what you should do.

Defrosting chicken isn’t as simple as taking it out of the freezer. Salmonella is real, y’all—according to FoodSafety.gov, roughly 4% of chicken packages at American grocery stores are contaminated with the bacteria. That bacteria can multiply rapidly in the temperature danger zone, between 40°F and 140°F. Translation: Leaving your chicken out on the counter can actually make you sick.

To prevent that, choose the right method and protect the surrounding environment from cross-contamination. Even with supposedly airtight packaging, the plastic may have holes, or chicken juice may transfer from other packages at the grocery store. It’s especially difficult to spot when the meat is frozen, so Steinberg says it’s better to be safe than sorry.

“You should put your [raw] chicken in a roasting pan or a baking sheet so the juices won’t spread,” she says. Everything that touches raw chicken should be thoroughly cleaned with hot, soapy water. If you want to take food safety even further, Steinberg suggests keeping a separate cutting board in a different color that you use exclusively for raw meat. And above all else: Wash your hands!

If you’re not in a rush, thawing chicken in the fridge yields the most consistent results. Because refrigerators should stay at 40°F and below, frozen chicken can gradually defrost without entering the temperature danger zone where bacteria multiply more rapidly.

Because of this, Steinberg says it’s the only USDA-approved thawing method that lets you refreeze raw chicken without cooking it first. “If you end up deciding that you don’t want to cook the chicken or you only want to use half of it, you can place it back in the freezer,” she says. There is a caveat, however: Once your chicken has fully thawed, you should either cook or refreeze it within one to two days.

If you opt for the refrigerator method, keep these safety measures in mind. Beyond keeping your meat contained on a plate or tray, place it on the bottom shelf. If juice drips, it’ll contaminate the fewest ingredients. Steinberg also suggests storing the chicken toward the back of your refrigerator. “The temperature is more consistent, unlike the areas closest to the door,” she says.

If you need to defrost chicken fast, one of the best ways is with cool, running water. Unlike fridge air, water conducts heat much more effectively. Keeping the water moving also helps maintain consistent thawing conditions. But you don't necessarily need to leave the faucet running: The USDA also recommends submerging chicken in cold water and changing it every 30 minutes.

So if cold water thaws meat quickly, would hot water do the job even faster? It might, but the potential food safety risks aren't worth it. "If you thaw chicken under warm or hot water, the outside of the meat can enter the temperature danger zone while the center is still frozen,” Steinberg says.

For the running-water method, place the chicken in leak-proof packaging in a bowl and run cool water (70°F or lower) over it. Thawing times depend on the size and thickness of the meat, but smaller packages may be ready in an hour or less. Once thawed, cook the chicken immediately before considering refreezing it.

The final USDA-approved method involves using your microwave’s defrost setting. While it’s certainly faster than letting meat thaw in the fridge, we suggest relying on this method only if you have no other option.

Steinberg says this technique leaves the least wiggle room for planning your dinner. “You have to cook it immediately,” she says. “You can’t defrost it and then decide to cook two hours later.”

The need to cook immediately is certainly one downside of the microwave method. However, another compelling argument against using the defrost setting is that it can make your chicken taste worse.

Microwaves heat food unevenly, especially with thicker pieces of meat. Some areas can start warming up or even cooking before the center fully thaws. It's not a big deal when reheating leftovers, but it can nearly ruin frozen proteins.

By the time the center is fully defrosted, the outer edges may already be partially cooked. Can you imagine chicken that tastes worse than unseasoned microwaved chicken? We can't.

It’s a safe and fast defrosting method when followed by immediate cooking—but at what cost? So we'd only vouch for this technique if your chicken will end up shredded or submerged in enough sauce to mask the texture.

#6681. 40 More Million-Dollar Watches Just Sold at Auction

This is an edition of the newsletter Box + Papers, Cam Wolf’s weekly deep dive into the world of watches. Sign up here.

Back in June, I reported on the bonanza of watches crossing the million-dollar-plus mark at auction. What once felt like a unicorn price for watchmakers, auction houses, and the industry as a whole no longer feels so magical. “I joke with people that $1 million is like the new $250,000 of five years ago,” Paul Boutros of Phillips auction house said over the summer.

In just the first half of 2026, the number of million-dollar watches sold nearly eclipsed the total from all of 2025. Now, after a raft of high-profile auctions in Geneva a couple of weeks ago, the industry has set yet another record. In just the last month alone (including Monaco Legend Group, which kicked things off in late October), 40 million-dollar watches hammered, according to numbers provided by EveryWatch. That’s more sold than in any entire year before 2020.

If you’re keeping score at home, we’ve seen 133 watches sell at or above seven figures this year. And we’ve still got plenty of year left.

The question is: How much steam does the auction world have left? And what’s driving this radical spike in big-ticket timepieces?

A $10 million Patek Philippe Perpetual Calendar Chronograph ref. 2499

Mike Nouveau, WatchTok King and dealer, has told me that if more kids knew how much growth potential there is in the vintage market, they’d put down the creator-style tiny microphones and start studying reference numbers. The vintage market spiked in the middle of the pandemic, when prices on sport watch grails like the Patek Philippe Nautilus and Rolex Daytona went crypto-mode as a new wave of speculators flooded the high-end collecting scene.

But while the steel sport watch craze has cooled—or at least leveled off—the market has continued riding a remarkably durable wave, helped in part by the arrival of a previously quiet category: the insiders-only independent brands. “For many years at auction, we always said, ‘You have Patek Philippe and Rolex. What’s the third brand that can compete?’” Alexandre Ghotbi, a deputy chairman at Phillips auction house, told me in 2024 for a story on the beloved watchmaker Rexhep Rexhepi. “Today’s third brand is not a brand—it’s a genre: independent artisanal watchmakers.”

Think F.P. Journe, Berneron, Phillipe Dufour, Rexhepi’s Atelier Akrivia—companies helmed by watchmaking auteurs turning out hyper-limited runs, most of which sell out long before a perfectly-lit product photo ever hits the web. Oftentimes, the only way to get your hands on one of their wares—if you haven’t yet achieved friend-of-the-brand status—is by raising a paddle at auction.

When I asked dealer Eric Wind if he thought the indie insanity would remain strong, he was unequivocal: “At the top end, yes.” The dealer Zoe Abelson, of Graal Watches, actually believes we haven’t reached the peak yet. “I do think there's still room for the pieces that are actually rare to continue to grow in value with a continuance in new interest in collecting watches and the yearning to build the most impressive collection,” she said.

Two weekends ago, a new independent brand joined the list of million-dollar watchmakers. Sylvain Pinaud cut his teeth restoring antique watches and established his eponymous brand in 2018. He’s known for showing his work—the instrumental components of his watches are often highlighted on the dial. A unique version of his Origine, a model that only launched in 2022, sold for 1,011,200 Swiss francs (roughly $1,211,500).

Pinaud’s success is indicative of what happens to the elite independent brands that hit the big time. Compared to many of the heavyweight Swiss makers working at scale, independent watchmakers are seen as artisans who hand-produce their designs in extremely limited quantities. It’s why a watchmaker like Kari Voutilainen, considered a master of his craft, has sold more million-dollar pieces this year than many of the big fellas getting rap lyric shoutouts. “There's a growing appreciation for what these watchmakers are producing,” said Ben Horesh, EveryWatch’s CEO. “It’s great to see more independents challenging the old guard."

Look at that list above. Voutilainen ranks just after Rolex and Patek Philippe but ahead of Cartier for the most million-dollar watches sold at auction in 2026. The list is heavy on independents, including Rexhepi’s Akrivia, George Daniels, Philippe Dufour, and Vianney Halter. The real headline, though, is seeing F.P. Journe—the godfather of the indie scene—at the very top. If one area of the market doesn’t feel entirely sustainable, it’s the inferno around FPJ’s pieces. For deep-pocketed newcomers to the “hobby” of catching big-ticket whales, the Geneva-based maker has come to represent the grailiest of grails. Nearly every Journe piece that comes to auction sells for multiples of its estimate. And I mean everything: an empty watch box made for a set of FPJs sold for $230,000 at Christie’s! “The less rare—or in Journe's case, current production—pieces that get swept up in the overall market growth will slow down soon,” Abelson said. “I don't think it's sustainable; at a certain point the values will price out enough people that there should be a correction.”

A $13 million F.P. Journe Chronomètre à Résonance "Régence”

If six-figure watches were once rare, 10-million-plus pieces were true spectacles. Between 2020 and 2023, not a single watch crossed that threshold. In the last decade, from 2015 to 2025, there were just seven 10-million watches total. But with some time still on the clock, seven watches have already topped that threshold in 2026. A solid chunk of that is thanks to the wild one-of-one Daytonas that Rolex made for a charity auction—three out of the four sold for seven figures—but it’s still an astounding feat. The rest of the list is filled out by:

These days, it’s hard to find a category of watches that isn’t doing well at auction. Cartier hasn’t fallen off—in fact, the brand keeps setting records: a very cool clock known as Portico No. 4 hammered for approximately $5,768,400 at Phillips the weekend before last, becoming the most expensive Cartier ever sold in the process. Breguet is, rightfully and finally, on the rise. And after relaunching just last summer, Urban Jürgensen’s vintage pieces are hotter than ever. A super sexy pink-gold version of the brand’s Reference 2 went for 358,400 Swiss francs (about $430,000) at Sotheby’s.

To put a fine point on all this, just look at how overall sales are soaring. Last year, Phillips set the record with $83,018,538 worth of timepieces sold in a single auction. It only took 12 months to shatter that number. This month saw Phillips reset the record with a $112.3 million auction. I would say 2026 is an inflection point for the industry…if I didn’t anticipate that we’ll be back here talking about even more record-setting sales every year for the foreseeable future.

#6679. This Buzzy New Wellness Retreat in Kerala Blends Ancient Traditions With Modern Medicine

As the birthplace of yoga and its sister science Ayurveda, India certainly has no shortage of wellness retreats. The country is quite literally filled with spiritual centers, located everywhere from the foothills of the Himalayas to the beaches of Goa to the sacred riverbanks of Varanasi. I’ve been fortunate enough to visit a fair amount of them over the past decade, thanks to both my work as the author of Destination Wellness, an exploration of ancient health traditions around the world, and the fact that my husband is a born-and-raised Delhiite. We live in New York, but go to India regularly to stay with family and travel around the rest of the country together.

That’s why I was immediately intrigued when I heard about Tulåh Clinical Wellness, a longevity-focused wellness center in Kerala that opened earlier this year and blends ancient Ayurveda with more modern diagnostic testing. While some wellness retreats in India are already known for their mix of global healing traditions (Six Senses Vana and Ananda in the Himalayas come to mind), Tulåh’s blend sounded new to me, closer to a clinical European med spa—albeit one steeped in traditional medicine. Its location stood out to me, too, given Kerala’s long history as the epicenter of Ayurveda in India. I’ve done two very traditional Ayurvedic retreats in Kerala myself, so as I read Tulåh’s extensive list of modern medical offerings—from MRIs to mammograms—I became increasingly curious about its approach. How would all that new testing and technology fit into the longstanding wellness scene in Kerala? And what would that mean for India at large?

To find out, I booked a weeklong program at Tulåh in early September, right at the tail end of monsoon season (actually considered one of the best times for Ayurvedic treatments in Kerala). It was drizzling when I got off the plane in the coastal city of Calicut, but by the time I arrived at the property half an hour later, the rain had stopped and the air smelled fresh—and not just because of the post-shower skies. Tulåh is set on 30 acres of rewilded forest and medicinal gardens in the Western Ghats, a lush mountain range whose abundance of healing herbs and plants perfumes its air with a consistently earthy scent.

My stay began with a watermelon elixir welcome drink and a tour of the property, which felt even more global than I expected—almost like an international wellness campus with a serious Indian pedigree. That’s partly because “the sanctuary,” as the staffers lovingly call it, is modeled after Auroville, an experimental, spiritually-minded community just north of Pondicherry in Tamil Nadu. Auroville brings people from different countries and cultures together with the goal of living in harmony, and Tulåh—which means “balance” in Sanskrit—has that same world-blending vibe. Designed by Dubai-based firm Lami Architects, the 65-suite property is built on the site of a former cotton mill and looks strikingly modern from the outside, with sleek, flowing curves inspired by the legendary Zaha Hadid. Yet inside its nine main buildings, the minimalist interiors focus largely on Indian craftsmanship, featuring smooth terrazzo floors sourced from artisans in Rajasthan, handwoven earth-toned rugs and marble from Uttar Pradesh, and plush furniture from a design studio in Kerala. Strolling around the grounds after my initial tour, I even heard the upbeat “Qui Es-Tu?” from the French electro-pop duo Poom playing on speakers placed throughout the tropical gardens, followed by a bamboo flutist performing peaceful South Indian Carnatic meditations in the lobby just a few minutes later.

This deliberate mix of influences is the brainchild of founder Faizal Kottikollon, an entrepreneur, engineer, and philanthropist who was born in Kerala, studied in the US, and later settled in Dubai. “Yoga and Ayurveda are India’s IP, but Ayurveda often gets siloed,” he told me one afternoon over a cup of herbal tea. “It gets marketed as an alternative therapy in the medical world, when it should be in the mainstream alongside other modern practices.”

He, of all people, would know. Back in 2022, Kottikollon was diagnosed with spinal cord compression, and his doctors recommended a very risky spinal surgery. He didn’t want to do that, so he turned instead to the traditional Ayurvedic practices he’d grown up around in Kerala. Ayurvedic practitioner Dr. Vishnuraj Prakash, whom Kottikollon later hired as the first doctor at Tulåh, suggested he do a 21-day panchakarma treatment along with mamsa kizhi massages with warm cloth bundles of goat meat, milk, rice, and various herbs. In Ayurveda, goat meat is thought to strengthen muscle tissues—and by all accounts it did. Kottikollon’s next MRI showed that his compression was healed. Today, he says he is 99% recovered.

“When we did the MRI after my panchakarma, my modern medicine doctors had to believe in Ayurveda, because the proof was right there,” he told me. “And that’s when I said, ‘Oh my god, this is the future of healthcare.’ Ayurveda had the solution to my problem for thousands of years, but my modern doctors never knew. That’s why it should be integrated with modern medicine rather than working on its own. People don’t talk to each other, because human beings are blocked by egos—but all doctors need to work together. And that’s what I’m trying to change.”

His plan (and his $100 million investment) seems to be working. At Tulåh, my days were filled with a true mix of traditional Ayurvedic practices and modern longevity diagnostics. It all started, as these sorts of retreats so often do, well before my stay, when I sent in various samples for the medical team to assess just a few months after their February opening. Then I went straight into two full days of diagnostic tests and consultations the day after I arrived. A nurse took my blood sample on my first morning, followed by a BCA (body composition analysis) and an Ayurvedic consultation with my designated practitioner, Dr. Urvashi Naithani. She read my pulse, asked some lifestyle questions, and ultimately identified a kapha imbalance in my system that was making me sluggish. In Ayurveda, everyone has a unique constitution shaped by three doshas: vata (air and space), pitta (fire and water), and kapha (earth and water). The goal in life is to keep all three doshas in balance at all times, though as I can attest, that’s very hard to do.

A shirodhara treatment on a Vichy Shower Bed.

My program continued with a couple of kapha-reducing Ayurvedic treatments interspersed with more modern longevity testing. That included a chest X-ray, a CAC scan, a DXA scan, an MRI (quite an accomplishment for a claustrophobe like me), a dental appointment, a psychological assessment, and a slew of mobility and fitness consultations. At times it felt a bit jarring to go from a soothing ancient therapy like shirodhara to a terrifying 45-minute scan in a metal tube, but I always knew it was all in pursuit of self-knowledge—and that made me feel really good. It was almost like being back in school, only the subject was myself.

Everything eventually culminated with the big “MDM meeting,” or the multidisciplinary team meeting, on my third full day. This meeting is essentially Kottikollon’s vision of integration come to life: when representatives from Tulåh’s nine departments (Ayurveda, functional medicine, modern medicine, Chinese medicine, fitness, physiotherapy, psychology, clinical yoga, and dental) convene to discuss your results and put together a custom plan for the rest of your stay and your routine after you leave. Back to the school metaphor, I couldn’t help but think of it as all my teachers from different subjects gossiping about me in the conference room… but with only my very best interests in mind.

If the team had determined I needed serious medical attention, Tulåh has an on-site ICU and operating room, as well as access to a nearby hospital that Kottikollon also owns. But in my case, the consensus across the board was that I simply needed to boost my energy and get much, much stronger. One of the biggest subjects the MDM team discusses is your Tulåh Life Index, a proprietary number they calculate to assess your body’s overall function based on your bloodwork, body composition results, lifestyle questions, and more. My score was 71 out of 100, which was not terrible (70 and above is the goal), but not great either—thanks largely to my lack of muscle mass. In my defense, there was a good reason for that. As I told the doctors during my consultations, I stopped strength training regularly during a five-year period of IVF treatments, when fertility doctors advise against lifting weights because of the risk of ovarian torsion. Though I could’ve done more strength training between IVF rounds, I was still a bit too scared for my ovaries to fully get back into it. Now that I’m finally emerging from the IVF tunnel thanks to turning to surrogacy, the doctors recommended I make regaining my muscle mass a top priority—especially since I’m now 41, when these things begin to matter even more. I knew this already, technically, but hearing it from a team of professionals based on my own numbers made it feel extra real to me—and all the more urgent.

What followed was a few more packed days of treatments and meals customized to my new high-strength, high-energy lifestyle. My meals were delicious—lots of high-protein South Indian fish curries and North Indian specialties like chicken tikka and chana masala, all made with predominantly organic and locally-grown ingredients. And unlike my past Ayurvedic retreats in Kerala, where the plan mostly revolved around oil treatments and yoga, therapies at Tulåh also included aquatic fitness, personal strength training sessions, clinical yoga with a focus on alignment, and daily sound baths in the incredible Sonorium (I fell asleep every time). Throughout it all, the staff was so caring and lovely as well. During a qawwali performance in the Sonorium one night, I even saw a young teacher offer an older Indian uncle a pillow for behind his back without him ever asking.

My Ayurvedic treatments were still my favorite, though. In a plot twist that will undoubtedly delight all Ayurveda lovers, Kottikollon and his team have combined the Vichy shower—named after the thermal spa town of Vichy, France—with a traditional Ayurvedic massage bed to create the recently patented Vichy Shower Bed, which has six showerheads directly above the heated, ergonomically designed table. This means that, rather than shuffling you to the shower after your treatment so you can rinse off all the medicated oil, practitioners do it for you right there on the bed—including a shampoo and condition. In my experience, Ayurvedic oil is often near impossible to get off, so this perk was absolute bliss for me. And it’s one that Kottikollon hopes will make Ayurveda more accessible to the mainstream as well. “Traditional wooden Ayurvedic beds can be slippery and leave you with oil all over, and I believe this is part of the reason why Ayurveda has not been adopted in the current world,” he told me. “But Ayurveda can solve so many problems—which is why I want this bed to be at all the spas and hospitals in the world along with all the other options.”

A treatment room with a Vichy Shower Bed.

I’ll co-sign that. While I wasn’t sure how it would feel to combine Ayurveda with all things modern, I ended up loving the 360-degree approach. Not having to pick a lane (or a century) was so convenient—like one-stop shopping for longevity. If anything, seeing the ancient practices I’ve come to love used as part of a diagnostics-informed treatment plan even helped me appreciate them in a new, deeper way.

I’m also happy to report I’ve followed through on my strength and energy mission, at least somewhat, since I checked out of Tulåh a month ago. As a frequent traveler, it’s hard for me to get into a super steady routine, but I did lift weights at my hotel gym in Japan last week as opposed to just running on the treadmill—and that felt like progress to me. At home in New York, I’ve also been consulting Tulåh’s Home app, which provides personalized recipes, workout plans, yoga poses and meditations based on my medical results. I don’t use it every day (maybe you’ve heard of a little thing called the NYC restaurant scene?), but I’ve made enough of the recipes to tell you they’re easy and good. And the yoga nidra meditation has become my new go-to for getting out of an afternoon slump.

We have a saying in my family of journalists: “Everything’s been said, but not everyone has said it.” And so, in the grand tradition of honoring your roots, allow me to state the obvious: Knowledge really is power. It feels so good to know exactly what I need to do. Now I just need to keep doing it.
